cards.q: What are the three steps of the cycle the CPU repeats?
cards.a:
Fetch, decode, execute

Fetch copies the instruction the program counter points at and moves the counter on, decode works out what the number means, and execute does it. Compiling and linking happen before the program ever runs.
cards.lessonTitle: What Happens When a Program Runs

cards.q: What is the difference between memory and storage?
cards.a:
Memory (RAM) holds the running program and its values and is emptied at power-off; storage keeps files long term

A program file has to be copied from storage into memory before it can run. Slots inside the CPU itself are registers, not memory.
cards.lessonTitle: What Happens When a Program Runs

cards.q: What is a register?
cards.a:
A small, very fast storage slot inside the CPU itself

Arithmetic happens in registers: values are copied in from memory first and copied back afterwards.
cards.lessonTitle: What Happens When a Program Runs

cards.q: Why can a debugger show you every value in a running program?
cards.a:
Because the CPU can be paused between two instructions, when every value is fixed

Paused between two instructions, every register and every memory cell holds a definite number that a tool can read. No log of values is kept.
cards.lessonTitle: What Happens When a Program Runs

cards.q: What does the program counter hold?
cards.a:
The number of the memory cell that holds the next instruction

It is the CPU's bookmark. Fetch reads the cell it names, then moves it on by one.
cards.lessonTitle: What Happens When a Program Runs

cards.q: In the first demonstration, which instruction changed memory?
cards.a:
`STORE 12`

`LOAD` and `ADD` only change register A, inside the CPU. `STORE` is the one that copies a value out into a memory cell.
cards.lessonTitle: What Happens When a Program Runs

cards.q: Cell 5 of a program's memory holds the number 110. What is it?
cards.a:
Either: it depends on how the cell is used

Memory does not label its contents. The same number is an instruction if the program counter reaches it, and plain data if an instruction reads it.
cards.lessonTitle: What Happens When a Program Runs

cards.q: How does this machine repeat a group of instructions?
cards.a:
A jump puts an earlier cell number into the program counter

Loops and decisions are both made from jumps. `JUMP` always changes the program counter; `JUMPZ` changes it only when register A is zero.
cards.lessonTitle: What Happens When a Program Runs

cards.q: Where do the names of your C++ variables go when the program is compiled?
cards.a:
They become memory cell numbers and are gone

Names are for people and for the compiler. A debugger can show them again only because the compiler can write them to a separate symbol file.
cards.lessonTitle: What Happens When a Program Runs

cards.q: How many different values can one byte hold, and why?
cards.a:
256, because each of the eight bits doubles the number of combinations

2 multiplied by itself eight times is 256. Unsigned that is 0 to 255, so 255 is the largest value but not the count of values.

cards.q: Why does one hexadecimal digit correspond to exactly four bits?
cards.a:
Because sixteen is two to the power of four

Four bits form sixteen combinations and hexadecimal has sixteen digits, so each digit matches one combination. A byte is eight bits, which is why it takes two hex digits.

cards.q: How do you negate a number in two's complement?
cards.a:
Flip every bit, then add one

5 is `0000 0101`; flipped it is `1111 1010`; add one and it is `1111 1011`, which is -5. Flipping alone gives -6, and flipping only the top bit does not negate at all.

cards.q: What does "little-endian" mean?
cards.a:
The lowest-value byte of a multi-byte value is stored at the lowest address

The `int` 1000, which is `0x000003E8`, sits in memory as `E8 03 00 00`. Only the order of the bytes changes, not the bits inside them; highest byte first is big-endian.

cards.q: What happens when an unsigned value goes past its largest value?
cards.a:
It wraps round to zero and carries on from there

Nothing reports an error, and nothing clamps the value. For signed types going past the end is undefined behaviour, which is worse.

cards.q: What is `0100 0001` as an unsigned number?
cards.a:
65

The bits that are on are worth 64 and 1. In hexadecimal the same byte is `0x41`, which is where the wrong answer 41 comes from.

cards.q: Why is hexadecimal used instead of decimal when looking at memory?
cards.a:
Each hex digit is exactly four bits, so a byte is two digits

Hexadecimal is only a way of writing numbers. Its advantage is the exact fit: four bits per digit, two digits per byte.

cards.q: A signed byte holds the bits `1111 1111`. What value is that?
cards.a:
-1

In two's complement the top bit is worth -128, and the other seven add up to 127. Read as unsigned, the same bits are 255.

cards.q: An `int` on a PC holds the value `0x0A0B0C0D`. In what order do its bytes sit in memory, from the lowest address up?
cards.a:
`0D 0C 0B 0A`

PCs are little-endian: the lowest byte is stored first. The digits inside each byte are not reversed, only the order of the bytes.

cards.q: A `std::uint8_t` holds 200 and the program adds 100 to it. What does it hold now?
cards.a:
44

300 does not fit in eight bits, so it wraps: 300 - 256 = 44. Unsigned arithmetic always wraps round like this.

cards.q: What is the difference between `p`, `*p` and `&p` for a pointer `p`?
cards.a:
`p` is the address held, `*p` the value at that address, `&p` the address of the pointer itself

A pointer is a variable too, so it lives somewhere and has its own address, `&p`, which is different from the address it holds.

cards.q: Why does adding one to an `int*` move it by four bytes?
cards.a:
Because pointer arithmetic counts in elements, and an `int` is four bytes

The compiler multiplies by the size of the type pointed at, so `p + 1` is the address of the next `int`. A `char*` plus one moves by one byte.

cards.q: What is padding, and why does the compiler add it?
cards.a:
Unused bytes between values or struct members so each value sits at an aligned address

Keeping each value at an address that is a multiple of its size lets the processor read it fastest.

cards.q: Why is dereferencing `nullptr` a crash, and why is that a good thing?
cards.a:
Nothing lives at address 0, so any access is stopped as an access violation and the program fails at the faulty line

Failing immediately at the bad line is far better than silently corrupting memory. There is no compiler-inserted check: the operating system stops the access.

cards.q: Why are memory locations often described as a base plus an offset?
cards.a:
Because absolute addresses change between runs, but the distance from a base to a value does not

Find the base (the start of a struct or loaded program) at run time and add the fixed offset, and you reach the value every time.

cards.q: What is the address of a variable?
cards.a:
The position in memory of its first byte

Memory is a numbered row of bytes. A variable occupies one or more of them, and its address is the number of the first.

cards.q: An `int` is at address `0x1000`. `int* p` points at it. What address is `p + 1`?
cards.a:
`0x1004`

Adding one to a pointer moves it by one element. An `int` is four bytes, so the next `int` starts four bytes further on.

cards.q: After `int score{ 7 }; int* p{ &score }; *p = 20;` what is true?
cards.a:
`score` is now 20

`*p` means "the int that p points at", which is `score` itself. Nothing was copied. `p` still holds the address of `score`.

cards.q: A struct has a `char`, then an `int`, then a `char`. Why is `sizeof` 12 and not 6?
cards.a:
Padding keeps the `int` and the struct size at multiples of 4

The `int` needs to be aligned, so three unused bytes follow the first `char`. Three more follow the last `char` so that the next struct in an array would also be aligned.

cards.q: What happens when a program dereferences a null pointer on Windows?
cards.a:
Windows stops it with an access violation

Nothing is ever placed at address 0, precisely so that this mistake is caught the moment it happens.

cards.q: The same program prints a different address for the same variable each time it runs. Why?
cards.a:
Windows places the program and its stack differently each run

Addresses are assigned at run time and Windows randomises them on purpose. The distances between things inside the program stay the same, which is why locations are described as a base plus an offset.

cards.q: Name the four stages of a build, in order.
cards.a:
Preprocessor, compiler, assembler, linker

The first three run once per `.cpp` file; the linker runs once for the whole program, joining the object files.
cards.lessonTitle: How Source Code Becomes Machine Code

cards.q: Why is each `.cpp` file compiled separately?
cards.a:
So that changing one file only means recompiling that one file

The linker then joins the pieces. A consequence is that one file cannot see another's definitions, only the declarations it includes.
cards.lessonTitle: How Source Code Becomes Machine Code

cards.q: What is the difference between a compiler error and a linker error?
cards.a:
A compiler error means one file is not valid C++; a linker error means the valid pieces do not fit together

A linker error such as LNK2019 means something declared was never defined, or something was defined twice. Both kinds of error happen while building.
cards.lessonTitle: How Source Code Becomes Machine Code

cards.q: What does `.pdb` stand for in Visual Studio, and what is it for?
cards.a:
Program database: the debug symbols linking machine code to source lines and variable names

The debugger needs the `.pdb` to show your own code and variable names instead of raw instructions. Precompiled headers are a different file (`.pch`).
cards.lessonTitle: How Source Code Becomes Machine Code

cards.q: Which stage turns `#include <vector>` into thousands of lines of code?
cards.a:
The preprocessor

The preprocessor handles every `#` line, and `#include` is a straight paste of the file's text.
cards.lessonTitle: How Source Code Becomes Machine Code

cards.q: What does an object file (`.obj`) contain?
cards.a:
One file's machine code, plus the names it defines and needs

Each `.cpp` file becomes one object file. The linker later joins them and fills in the addresses that were missing.
cards.lessonTitle: How Source Code Becomes Machine Code

cards.q: A build fails with `LNK2019: unresolved external symbol`. What is the most likely cause?
cards.a:
A function is declared and called but never defined

Linker errors appear after compiling has succeeded. Something is used but never defined in anything the linker was given.
cards.lessonTitle: How Source Code Becomes Machine Code

cards.q: In the assembler output above, why does the byte `32` appear in the encoding of `lea eax, [rcx+50]`?
cards.a:
50 in decimal is `0x32` in hexadecimal

Numbers inside instructions are stored as bytes like everything else. Fifty is three sixteens and two, which is `0x32`.
cards.lessonTitle: How Source Code Becomes Machine Code

cards.q: What is a stack frame?
cards.a:
The block of stack memory for one call of a function: return address, locals and bookkeeping

Each call gets its own frame, and the frame is released when that call returns.
cards.lessonTitle: Function Calls and the Stack: A First Look

cards.q: What does the `rsp` register hold?
cards.a:
The address of the current top of the stack, its lowest address in use

The stack grows downward, so making room on it means subtracting from `rsp`. The next instruction's address is in `rip`.
cards.lessonTitle: Function Calls and the Stack: A First Look

cards.q: Why is returning `&localVariable` a bug?
cards.a:
The local's frame is released on return, so the memory gets reused

The address still exists as a number, but what lives there soon becomes something else, such as the next call's frame.
cards.lessonTitle: Function Calls and the Stack: A First Look

cards.q: What causes a stack overflow?
cards.a:
Using more stack than reserved, e.g. endless recursion

The stack has a fixed reserved size (about 1 MB by default on Windows). `new` uses the heap, and integer overflow is a different problem.
cards.lessonTitle: Function Calls and the Stack: A First Look

cards.q: What two things does every function call need the stack for?
cards.a:
Remembering where to return to, and holding the call's local variables

The return address lets the CPU come back to the right place in the caller; the frame gives each call its own locals.
cards.lessonTitle: Function Calls and the Stack: A First Look

cards.q: On x64 Windows, a function calls itself three levels deep. Where is the deepest call's frame?
cards.a:
At the lowest address, below the others

The stack grows downwards: each new frame is placed below the previous one.
cards.lessonTitle: Function Calls and the Stack: A First Look

cards.q: What does the `ret` instruction do?
cards.a:
Pops the return address off the stack and jumps to it

`call` pushed the return address; `ret` takes it back off and carries on from there.
cards.lessonTitle: Function Calls and the Stack: A First Look

cards.q: Why does `int grid[1000000];` inside a function usually crash?
cards.a:
It needs 4 MB of stack; the default is 1 MB

Locals live in the frame. A frame bigger than the whole stack overflows it immediately.
cards.lessonTitle: Function Calls and the Stack: A First Look

cards.q: What is the difference between user mode and kernel mode?
cards.a:
Kernel mode has full control of hardware and memory; user mode is restricted and asks the kernel through system calls

Normal programs run in user mode and cannot touch anything outside their own process without a system call.
cards.lessonTitle: What the Operating System Does for a Program

cards.q: What does the Windows loader do when a program starts?
cards.a:
It maps the program and its DLLs into a new process, links imports, starts a thread

Compiling happened long before, at build time. The loader's job is setting up the process so the first instruction can run.
cards.lessonTitle: What the Operating System Does for a Program

cards.q: What is a handle?
cards.a:
A small number a process uses to refer to a kernel object it has opened

The kernel checks every use of a handle against the process's rights. It is not an address the program could follow itself.
cards.lessonTitle: What the Operating System Does for a Program

cards.q: Why can one process not simply read another process's variables through a pointer?
cards.a:
Each process has its own address space, so the address means nothing elsewhere

The same pointer value in two processes refers to two different places. Reading another process needs the kernel's help through a system call.
cards.lessonTitle: What the Operating System Does for a Program

cards.q: Two processes print the same pointer value. What does that tell you?
cards.a:
Nothing: each has its own address space

Virtual addresses are private to each process. The OS maps them to physical memory separately for each one.
cards.lessonTitle: What the Operating System Does for a Program

cards.q: What is a process?
cards.a:
A running copy of a program, with its own memory and threads

The `.exe` is the file on disk. Starting it creates a process. Starting it twice creates two processes.
cards.lessonTitle: What the Operating System Does for a Program

cards.q: How big is one page of memory on x64 Windows?
cards.a:
4,096 bytes (`0x1000`)

65,536 is the allocation granularity, which chapter 6 explains. A page is 4 KB.
cards.lessonTitle: What the Operating System Does for a Program

cards.q: How does a normal Windows program read a file from disk?
cards.a:
It calls a Windows API function, which makes a system call into the kernel

User-mode code cannot touch hardware. The kernel and its drivers do that on the program's behalf.
cards.lessonTitle: What the Operating System Does for a Program

cards.q: What is the difference between a project and a solution?
cards.a:
A project builds one program or library; a solution is a container for related projects

Opening the `.sln` file opens the solution and every project inside it.
cards.lessonTitle: Setting Up Visual Studio for This Course

cards.q: Name two ways a Debug build differs from a Release build.
cards.a:
Debug is unoptimised and adds checks such as `0xCC` fill

Release is faster but harder to follow in a debugger. Platform (x64 or x86) is a separate setting from the configuration. Release is optimised: faster, but harder to follow.
cards.lessonTitle: Setting Up Visual Studio for This Course

cards.q: Where does Visual Studio put the program it builds?
cards.a:
In a platform and configuration folder such as `x64\Debug\`

Each platform and configuration combination gets its own output folder, so Debug and Release builds do not overwrite each other.
cards.lessonTitle: Setting Up Visual Studio for This Course

cards.q: Which workload do you need in the Visual Studio installer for this course?
cards.a:
Desktop development with C++

It brings the MSVC compiler, the Windows SDK and the C++ debugger.
cards.lessonTitle: Setting Up Visual Studio for This Course

cards.q: A variable shows as `-858993460` in the debugger. What does that suggest?
cards.a:
It was read before being given a value, in a Debug build

-858993460 is `0xCCCCCCCC`, the pattern Debug builds use to fill uninitialised stack memory.
cards.lessonTitle: Setting Up Visual Studio for This Course

cards.q: Why should the platform be set to x64?
cards.a:
The course describes 64-bit pointers, registers and calls

Both build fine, but a 32-bit program has different pointer sizes, registers and calling conventions from everything the course explains.
cards.lessonTitle: Setting Up Visual Studio for This Course

cards.q: What does a breakpoint do?
cards.a:
It pauses the program just before that line runs

The program is paused, not ended: you can look at its state and then carry on.
cards.lessonTitle: Your First Debugging Session: Watching Memory Change

cards.q: What is the difference between Step Over and Step Into?
cards.a:
Step Over (F10) runs the whole line including calls; Step Into (F11) goes into the called function

Step Over still runs any calls on the line, it just does not stop inside them.
cards.lessonTitle: Your First Debugging Session: Watching Memory Change

cards.q: How do you see the raw bytes of a variable?
cards.a:
Type its address, such as `&hero`, into the Memory window

Hovering and the Watch window show the value interpreted by its type, not the bytes. The Memory window is under Debug, Windows, Memory.
cards.lessonTitle: Your First Debugging Session: Watching Memory Change

cards.q: What does the Call Stack window show?
cards.a:
The chain of function calls that led to the current line, newest at the top

Each entry is one stack frame, and double-clicking it shows that frame's locals.
cards.lessonTitle: Your First Debugging Session: Watching Memory Change

cards.q: The yellow arrow is on the line `total = addGold(hero, 10);`. Which key runs that line and stops on the next line of `main`?
cards.a:
F10 (Step Over)

Step Over runs the whole line, including the call, and stops at the next line of the same function.
cards.lessonTitle: Your First Debugging Session: Watching Memory Change

cards.q: While paused inside `addGold`, what does the Call Stack window show at the top?
cards.a:
`addGold`, with `main` below it

The newest frame is listed first. `main` is waiting underneath for `addGold` to return.
cards.lessonTitle: Your First Debugging Session: Watching Memory Change

cards.q: The Memory window shows `1e 00 00 00` where an `int` lives. What is its value?
cards.a:
30

Little-endian: the lowest byte comes first, so the value is `0x0000001E`, which is 30.
cards.lessonTitle: Your First Debugging Session: Watching Memory Change

cards.q: Why is `&hero.gold` exactly 4 more than `&hero`?
cards.a:
`gold` is stored straight after `health`, which takes 4 bytes

A struct's members are laid out in order. Chapter 2 shows when the compiler adds gaps between them.
cards.lessonTitle: Your First Debugging Session: Watching Memory Change

cards.q: List the parts of an x64 Windows stack frame, from the caller's side down.
cards.a:
Shadow space, return address, saved registers, locals, space for the function's own calls

The caller reserves the 32-byte shadow space, `call` then pushes the return address, and the called function saves registers and makes room for its locals and its own calls below that.
cards.lessonTitle: The Stack: Frames, Locals and Return Addresses

cards.q: Why are frame sizes often 8 more than you would expect?
cards.a:
The 8-byte return address left `rsp` 8 off a multiple of 16

At each `call`, `rsp` must be a multiple of 16. After the return address is pushed it is 8 off, and the extra 8 in the frame fixes that for the function's own calls.
cards.lessonTitle: The Stack: Frames, Locals and Return Addresses

cards.q: How do you turn a recursive search into one that cannot overflow the stack?
cards.a:
Keep the work still to do in a container such as `std::vector` used as a stack, and loop until it is empty

Take one item out, process it, push its neighbours. The container lives on the heap and can grow as large as needed; a bigger stack only moves the limit.
cards.lessonTitle: The Stack: Frames, Locals and Return Addresses

cards.q: What is the 32-byte shadow space for?
cards.a:
Room where the callee may store its four register arguments

The first four arguments travel in `rcx`, `rdx`, `r8` and `r9`. The caller always reserves 32 bytes so the called function has a place to spill them.
cards.lessonTitle: The Stack: Frames, Locals and Return Addresses

cards.q: At the moment of a `call` instruction, `rsp` must be a multiple of what?
cards.a:
16

The x64 Windows convention requires 16-byte alignment at every call. The pushed return address then leaves `rsp` 8 off inside the function, and the function fixes that when it sets up its frame.
cards.lessonTitle: The Stack: Frames, Locals and Return Addresses

cards.q: A flood fill on a huge open map crashes with a stack overflow. What is the best fix?
cards.a:
Keep the cells to visit in a heap container and loop

Any depth that depends on input data can outgrow any fixed stack. An explicit container grows on the heap instead.
cards.lessonTitle: The Stack: Frames, Locals and Return Addresses

cards.q: Which of these does the called function have to restore before it returns?
cards.a:
`rbx`

`rbx`, `rbp`, `rdi`, `rsi` and `r12` to `r15` are non-volatile: callers rely on them being unchanged. `rax` carries the return value and `rcx` the first argument; both may be overwritten.
cards.lessonTitle: The Stack: Frames, Locals and Return Addresses

cards.q: Name two reasons to put data on the heap instead of the stack.
cards.a:
Its size is known only at run time, or it must outlive its function

Very large data also belongs on the heap because the stack is small. Heap memory is not faster than the stack; it is usually slower to get.
cards.lessonTitle: The Heap: Asking for Memory at Run Time

cards.q: What is a memory leak?
cards.a:
Heap memory that is never freed once it is no longer needed

The memory stays reserved until the process ends. Reading past an array is an overrun, and using freed memory is use-after-free.
cards.lessonTitle: The Heap: Asking for Memory at Run Time

cards.q: What do the Debug heap patterns `CD`, `DD` and `FD` mean?
cards.a:
`CD` is allocated but not yet written, `DD` is freed, `FD` is the guard area around each block

The `FD` guard bytes detect writes past either end of a block. Seeing `DD` through a pointer means the memory has already been freed.
cards.lessonTitle: The Heap: Asking for Memory at Run Time

cards.q: What is an arena allocator?
cards.a:
One large block from which pieces are handed out by moving an offset forward, reset all at once

Individual pieces are never freed; the whole block is reset at once, for example at the end of a frame or level. That is why it is so cheap.
cards.lessonTitle: The Heap: Asking for Memory at Run Time

cards.q: A level's size is read from a file when the game starts. Where should its tile data go?
cards.a:
On the heap, for example in a `std::vector`

Its size is only known at run time and it must outlive the function that loads it. Both point to the heap.
cards.lessonTitle: The Heap: Asking for Memory at Run Time

cards.q: In a Debug build, you look at a pointer's target and see `DD DD DD DD`. What has happened?
cards.a:
The memory was freed, but is still being used

`DD` is the Debug heap's "dead memory" fill, written when a block is freed.
cards.lessonTitle: The Heap: Asking for Memory at Run Time

cards.q: Why do games avoid allocating many small objects every frame?
cards.a:
Each allocation costs time and scatters data, and it adds up

Allocation is a search plus bookkeeping. Reserving, pooling and arenas avoid repeating it every frame.
cards.lessonTitle: The Heap: Asking for Memory at Run Time

cards.q: What frees the memory owned by a `std::vector` local?
cards.a:
The vector's destructor, when the vector goes out of scope

Containers and smart pointers free their heap memory in their destructors. That is the RAII idea in lesson 2.04.
cards.lessonTitle: The Heap: Asking for Memory at Run Time

cards.q: What are the three storage durations, and where does each one's memory come from?
cards.a:
Automatic (the stack), dynamic (the heap), static (the program's image, laid out by the linker)

Static storage is laid out by the linker and mapped in by the loader, so it exists for the whole run of the program.
cards.lessonTitle: Static Storage and the Layout of a Program in Memory

cards.q: What is the difference between `.data` and `.rdata`?
cards.a:
`.data` holds writable globals that start with a value; `.rdata` holds read-only data such as string literals

Writing to `.rdata` crashes. Zero-initialised globals go in `.bss`, which takes no space in the file.
cards.lessonTitle: Static Storage and the Layout of a Program in Memory

cards.q: How does a function with a `static` local avoid initialisation-order problems?
cards.a:
The local is initialised the first time the function is called, so it is ready whenever anything uses it

The order in which globals in different files are set up is not fixed, but a function's `static` local is set up on first use, whatever that order was.
cards.lessonTitle: Static Storage and the Layout of a Program in Memory

cards.q: Which section holds the characters of the string literal `"Game Over"`?
cards.a:
`.rdata`

Literals are read-only data. Writing to them is an access violation.
cards.lessonTitle: Static Storage and the Layout of a Program in Memory

cards.q: A `static int counter{ 0 };` inside a function. How many times is `counter` initialised?
cards.a:
Once, the first time the function runs

A static local lives in static storage for the whole program and is initialised the first time control reaches its declaration.
cards.lessonTitle: Static Storage and the Layout of a Program in Memory

cards.q: Two addresses are `00007FF6C1A21000` and `00007FF6C1A3B0E0`. What is the most likely relationship?
cards.a:
Both are inside the same loaded image, such as the `.exe`

They share their high digits and differ only in the low ones: about 100 KB apart, typical of sections within one module.
cards.lessonTitle: Static Storage and the Layout of a Program in Memory

cards.q: Why does a zero-initialised global array of a million `int`s not make the `.exe` four megabytes bigger?
cards.a:
Zeroed data takes no file space; the loader supplies zeroes

The file only records how much zeroed memory is needed, not the zeros themselves.
cards.lessonTitle: Static Storage and the Layout of a Program in Memory

cards.q: When does an object's lifetime begin and end?
cards.a:
It begins when its constructor finishes and ends when its destructor starts

Outside that window, using the object is undefined behaviour, even if its memory still exists.
cards.lessonTitle: Object Lifetime: When Memory Is Valid

cards.q: Why is `const char* p = makeString().c_str();` a bug?
cards.a:
The returned string is a temporary destroyed at the end of the line

The temporary only lives until the end of the full expression. Keep the string in a named variable first if you need the pointer later.
cards.lessonTitle: Object Lifetime: When Memory Is Valid

cards.q: Name three kinds of resource that RAII can manage.
cards.a:
Heap memory, open files and Windows handles

RAII ties a resource to an object: the constructor acquires it and the destructor releases it, whatever the resource is. Locks, or any "undo this when finished" action, work the same way.
cards.lessonTitle: Object Lifetime: When Memory Is Valid

cards.q: Three locals `a`, `b`, `c` are declared in that order in one block. In which order are they destroyed?
cards.a:
`c`, `b`, `a`

Reverse order of construction, so later objects, which may depend on earlier ones, go first.
cards.lessonTitle: Object Lifetime: When Memory Is Valid

cards.q: How long does the temporary in `std::cout << makeName() << '\n';` live?
cards.a:
Until the end of the full expression, at the semicolon

Temporaries die at the end of the full expression they were created in.
cards.lessonTitle: Object Lifetime: When Memory Is Valid

cards.q: Why can `Enemy& first = enemies[0]; enemies.push_back(e); first.health = 0;` be a bug?
cards.a:
`push_back` may move the elements, leaving `first` dangling

When capacity runs out, the vector reallocates and frees the old block.
cards.lessonTitle: Object Lifetime: When Memory Is Valid

cards.q: What is RAII?
cards.a:
Releasing a resource in the destructor of its owner

Because destructors run automatically, the resource is released on every path out of the scope.
cards.lessonTitle: Object Lifetime: When Memory Is Valid

cards.q: State the three layout rules for a struct.
cards.a:
Each member starts at a multiple of its alignment; the struct's alignment is its largest member's; its size is a multiple of that

Members are never reordered by the compiler. Padding can appear between members and at the end.

cards.q: How do you usually reduce a struct's padding?
cards.a:
Declare the members in order of decreasing alignment: 8-byte first, then 4, 2 and 1

Largest first leaves no gaps between members. `#pragma pack` removes padding too, but makes access slower and is meant for fixed file or network layouts.

cards.q: Why should structs with padding not be compared with `memcmp`?
cards.a:
Padding bytes hold no set value, so equal structs can differ

Compare the members one by one (or with a defaulted `operator==`) instead.

cards.q: What is the size of `struct A { char c; double d; };` on x64 Windows?
cards.a:
16

`d` needs an offset that is a multiple of 8, so 7 padding bytes follow `c`. 1 + 7 + 8 = 16.

cards.q: What is the alignment of `struct B { char c; int i; short s; };`?
cards.a:
4

A struct's alignment is the largest alignment of its members, here the `int`'s 4.

cards.q: Why is `struct C { int i; char c; };` 8 bytes, not 5?
cards.a:
Tail padding makes the size a multiple of its alignment

In an array, the second element starts right after the first. Size 8 keeps its `int` at a multiple of 4.

cards.q: When is `#pragma pack(push, 1)` the right tool?
cards.a:
When matching an outside layout, like a file header

Packing removes padding at the cost of misaligned access. Reordering members is the usual way to save space.

cards.q: Which parts of a class take up space in each object?
cards.a:
Non-static data members, padding, and a vptr if it has virtuals

Member functions are code, stored once; static members live in static storage; access specifiers cost nothing.
cards.lessonTitle: How Structs and Classes Are Laid Out

cards.q: Why can a `Monster*` be used as an `Entity*` without changing the address?
cards.a:
With single inheritance the `Entity` subobject is at offset 0 of the `Monster`

The base comes first in the derived object's layout, so both pointers hold the same address.
cards.lessonTitle: How Structs and Classes Are Laid Out

cards.q: What is `this`?
cards.a:
A hidden argument holding the address of the object called on

On x64 Windows it arrives in the first argument register, `rcx`. It is a pointer, not a copy.
cards.lessonTitle: How Structs and Classes Are Laid Out

cards.q: A class has three `int` members, ten member functions and a `static int`. What is its `sizeof`?
cards.a:
12

Only the non-static data members are stored in each object.
cards.lessonTitle: How Structs and Classes Are Laid Out

cards.q: Where does a derived class's base subobject go?
cards.a:
At the start of the derived object, at offset 0

The base's members come first, so a pointer to the derived object is also a valid pointer to its base.
cards.lessonTitle: How Structs and Classes Are Laid Out

cards.q: Why is `sizeof(WithVirtual)` 16 when its only data member is an `int`?
cards.a:
A hidden 8-byte vptr is added, and the size is padded to 16

The vptr points to the class's table of virtual functions. The functions themselves are in the code section.
cards.lessonTitle: How Structs and Classes Are Laid Out

cards.q: How does a member function know which object it is working on?
cards.a:
The object's address is passed as a hidden argument, `this`

`obj.f(x)` is compiled much like `f(&obj, x)`.
cards.lessonTitle: How Structs and Classes Are Laid Out

cards.q: How is the address of `a[i]` worked out?
cards.a:
The address of `a[0]` plus `i` times the size of one element

Array elements sit side by side with nothing between them, so the arithmetic is all it takes.
cards.lessonTitle: Arrays and Multi-Dimensional Data in Memory

cards.q: What does row-major order mean?
cards.a:
Each complete row is stored after the previous one, so (row, column) is at row × width + column

Built-in two-dimensional arrays in C++ are row-major. Column × height + row would be column-major, the other order.
cards.lessonTitle: Arrays and Multi-Dimensional Data in Memory

cards.q: Why does loop order affect speed over a big grid?
cards.a:
Rows use each 64-byte cache line fully; columns fetch a new line each step

Same number of elements, very different number of cache-line fetches. Make the inner loop walk along rows for a row-major grid.
cards.lessonTitle: Arrays and Multi-Dimensional Data in Memory

cards.q: An array of `double` starts at address `0x1000`. Where is element 3?
cards.a:
`0x1018`

3 × 8 bytes = 24 = `0x18`, so element 3 is at `0x1000 + 0x18`.
cards.lessonTitle: Arrays and Multi-Dimensional Data in Memory

cards.q: A tile map is 10 wide and stored row-major. Which index holds the tile at x = 3, y = 2?
cards.lessonTitle: Arrays and Multi-Dimensional Data in Memory

cards.q: Which loop order is faster for a large row-major grid?
cards.a:
Rows in the outer loop, columns in the inner loop

The inner loop should walk through memory in order, so each cache line fetched is fully used.
cards.lessonTitle: Arrays and Multi-Dimensional Data in Memory

cards.q: Inside `void f(int a[])`, what is `sizeof(a)` on x64?
cards.a:
8, the size of a pointer

An array parameter is really a pointer. The length is not passed.
cards.lessonTitle: Arrays and Multi-Dimensional Data in Memory

cards.q: How does `strlen` find the length of a C string?
cards.a:
It walks along from the first character, counting, until it finds the zero byte

A C string stores no length; that is why `strlen` costs time proportional to the string and why a missing zero byte runs off the end.
cards.lessonTitle: Strings in Memory: C Strings, std::string and Encodings

cards.q: What is the small string optimisation?
cards.a:
Storing short strings directly inside the `std::string` object, so they need no heap allocation

On MSVC, strings of up to 15 characters fit in the object's own buffer.
cards.lessonTitle: Strings in Memory: C Strings, std::string and Encodings

cards.q: What is the difference between UTF-8 and UTF-16?
cards.a:
Both cover Unicode; UTF-8 uses 1-4 bytes, UTF-16 uses 2 or 4

Both cover all of Unicode. On Windows, `wchar_t` strings are UTF-16. UTF-8 matches ASCII for English text; Windows uses UTF-16 internally.
cards.lessonTitle: Strings in Memory: C Strings, std::string and Encodings

cards.q: How many bytes does `char word[]{ "Lava" };` occupy?
cards.a:
5

Four characters plus the terminating zero byte.
cards.lessonTitle: Strings in Memory: C Strings, std::string and Encodings

cards.q: On 64-bit MSVC, which of these strings is stored inside the `std::string` object with no heap allocation?
cards.a:
`"Goblin"`

Up to 15 characters fit in the small buffer.
cards.lessonTitle: Strings in Memory: C Strings, std::string and Encodings

cards.q: In memory you see `48 00 50 00 00 00`. What is most likely there?
cards.a:
The UTF-16 string `"HP"`

`0x48` is `H`, `0x50` is `P`; the zero byte after each is the high half of a 2-byte UTF-16 unit, and `00 00` ends it.
cards.lessonTitle: Strings in Memory: C Strings, std::string and Encodings

cards.q: What does `'5' - '0'` evaluate to?
cards.a:
5

Digits are consecutive in ASCII, so subtracting `'0'` gives the digit's value.
cards.lessonTitle: Strings in Memory: C Strings, std::string and Encodings

cards.q: Why are memory bugs harder to find than logic bugs?
cards.a:
The symptom often appears far from the cause, and only sometimes

The bad write lands on some unrelated value, which only misbehaves when it is used later. That is why watching the corrupted variable with a data breakpoint helps.
cards.lessonTitle: Memory Bugs: Overruns, Dangling Pointers and Leaks

cards.q: What is the difference between a dangling pointer and a leak?
cards.a:
A dangling pointer refers to memory that was freed or whose object ended; a leak is memory still allocated that nothing will free

They are opposites: one keeps a reference without memory, the other keeps memory without a reference.
cards.lessonTitle: Memory Bugs: Overruns, Dangling Pointers and Leaks

cards.q: How do ids or handles help avoid use-after-free bugs?
cards.a:
Code looks the object up by id, and a lookup of a gone object fails

Instead of holding a pointer that can dangle, code asks "is object 42 still there?" each time and gets a clear answer.
cards.lessonTitle: Memory Bugs: Overruns, Dangling Pointers and Leaks

cards.q: A player's gold changes to a huge random number right after they rename their character. What kind of bug is most likely?
cards.a:
A buffer overrun from the name into the gold

The name copy wrote past the end of its array into the next member.
cards.lessonTitle: Memory Bugs: Overruns, Dangling Pointers and Leaks

cards.q: In a Debug build a variable reads `-572662307` (`0xDDDDDDDD`). What does that point to?
cards.a:
Use of heap memory after it was freed

The Debug heap fills freed blocks with `DD`.
cards.lessonTitle: Memory Bugs: Overruns, Dangling Pointers and Leaks

cards.q: Which habit prevents leaks from early returns and exceptions?
cards.a:
Giving every allocation an owner such as `std::unique_ptr`

Owners free memory in their destructors, which run on every path out of the scope.
cards.lessonTitle: Memory Bugs: Overruns, Dangling Pointers and Leaks

cards.q: What is the best tool for finding which instruction changes a variable unexpectedly?
cards.a:
A data breakpoint on that variable's address

A data breakpoint stops the program on the exact write, with the call stack showing who made it.
cards.lessonTitle: Memory Bugs: Overruns, Dangling Pointers and Leaks

cards.q: How does AddressSanitizer know an access is invalid?
cards.a:
It checks shadow memory, which marks red zones and freed memory, on every access

The compiler inserts the shadow check before each memory access, which is why ASan needs a rebuild and slows the program down.

cards.q: What three locations can an ASan use-after-free report give you?
cards.a:
Where the bad access happened, where the memory was freed, and where it was originally allocated

Each comes with a call stack, so you can see the whole story of the block.

cards.q: Why keep a separate ASan build configuration?
cards.a:
ASan is slow and clashes with some options, such as Edit and Continue

Normal debugging stays fast, and the ASan build is run regularly to catch memory bugs.

cards.q: When does AddressSanitizer report a buffer overrun?
cards.a:
At the moment the bad read or write happens

Every access is checked as it happens, which is what makes ASan so much more useful than finding the damage later.

cards.q: A report says "0 bytes to the right of 16-byte region". What happened?
cards.a:
The code touched the byte just after a 16-byte block

"To the right" means past the end; "0 bytes" means immediately after it.

cards.q: Which of these does ASan not catch?
cards.a:
An overrun between members of one struct

Both members belong to one live object, so the access is to valid memory as far as ASan can tell.

cards.q: What is shadow memory?
cards.a:
Where ASan records which bytes are valid to use

One shadow byte describes eight bytes of real memory.

cards.q: How can you tell a pointer from other data in the Memory window?
cards.a:
8 aligned bytes ending in `00 00`, such as `f6 7f 00 00`

User-mode addresses on x64 Windows are far below the top of the 64-bit range, and little-endian order puts their zero high bytes last.
cards.lessonTitle: Reading the Memory Window in Visual Studio

cards.q: What are the three parts of a 32-bit float?
cards.a:
One sign bit, an 8-bit exponent stored with a bias of 127, and a 23-bit fraction

1 + 8 + 23 = 32 bits. The exponent's bias of 127 is why `1.0f` is stored as `00 00 80 3f`.
cards.lessonTitle: Reading the Memory Window in Visual Studio

cards.q: What steps decode an unknown object in memory?
cards.a:
Work out member offsets, split the bytes, read each member by its kind

Each member needs the right reading rule: integer, float, pointer or padding. Checking against the Locals window confirms you got the offsets right. Then check the result against the Locals window.
cards.lessonTitle: Reading the Memory Window in Visual Studio

cards.q: You see the eight bytes `30 12 4a 9c f6 7f 00 00`. What is it most likely to be?
cards.a:
A pointer into the program's own code or data

Eight bytes ending in `f6 7f 00 00` is the typical shape of an address in the program's image.
cards.lessonTitle: Reading the Memory Window in Visual Studio

cards.q: What `float` is stored as the bytes `00 00 80 3f`?
cards.a:
1.0

Read little-endian, the bits are `0x3F800000`: sign 0, exponent 127, fraction 0, which is 1.0.
cards.lessonTitle: Reading the Memory Window in Visual Studio

cards.q: An int that should be small reads 1,065,353,216 in the Watch window. What is a likely explanation?
cards.a:
The memory holds the float 1.0, read as an int

1,065,353,216 is `0x3F800000`, the bit pattern of 1.0f.
cards.lessonTitle: Reading the Memory Window in Visual Studio

cards.q: Why do user-mode pointers on x64 Windows always end in `00 00` in memory?
cards.a:
Their top two bytes are zero, and little-endian stores them last

The highest bytes of the value come last in memory, and for user-mode addresses they are zero.
cards.lessonTitle: Reading the Memory Window in Visual Studio

cards.q: What does a pointer to a pointer hold?
cards.a:
The address of another pointer variable

An `int**` holds the address of an `int*`. Dereference it once to get that pointer, twice to get the `int`.

cards.q: Give two common reasons to use a pointer to a pointer.
cards.a:
To let a function re-aim the caller's pointer, and for arrays of pointers

A function given an `Enemy*` can only change the enemy; given an `Enemy**` it can change which enemy the caller's pointer refers to.

cards.q: How many bytes does `argv + 1` move on x64?
cards.a:
Eight, the size of one pointer

Pointer arithmetic moves by the size of the thing pointed at, and `argv` points at `char*` pointers, which are 8 bytes on x64.

cards.q: `int x{ 5 }; int* p{ &x }; int** pp{ &p };` What is the type of `*pp`?
cards.a:
`int*`

One `*` removes one level: `*pp` is `p`, an `int*`.

cards.q: Why does a function need an `Enemy**` parameter to change which enemy the caller's `Enemy*` points at?
cards.a:
It needs the caller's pointer's address to write into it

Arguments are copies. To change the caller's variable, a function needs its address, and here the variable is itself a pointer.

cards.q: In `int main(int argc, char** argv)`, what is `argv[2][0]`?
cards.a:
The first character of the third command-line argument

`argv[2]` is the third pointer in the array; `[0]` takes the first character it points at.

cards.q: What two steps does following `p->member` take?
cards.a:
Read the address held in `p`, then access the bytes at that address plus the member's offset

The member's offset is fixed at compile time, so `p->member` is just one address calculation and one memory access.

cards.q: How can you tell from a crash address that a null pointer was followed?
cards.a:
The address is small, equal to the offset of the member being read from address zero

Reading `p->member` with `p` null reads address 0 + offset, so a crash at `0x10` suggests reading the member at offset 16 of a null object.

cards.q: Name two ways games reduce pointer chasing.
cards.a:
Storing objects by value inside their owners, and keeping objects in arrays referred to by index or handle

Objects next to each other in memory share cache lines; every pointer hop to a scattered heap object can be a cache miss.

cards.q: A crash says "access violation reading location 0x0000000000000010". What is the most likely cause?
cards.a:
Reading the member at offset 16 through a null pointer

Null plus a member offset gives a tiny address like 0x10. Look for an unchecked pointer whose member at offset 16 was being read.

cards.q: Why is following a long chain of pointers through scattered heap objects slow?
cards.a:
Each read waits for the last, and each may miss the cache

Dependent loads cannot overlap, so every cache miss along the chain is paid in full.

cards.q: When should a member be a pointer rather than a value?
cards.a:
When the link is optional, or the object is owned elsewhere

If an object always has exactly one of something, a value member is simpler, safer and faster.

cards.q: How is a reference parameter passed at the machine level?
cards.a:
As an address, exactly like a pointer

The machine code for `void f(int& x)` and `void f(int* x)` is usually identical: the address arrives in a register.

cards.q: Why are references safer than pointers?
cards.a:
They cannot be null, cannot be re-aimed, and need no `*` or `->`

These rules remove several common mistakes, but a reference can still dangle if the object it refers to is destroyed.

cards.q: When should you still use a pointer instead of a reference?
cards.a:
When it may be null, must be re-aimed, or must be stored

A reference must refer to something and cannot be re-aimed, which also makes it awkward as a class member or container element. Storing a reference in a container or an assignable class is awkward because it cannot be re-aimed.

cards.q: What does `void f(int& x)` receive in its first register when called?
cards.a:
The address of the caller's `int`

A reference parameter is passed exactly like a pointer.

cards.q: Which of these can a pointer do that a reference cannot?
cards.a:
Be re-aimed at a different object later

A reference is bound once, when it is created, and always refers to that object.

cards.q: Which is the best parameter type for a function that reads a large `Level` without changing it?
cards.a:
`const Level&`

No copy, no null check, and the `const` documents that the function only reads it.

cards.q: What is the difference in machine code between a direct call and a call through a function pointer?
cards.a:
A direct call's target is fixed at link time; a pointer call reads it at run time

An indirect call such as `call rax` reads its target from a register or memory, so the same instruction can reach different functions.

cards.q: What is a callback?
cards.a:
A function passed to other code so that code can call it when needed

The caller decides part of the behaviour, for example what to do with each item a search finds.

cards.q: When would you choose `std::function` over a plain function pointer?
cards.a:
When it must store a callable with data, like a capturing lambda

A plain function pointer can only hold a function (or a capture-less lambda). Windows APIs need plain function pointers, and `std::function` costs a little more.

cards.q: What does `int (*f)(float)` declare?
cards.a:
A pointer to a function that takes a `float` and returns an `int`

Read from the name outwards: `f` is a pointer (`*f`) to a function taking `(float)` returning `int`.

cards.q: Which kind of lambda can be converted to a plain function pointer?
cards.a:
One that captures nothing

A captureless lambda has no data to carry, so it is just a function. Capturing lambdas are objects.

cards.q: Why do Windows API callbacks use plain function pointers instead of `std::function`?
cards.a:
The Windows API is a C interface, and C has no `std::function`

C++ types like `std::function` cannot cross a C boundary.

cards.q: What is a vtable?
cards.a:
A per-class array of function pointers, one slot per virtual function

Objects use their class's vtable, reached through the hidden vptr, to find the right function at run time.
cards.lessonTitle: Virtual Functions and Vtables in Memory

cards.q: Why does every class put a given virtual function in the same slot?
cards.a:
So a base pointer can call it by slot without knowing the real class

The caller compiles `call [vtable + slot * 8]`; whichever class the object really is, its table has the right function in that slot.
cards.lessonTitle: Virtual Functions and Vtables in Memory

cards.q: What does a virtual call cost compared with a normal call?
cards.a:
Two extra dependent memory reads (vptr and table entry), an indirect call, and usually no inlining

The cost is small for one call but adds up in tight loops over many objects, mostly because the call cannot be inlined.
cards.lessonTitle: Virtual Functions and Vtables in Memory

cards.q: Where is the vptr stored?
cards.a:
In each object, normally at offset 0

Every object of a class with virtual functions carries its own vptr, set by its constructor.
cards.lessonTitle: Virtual Functions and Vtables in Memory

cards.q: Two `Goblin` objects exist. How many Goblin vtables are there?
cards.a:
One, shared by both

The vtable belongs to the class and lives in `.rdata`. Objects only hold pointers to it.
cards.lessonTitle: Virtual Functions and Vtables in Memory

cards.q: What does `call QWORD PTR [rax+8]` do in a virtual call?
cards.a:
Calls the function in vtable slot 1, read via `rax`

`rax` holds the vptr; `[rax+8]` is the second 8-byte entry of the table.
cards.lessonTitle: Virtual Functions and Vtables in Memory

cards.q: A virtual function is called from inside the base class's constructor while a `Dragon` is being built. Which version runs?
cards.a:
The base class's version

During the base constructor the vptr still points at the base class's vtable.
cards.lessonTitle: Virtual Functions and Vtables in Memory

cards.q: What does each node of a singly linked list hold?
cards.a:
An element's value and a pointer to the next node, or `nullptr` in the last node

Pointers in both directions make a doubly linked list. A singly linked list only links forward.

cards.q: Why is inserting at the front of a list cheap?
cards.a:
Because it creates one node and changes two pointers, whatever the list's length

Nothing has to move, unlike inserting at the front of a vector, which shifts every element.

cards.q: Give two situations where games use linked structures sensibly.
cards.a:
Intrusive lists inside existing objects, and pool free lists

Lists are slow to walk, so they appear where links are cheap to keep and walking is rare or short. An intrusive list keeps the link inside objects that already exist, such as the objects in one grid cell.

cards.q: What is the cost of reading the 1000th element of a linked list?
cards.a:
Following 999 `next` pointers from the head

There is no index arithmetic: the only way to a node is through the ones before it.

cards.q: In `removeFirst`, why does `link` have type `Node**`?
cards.a:
It points at the link (`head` or a `next`) that may change

Changing a pointer requires its address. `*link = dead->next` updates whichever pointer pointed at the dead node.

cards.q: Why is a `std::vector` usually faster to loop over than a linked list with the same elements?
cards.a:
Its elements are contiguous and cache-friendly; list nodes are scattered

Contiguous memory is streamed efficiently; pointer chasing waits on memory at every step.

cards.q: What three pointers make up a `std::vector`, and how are size and capacity worked out?
cards.a:
Start of the block, end of the elements in use, end of the block; size is used end minus start, capacity is block end minus start

Size and capacity are not stored as numbers; they are worked out from the three pointers.

cards.q: Why can a pointer to a vector element become invalid after `push_back`?
cards.a:
If the vector is full, `push_back` moves every element to a new block and frees the old one

If there is spare capacity the elements stay put, but you cannot rely on that unless you have reserved enough.

cards.q: When is swap-and-pop the right way to remove an element?
cards.a:
When the order of the elements does not matter

Moving the last element into the gap removes in constant time, but it changes the order.

cards.q: A vector has size 6 and capacity 6. What happens on `push_back`?
cards.a:
It moves the 6 elements to a bigger block, then adds the new one

A heap block cannot grow in place, so the vector moves to a new, larger one.

cards.q: Why does a vector grow by a factor (such as 1.5×) instead of by one element at a time?
cards.a:
So the cost of many `push_back`s averages to a constant each

Growing by one would copy everything on every push: the cost would grow with the square of the size.

cards.q: What does `v.reserve(100)` do to an empty vector's size?
cards.a:
Nothing: the size stays 0, only the capacity changes

`reserve` makes room; `resize` changes the number of elements.

cards.q: What is the cost of swap-and-pop removal?
cards.a:
Constant, whatever the size of the vector

One move and one `pop_back`. The order of the elements changes, which is the price.

cards.q: What two properties should a hash function have?
cards.a:
It must give the same hash for the same key, and it should spread keys evenly

Same key, same hash, or lookups would fail. Collisions cannot be avoided entirely; a good spread just keeps them rare.

cards.q: What is the load factor, and why does it matter?
cards.a:
The number of entries divided by the number of buckets; a high one means more collisions, so tables rehash past a limit

Growing and rehashing keeps buckets short so lookups stay fast.

cards.q: When would you choose `std::map` over `std::unordered_map`?
cards.a:
When you need the keys in sorted order, or a key's neighbours

`std::map` is a sorted tree; `std::unordered_map` is usually faster for plain lookup but has no order.

cards.q: What does a hash table do with a key's hash?
cards.a:
Uses it to pick the one bucket a lookup must search

`hash % bucketCount` picks the bucket; only the entries there are compared.

cards.q: Two different keys land in the same bucket. What is that called?
cards.a:
A collision

Collisions are normal; the table's strategy (chaining or probing) handles them.

cards.q: Why does a hash table rehash when its load factor gets high?
cards.a:
To keep buckets short so lookups stay fast

Keeping entries per bucket low keeps lookups near constant time.

cards.q: You need to print all items in alphabetical order. Which container fits best?
cards.a:
`std::map<std::string, Item>`

`std::map` keeps its keys sorted; `unordered_map` has no meaningful order.

cards.q: What is a scene graph, and why do positions in it add up on the way down?
cards.a:
A tree of attached objects, each placed relative to its parent

A sword attached to a hand moves with the hand because its position is stored relative to the hand.

cards.q: What is the difference between depth-first and breadth-first search?
cards.a:
Depth-first follows one branch first (a stack); breadth-first goes by distance (a queue)

Visiting by distance is why breadth-first search finds the shortest path when every step costs the same.

cards.q: How do you recover the actual path, not just its length, from a BFS?
cards.a:
Record where each place was reached from, then follow it back

One "came from" entry per place is all it takes; following them from the target to the start gives the path in reverse.

cards.q: What makes a tree different from a general graph?
cards.a:
Every node except the root has exactly one parent, and there are no loops

A binary tree has at most two children; a tree in general may have any number.

cards.q: Why does breadth-first search find the shortest path when every step costs the same?
cards.a:
It visits places by distance, so it reaches the target by a shortest route

The queue ensures all places at distance n are handled before any at distance n + 1.

cards.q: What data structure drives a breadth-first search?
cards.a:
A queue

First in, first out: places are explored in the order they were discovered.

cards.q: What kind of structure is `std::map` built on?
cards.a:
A balanced binary search tree

That is why it keeps keys in order and looks them up in logarithmic time.

cards.q: What three things does a container of game objects usually need to do well?
cards.a:
Loop quickly over live objects, add and remove them cheaply, and let other code refer to an object safely

The patterns in the lesson each trade these three off differently.
cards.lessonTitle: Containers of Game Objects: Entity Lists and Pools

cards.q: How does a generational handle detect that its object is gone?
cards.a:
The slot's generation changes on free, so the handle's no longer matches

The handle remembers the generation from when it was made, so a reused slot is recognised as a different object.
cards.lessonTitle: Containers of Game Objects: Entity Lists and Pools

cards.q: Why are handles safer to store than pointers?
cards.a:
A stale handle is caught on lookup; a stale pointer is not

The lookup turns a silent memory bug into a clear "the object is gone" result.
cards.lessonTitle: Containers of Game Objects: Entity Lists and Pools

cards.q: Why does a dense vector with swap-and-pop not give objects stable references?
cards.a:
Removing one moves another into its slot

The last element is moved to fill the gap, so its index changes.
cards.lessonTitle: Containers of Game Objects: Entity Lists and Pools

cards.q: What does a pool's free list link together?
cards.a:
The unused slots, through an index stored in each

Allocating takes the head of the free list; freeing pushes the slot back on.
cards.lessonTitle: Containers of Game Objects: Entity Lists and Pools

cards.q: A handle says (slot 12, generation 5). The pool's slot 12 has generation 6. What does a lookup return?
cards.a:
Nothing: the object the handle referred to has been destroyed

A different generation means the slot has been freed since the handle was made.
cards.lessonTitle: Containers of Game Objects: Entity Lists and Pools

cards.q: What is the difference between a solution and a project?
cards.a:
A project builds one output (exe, dll or lib) from its sources and settings; a solution groups related projects

The solution also records which projects to build in which configuration.

cards.q: Why might a setting work in Debug but not in Release?
cards.a:
Each configuration has its own settings, so a Debug-only change misses Release

Check the Configuration and Platform boxes at the top of the Property Pages before changing a setting, or choose All Configurations.

cards.q: What is a property sheet for?
cards.a:
Holding settings shared by several projects, so they are set once and stay consistent

Each project that imports the sheet picks up its settings, so changing them in one place changes them everywhere.

cards.q: What does adding a project reference from `game` to `engine` do?
cards.a:
Builds `engine` first and links its output into `game`

It sets the build order and the linking. Include directories are a separate setting.

cards.q: Where are a project's compiler and linker settings stored?
cards.a:
In the `.vcxproj` file and its property sheets

The solution only lists projects; each project file holds its own settings.

cards.q: What does `$(Configuration)` expand to?
cards.a:
The configuration being built, such as `Debug`

Macros let one setting work for every configuration and machine.

cards.q: What does the one definition rule require?
cards.a:
Each used function and variable is defined exactly once in the program

Declarations may be repeated freely. It is definitions of ordinary functions and variables that must be unique. Classes, templates and inline functions may be defined in several files, but only if every definition is identical.
cards.lessonTitle: Preprocessor, Compiler, Linker: Who Does What

cards.q: Why do class definitions go in headers but function bodies usually do not?
cards.a:
Classes may be defined (identically) in every translation unit; ordinary functions must be defined only once

A function body in a header included by two `.cpp` files is defined twice, which breaks the one definition rule unless it is marked `inline`.
cards.lessonTitle: Preprocessor, Compiler, Linker: Who Does What

cards.q: What is name mangling?
cards.a:
Encoding a function's namespace, class and parameter types into its symbol

That is how overloads such as `heal(int)` and `heal(unsigned)` get distinct symbols, and why they do not link to each other.
cards.lessonTitle: Preprocessor, Compiler, Linker: Who Does What

cards.q: Which is a definition, not just a declaration?
cards.a:
`int g_lives{ 3 };`

It creates the variable's storage. The others only announce that something exists elsewhere.
cards.lessonTitle: Preprocessor, Compiler, Linker: Who Does What

cards.q: Two `.cpp` files include a header containing `int square(int x) { return x * x; }`. What happens?
cards.a:
The linker reports that `square` is already defined

Each file gets a definition, breaking the one definition rule. Marking it `inline` fixes it.
cards.lessonTitle: Preprocessor, Compiler, Linker: Who Does What

cards.q: Why does a declaration `void heal(int)` not link to a definition `void heal(unsigned)`?
cards.a:
Parameter types are part of the mangled symbol name

C++ symbols encode the parameter types so that overloads can coexist.
cards.lessonTitle: Preprocessor, Compiler, Linker: Who Does What

cards.q: What does `extern "C"` change?
cards.a:
It turns off name mangling, so the symbol is the plain name

Plain names are what C code, other languages and `GetProcAddress` expect.
cards.lessonTitle: Preprocessor, Compiler, Linker: Who Does What

cards.q: Why fix the first error first?
cards.a:
Because later errors are often caused by the compiler misreading code after the first mistake

One missing semicolon or bracket can produce dozens of errors; fixing it often clears the rest.

cards.q: How can you tell a compiler error from a linker error?
cards.a:
Compiler errors have codes starting with `C`; linker errors start with `LNK`

Linker errors only appear once every file has compiled, and they name symbols rather than source lines.

cards.q: What does C2664 usually tell you, and what should you read in it?
cards.a:
An argument has the wrong type; compare the "from X to Y" types

The two types often differ only by a `const`, a `*` or a `&`, so compare them character by character. Look closely at const-ness, pointers and references: the two types often differ only there.

cards.q: A build shows 40 errors. What should you do first?
cards.a:
Fix the first error in the Output window and rebuild

Most of the rest are probably a cascade from the first.

cards.q: `error C2280: attempting to reference a deleted function` appears when pushing a `std::unique_ptr` into a vector. What is the fix?
cards.a:
Move it in: `v.push_back(std::move(ptr));`

`unique_ptr` cannot be copied; its copy constructor is deleted. It can be moved.

cards.q: `LNK1168: cannot open game.exe for writing`. What is the most likely cause?
cards.a:
The program is still running from the last build

Windows will not let the linker overwrite an executable that is running.

cards.q: Which warning tells you a function can end without returning a value?
cards.a:
C4715

Falling off the end of a non-void function is undefined behaviour.

cards.q: How does the linker decide which parts of a static library go into the program?
cards.a:
It takes each object file that defines a symbol still needed

Unused object files are left out, which is why a program using one function from a large library stays small. It repeats until nothing more is needed, so unused object files are left out.

cards.q: Why must a library be built with the same runtime library and configuration as the program?
cards.a:
Mismatches disagree about the runtime and standard type layouts

LNK2038 "mismatch detected" errors are the linker catching exactly this.

cards.q: When would you choose a DLL over a static library?
cards.a:
When code must be loaded or replaced at run time, as with plugins

A static library is copied into each program at link time; a DLL stays a separate file loaded when needed.

cards.q: What does a static library contain?
cards.a:
Object files and an index of their symbols

It is an archive of compiled code, ready to be linked.

cards.q: The game uses only `length` from `engine.lib`. What gets copied into `game.exe`?
cards.a:
The object file that defines `length`, and what it needs

The linker pulls in object files on demand, by symbol.

cards.q: `LNK2038: mismatch detected for '_ITERATOR_DEBUG_LEVEL'`. What does it mean?
cards.a:
Debug-built and Release-built code are mixed

Debug and Release standard containers have different layouts; mixing them is unsafe.

cards.q: What are the two ways a program can use a DLL?
cards.a:
Load-time linking through an import library, or run-time loading with `LoadLibrary` and `GetProcAddress`

With load-time linking the loader resolves the DLL when the program starts; with run-time loading the program loads it and looks functions up itself.
cards.lessonTitle: Dynamic Libraries: Building and Loading Your Own DLL

cards.q: Why should only simple C types cross a DLL boundary?
cards.a:
Each side may lay out standard library types differently

An `int` or a plain struct of fixed types means the same on both sides; a `std::string` may not. The DLL and the program may use different compilers, settings or heaps.
cards.lessonTitle: Dynamic Libraries: Building and Loading Your Own DLL

cards.q: What does `GetProcAddress` return, and what must you do with it?
cards.a:
An exported function's address; cast it to the exact signature

Calling through a pointer with the wrong signature compiles fine and then corrupts the call, so the signature must match exactly.
cards.lessonTitle: Dynamic Libraries: Building and Loading Your Own DLL

cards.q: What is the import library (`plugin.lib`) produced alongside `plugin.dll` for?
cards.a:
It tells the linker which symbols are in the DLL

The import library holds no code. It lets the linker record the DLL dependency in the program's import table.
cards.lessonTitle: Dynamic Libraries: Building and Loading Your Own DLL

cards.q: Why is `extern "C"` usually used for DLL exports meant for `GetProcAddress`?
cards.a:
It exports the plain function name instead of a mangled C++ name

`GetProcAddress` looks names up exactly as they appear in the export table.
cards.lessonTitle: Dynamic Libraries: Building and Loading Your Own DLL

cards.q: A program links to `plugin.dll` at load time, and the DLL is missing. What happens?
cards.a:
The program fails to start, with a message naming the missing DLL

Load-time dependencies are resolved before `main` runs. Run-time loading lets a program cope with a missing DLL.
cards.lessonTitle: Dynamic Libraries: Building and Loading Your Own DLL

cards.q: Why should `DllMain` do as little as possible?
cards.a:
It runs under the loader lock, where waiting can deadlock

Do real setup in a separate exported function the program calls after loading.
cards.lessonTitle: Dynamic Libraries: Building and Loading Your Own DLL

cards.q: What three jobs does vcpkg do for each dependency?
cards.a:
Downloads the source, builds it to match the project's triplet, and connects headers, libraries and DLLs to the project

The triplet describes platform and runtime, so the library is built to match the project's settings.

cards.q: What does manifest mode mean?
cards.a:
The project's dependencies are listed in `vcpkg.json`, and vcpkg installs them automatically on build

The manifest lives with the project, so anyone who builds it gets the same dependencies.

cards.q: Which files from vcpkg belong in version control?
cards.a:
`vcpkg.json` (and `vcpkg-configuration.json` if present), not the `vcpkg_installed` output

The manifest is enough to recreate the build output, which is large and machine-specific.

cards.q: What does `vcpkg.json` describe?
cards.a:
The libraries a project depends on

Anyone building the project gets the same dependencies from the manifest.

cards.q: What is a vcpkg triplet?
cards.a:
The target platform and linking, e.g. `x64-windows-static`

It ensures the libraries are built to match the project.

cards.q: Why add a baseline to the manifest?
cards.a:
To pin library versions for later builds

Without it, versions follow whatever vcpkg copy is installed.

cards.q: How does Windows involve the debugger when a breakpoint is hit?
cards.a:
The `int 3` instruction raises a breakpoint exception, and Windows delivers it to the attached debugger

The debugger writes `int 3` over the instruction at the breakpoint; because a debugger is attached, Windows hands it the event instead of the program.
cards.lessonTitle: The Debugger: Breakpoints, Stepping and the Call Stack

cards.q: How do you find out why a function was called with a bad argument?
cards.a:
In the Call Stack window, double-click the caller's frame and look at its variables in Locals and Watch

The caller's frame shows where the bad value came from, which is usually where the real bug is.
cards.lessonTitle: The Debugger: Breakpoints, Stepping and the Call Stack

cards.q: Why attach to a process instead of starting it in the debugger?
cards.a:
When the bug appears only after a while, or another program starts it

Debug, Attach to Process lets you join a program already running, in whatever state it has reached.
cards.lessonTitle: The Debugger: Breakpoints, Stepping and the Call Stack

cards.q: What does the debugger write into your program's code to make a breakpoint?
cards.a:
The byte `0xCC` (`int 3`) over the instruction's first byte

The CPU raises an exception when it executes `int 3`, and Windows passes it to the debugger.
cards.lessonTitle: The Debugger: Breakpoints, Stepping and the Call Stack

cards.q: A line calls three functions. How do you step into only the second?
cards.a:
Right-click → Step Into Specific, and choose it

Step Into Specific lists every call on the line.
cards.lessonTitle: The Debugger: Breakpoints, Stepping and the Call Stack

cards.q: Your game freezes. What do you do in the debugger first?
cards.a:
Break All, then read each thread's stack

Break All pauses the program wherever it is, which shows what it is stuck doing.
cards.lessonTitle: The Debugger: Breakpoints, Stepping and the Call Stack

cards.q: Where do you go to stop as soon as any C++ exception is thrown, even if it is caught later?
cards.a:
Exception Settings, ticking C++ Exceptions

By default the debugger only stops on unhandled exceptions.
cards.lessonTitle: The Debugger: Breakpoints, Stepping and the Call Stack

cards.q: What are format specifiers for?
cards.a:
Changing how Watch shows a value: hex, arrays, strings

For example `data,20` shows 20 elements of `data`, and `x,h` shows `x` in hex. The program itself is not changed.
cards.lessonTitle: Watch, Locals, Memory and Registers Windows

cards.q: Which registers hold the first four integer arguments on x64 Windows, and which the return value?
cards.a:
RCX, RDX, R8 and R9 for the arguments; RAX for the return value

RDI, RSI, RDX, RCX is the Linux convention; Windows uses RCX, RDX, R8, R9.
cards.lessonTitle: Watch, Locals, Memory and Registers Windows

cards.q: What does the Disassembly window show?
cards.a:
The generated instructions, interleaved with source lines

You can also show each instruction's bytes, and step one instruction at a time with F10 while it has focus.
cards.lessonTitle: Watch, Locals, Memory and Registers Windows

cards.q: How do you see 20 elements of an `int* data` in the Watch window?
cards.a:
Type `data,20`

The `,N` format specifier shows N elements starting at the pointer.
cards.lessonTitle: Watch, Locals, Memory and Registers Windows

cards.q: Which register holds the address of the next instruction to run?
cards.a:
RIP

RIP is the instruction pointer; RSP is the stack pointer.
cards.lessonTitle: Watch, Locals, Memory and Registers Windows

cards.q: You just stepped out of a function. Where can you see what it returned?
cards.a:
In `$ReturnValue`, or the Autos window

The debugger records the return value as you step out or over a call.
cards.lessonTitle: Watch, Locals, Memory and Registers Windows

cards.q: What does F10 do while the Disassembly window has focus?
cards.a:
Steps one machine instruction

In the Disassembly window, stepping is per instruction.
cards.lessonTitle: Watch, Locals, Memory and Registers Windows

cards.q: What is the difference between a breakpoint and a data breakpoint?
cards.a:
A data breakpoint stops when an address is written, by any code

A data breakpoint answers "who changed this?", which an ordinary breakpoint cannot. A tracepoint is the one that prints without stopping.

cards.q: What are the hardware limits on data breakpoints?
cards.a:
Four at a time, each covering 1, 2, 4 or 8 bytes at an address aligned to that size

The CPU has four debug address registers, which is where the limit comes from.

cards.q: How would you find the code that writes past the end of a heap block?
cards.a:
Set a data breakpoint on the bytes just after the block's end

The debugger then stops on the exact instruction that writes there.

cards.q: How do you make a breakpoint stop only on the 500th time it is reached?
cards.a:
Give it a hit count condition of `= 500`

Hit counts let the debugger count for you.

cards.q: What does a tracepoint do?
cards.a:
Prints a message, with values, without stopping

It is logging added from the debugger, without changing the code.

cards.q: Why can there be at most four data breakpoints at once?
cards.a:
They use the CPU's four debug address registers

The processor checks memory accesses against `DR0` to `DR3` in hardware.

cards.q: A data breakpoint is set on a local variable, and its function returns. What does the breakpoint watch now?
cards.a:
The same address, now reused by other stack data

Data breakpoints watch addresses, not variables.

cards.q: What is the as-if rule?
cards.a:
The compiler may transform the program any way that does not change its observable behaviour, provided it has no undefined behaviour

If the program has undefined behaviour, the optimiser's transformations can change what you see, which is why some bugs only show in Release.
cards.lessonTitle: Debug and Release Builds: What Optimisation Changes

cards.q: Name four things the optimiser does.
cards.a:
Keeps variables in registers, inlines functions, folds constants, removes dead code (also loop transforms and reordering)

The first group describes what a Debug build adds, the opposite of optimisation.
cards.lessonTitle: Debug and Release Builds: What Optimisation Changes

cards.q: How do you make a Release build debuggable without slowing it down?
cards.a:
Generate debug information with `/Zi`, which changes no code

Debug information goes in a separate `.pdb` and does not change the generated code. `assert` is removed in Release. Use `#pragma optimize("", off)` around one function that needs closer inspection.
cards.lessonTitle: Debug and Release Builds: What Optimisation Changes

cards.q: Why does the debugger say "variable is optimised away" in Release?
cards.a:
It lives only in a register, or was removed

With `/Zi` the debugger can sometimes still find it in a register, but not always.
cards.lessonTitle: Debug and Release Builds: What Optimisation Changes

cards.q: A program works in Debug and crashes in Release. What is the most likely cause?
cards.a:
Undefined behaviour that Debug happened to tolerate

Uninitialised values, overruns and data races behave differently once code is optimised.
cards.lessonTitle: Debug and Release Builds: What Optimisation Changes

cards.q: What happens to `assert(x > 0);` in a Release build?
cards.a:
It is removed entirely, because `NDEBUG` is defined

Asserts are a Debug-only safety net.
cards.lessonTitle: Debug and Release Builds: What Optimisation Changes

cards.q: What does inlining do?
cards.a:
Replaces a call with a copy of the called function's body

No call happens, which is faster and lets the optimiser work across the two.
cards.lessonTitle: Debug and Release Builds: What Optimisation Changes

cards.q: Why does Windows give programs handles instead of pointers to kernel objects?
cards.a:
Kernel memory is off-limits; a handle lets the kernel check each use

A pointer into kernel memory would be useless to user-mode code, and it would skip the kernel's permission check.

cards.q: What happens to a process's open handles when it exits?
cards.a:
Windows closes them all, and any object whose last handle that was is destroyed

Leaked handles are still a bug while the program runs, but they do not outlive the process.

cards.q: Why does the `UniqueHandle` class treat both `nullptr` and `INVALID_HANDLE_VALUE` as empty?
cards.a:
Because different Windows functions use different values to mean failure

`CreateFileW` fails with `INVALID_HANDLE_VALUE`, many others with null, so checking both makes the class safe whatever produced the handle.

cards.q: What is a handle?
cards.a:
A per-process number naming a kernel object it opened

The object lives in kernel memory; the handle is how your process names it.

cards.q: What does `CreateFileW` return when it fails?
cards.a:
`INVALID_HANDLE_VALUE`

Most other creation functions return `nullptr`; `CreateFileW` is one of the exceptions.

cards.q: A kernel object has two open handles. One is closed. What happens to the object?
cards.a:
Nothing yet: it goes when its last handle closes

Kernel objects are reference-counted.

cards.q: Why wrap handles in an RAII class?
cards.a:
So they are closed exactly once, automatically, on every path out of the scope

The destructor guarantees `CloseHandle` runs, even on early returns and exceptions.

cards.q: Name the three main ways Windows API functions report failure.
cards.a:
A `BOOL` returning `FALSE`, a null or invalid handle, or an `HRESULT` with its severity bit set

For the first two, `GetLastError` gives the reason. Windows API functions do not throw C++ exceptions.
cards.lessonTitle: Errors, GetLastError and Reading the Documentation

cards.q: What are the three fields of an HRESULT?
cards.a:
Severity, facility (which subsystem) and code
