In `0x80070005` the top bit says failure, facility 7 is Win32, and code 5 is access denied.
cards.lessonTitle: Errors, GetLastError and Reading the Documentation

cards.q: What is the two-call pattern?
cards.a:
Calling once to learn how big a buffer the result needs, then allocating it and calling again

Many functions report the required size when given a buffer that is too small or null.
cards.lessonTitle: Errors, GetLastError and Reading the Documentation

cards.q: A function returns `FALSE`. How do you find out why?
cards.a:
Call `GetLastError()` immediately afterwards

Many Windows functions record the reason per thread, for `GetLastError` to read.
cards.lessonTitle: Errors, GetLastError and Reading the Documentation

cards.q: What does `0x80070005` mean?
cards.a:
A failure HRESULT for Win32 error 5, access denied

Severity bit set, facility 7 (Win32), code 5.
cards.lessonTitle: Errors, GetLastError and Reading the Documentation

cards.q: Which section of a documentation page says whether to call `GetLastError`?
cards.a:
Return value

It describes what success and failure look like for that particular function.
cards.lessonTitle: Errors, GetLastError and Reading the Documentation

cards.q: Why use `FAILED(hr)` instead of `hr != 0`?
cards.a:
Some success codes, such as `S_FALSE`, are not zero

Only the severity bit separates success from failure.
cards.lessonTitle: Errors, GetLastError and Reading the Documentation

cards.q: Which of the A and W versions does Windows implement natively, and why does it matter?
cards.a:
The W versions; A converts via the code page and can lose characters

A file name with characters outside the code page cannot be opened reliably through an A function.
cards.lessonTitle: Strings on Windows: ANSI, UTF-16 and UTF-8

cards.q: What is the usual strategy for text in a Windows program?
cards.a:
Keep text as UTF-8 internally, convert to UTF-16 just before calling W functions, and convert results back

UTF-8 matches the rest of the world's files and libraries; the conversion happens only at the Windows boundary.
cards.lessonTitle: Strings on Windows: ANSI, UTF-16 and UTF-8

cards.q: What is a surrogate pair?
cards.a:
Two UTF-16 units that together encode one code point above U+FFFF

That is why `std::wstring{ L"😀" }.size()` can be 2: one character, two UTF-16 units.
cards.lessonTitle: Strings on Windows: ANSI, UTF-16 and UTF-8

cards.q: What does `CreateFileA` do with its file name?
cards.a:
Converts it from the code page to UTF-16 and calls `CreateFileW`

Windows works in UTF-16 internally; the A functions are converting wrappers.
cards.lessonTitle: Strings on Windows: ANSI, UTF-16 and UTF-8

cards.q: How many bytes does UTF-8 use for the character `é` (U+00E9)?
cards.a:
2

U+0080 to U+07FF take two bytes in UTF-8.
cards.lessonTitle: Strings on Windows: ANSI, UTF-16 and UTF-8

cards.q: A program keeps all its text as UTF-8. What should it do to open a file whose name the user typed?
cards.a:
Convert it to UTF-16 and call `CreateFileW`

Convert at the boundary, then call the W function.
cards.lessonTitle: Strings on Windows: ANSI, UTF-16 and UTF-8

cards.q: Why can `std::wstring{ L"😀" }.size()` be 2?
cards.a:
The emoji is above U+FFFF, so UTF-16 needs a surrogate pair of two units

Only code points up to U+FFFF fit in one UTF-16 unit.
cards.lessonTitle: Strings on Windows: ANSI, UTF-16 and UTF-8

cards.q: What does the share mode in `CreateFileW` control?
cards.a:
What other handles may do with the file while this one is open

A share mode of 0 locks others out completely, which is why another program can fail with error 32 (sharing violation).

cards.q: Where should a Windows game keep save files and settings?
cards.a:
Saves in Saved Games; settings and logs under AppData

The installation folder is usually not writable by normal users, and different users need their own saves. Both folders are found with `SHGetKnownFolderPath`.

cards.q: When would you use the Windows file API instead of `std::fstream` and `std::filesystem`?
cards.a:
When you need share modes, async I/O, mapped files or exact error codes

The standard library is portable and fine for most work; the Windows API exposes features it does not.

cards.q: Which creation disposition opens a file if it exists and creates it if not?
cards.a:
`OPEN_ALWAYS`

`CREATE_ALWAYS` also creates when missing, but truncates an existing file to empty.

cards.q: Another program cannot open your game's log while the game runs, getting error 32. Why?
cards.a:
The game's share mode does not allow others to read

Error 32 is a sharing violation: the existing handle's share mode forbids it.

cards.q: Why should save files not be written to the game's installation folder?
cards.a:
Under Program Files it is read-only for normal users

Use the per-user Saved Games or AppData folders.

cards.q: How do you update a save file so a crash can never leave it half-written?
cards.a:
Write a temporary file fully, then swap it in one step

The move or replace is atomic: the file is always either the old version or the new one.

cards.q: What is a window procedure?
cards.a:
The callback Windows calls with each message for the class

`DispatchMessageW` delivers each message to it.

cards.q: How does a message loop end?
cards.a:
`PostQuitMessage` queues `WM_QUIT`; `GetMessageW` then returns 0

A window closing does not end the loop by itself, which is why a process can keep running after its window has gone.

cards.q: How does a game's loop differ from a classic message loop?
cards.a:
It drains messages with `PeekMessageW`, then runs one frame

`GetMessageW` waits until a message arrives, which would freeze the game whenever nothing happens.

cards.q: What does `DispatchMessageW` do?
cards.a:
Calls the window procedure of the window the message is for

It finds the window's class and calls the function registered for it.

cards.q: A program's window closes but the process keeps running. What is the most likely cause?
cards.a:
`WM_DESTROY` never calls `PostQuitMessage`

The loop keeps waiting for messages for a window that no longer exists.

cards.q: Why do games use `PeekMessageW` instead of `GetMessageW`?
cards.a:
It returns at once when the queue is empty, so frames keep running

A game must update continuously, not only when messages arrive.

cards.q: What should a window procedure do with a message it does not handle?
cards.a:
Pass it to `DefWindowProcW` and return that

The default procedure implements the standard window behaviour.

cards.q: What are the main steps of a Win32 program's start-up?
cards.a:
Register a window class with a window procedure, create a window of that class, show it, then run the message loop

A window can only be created from a class that has already been registered.

cards.q: What is the client area of a window?
cards.a:
The part inside the borders and title bar, where the program draws

That is why `AdjustWindowRect` is used: to make the client area the size you want, the whole window must be a little larger.

cards.q: What must you do with every GDI object you create?
cards.a:
Delete it when finished, after deselecting it from any device context it was selected into

GDI objects are a limited resource; leaking them every frame eventually stops drawing working.

cards.q: Why does the program call `AdjustWindowRect` before `CreateWindowExW`?
cards.a:
The size includes borders, so it must grow to fit the client area

The client area is the drawable part inside the frame.

cards.q: What does drawing into an off-screen bitmap and copying it with `BitBlt` prevent?
cards.a:
Flicker: no half-drawn frame is ever shown

This technique is called double buffering.

cards.q: Why does the square move by `velocity * dt`?
cards.a:
So its speed is the same at any frame rate

A fixed step per frame would make it faster on faster computers.

cards.q: What is a virtual-key code?
cards.a:
A layout-independent number for a key, given in `wParam`

For typed text, use `WM_CHAR`, which carries the character; the virtual-key code names the key itself. Letter keys use their upper-case ASCII code.

cards.q: Where are a mouse message's coordinates, and in what coordinate system?
cards.a:
In `lParam` as two signed 16-bit halves, relative to the client area

They are signed because a captured mouse can be left of or above the client area; `GET_X_LPARAM` reads them as signed.

cards.q: When should a game read input from messages and when from the current key state?
cards.a:
Messages for presses and typing; the current state for held keys

A single press must not be missed, which messages guarantee; holding a key is about what is true right now.

cards.q: A key held down produces many `WM_KEYDOWN` messages. How do you tell the first one from the repeats?
cards.a:
Bit 30 of `lParam` is 0 for the first and 1 for repeats

Bit 30 records whether the key was already down.

cards.q: The player types `é`. Which message carries that character?
cards.a:
`WM_CHAR`

`TranslateMessage` turns key presses into characters according to the keyboard layout.

cards.q: Why use `GET_X_LPARAM` instead of `LOWORD` for a mouse x coordinate?
cards.a:
It reads the 16 bits as signed, so negatives work

Coordinates can be negative while the mouse is captured outside the window.

cards.q: Which is the right clock for measuring frame times?
cards.a:
`QueryPerformanceCounter`

It has sub-microsecond resolution; the others are about 15 ms coarse. `std::chrono::steady_clock` is a portable equivalent.

cards.q: What is DLL search-order hijacking, and how do you prevent it?
cards.a:
Planting a DLL in a folder searched first; prevented by restricting the search

The program loads whichever DLL with that name it finds first, so the defence is controlling where it looks. Use `SetDefaultDllDirectories`, full paths, and folders untrusted users cannot write to.

cards.q: What is an `HMODULE`?
cards.a:
The address at which a module (an exe or DLL) is loaded in the process; its headers start there

That is why `GetModuleHandleW(nullptr)` gives the base address of the program's own image.

cards.q: How can a program use a function that might not exist on the user's version of Windows?
cards.a:
Look it up with `GetProcAddress` and call it only if found

A direct call to a missing function makes the program fail to start; a run-time lookup lets it carry on without it.

cards.q: Why is the current working directory in the DLL search order a security risk?
cards.a:
Whoever controls that folder can plant a DLL there

This is DLL search-order hijacking.

cards.q: What does `GetModuleHandleW(nullptr)` return?
cards.a:
The load address of the program's own `.exe`

It is the same value as the `HINSTANCE` given to `wWinMain`.

cards.q: A game wants to use a function that only exists on Windows 11 but still start on Windows 10. What should it do?
cards.a:
Find it with `GetProcAddress` and use it only if found

A normal import of a missing function stops the program from starting at all.

cards.q: What does delay loading do?
cards.a:
Loads a DLL the first time one of its functions is called, instead of at start-up

Unused DLLs are never loaded, and a missing optional DLL does not stop the program starting.

cards.q: What are virtual terminal sequences?
cards.a:
Escape-character strings the console treats as commands

`\x1b[5;10H`, for example, moves the cursor to row 5, column 10 instead of printing anything.

cards.q: How does a console game read single key presses without blocking?
cards.a:
It reads waiting events with `ReadConsoleInputW`, only if any wait

`std::cin` waits for Enter; reading the console's input events gives each key press as it happens. `GetNumberOfConsoleInputEvents` says whether any are waiting.

cards.q: How can a windowed game show `std::cout` output during development?
cards.a:
Call `AllocConsole` to create a console and reopen `stdout` on `CONOUT$`

A windowed program has no console by default; `AllocConsole` creates one and reopening `stdout` sends output there.

cards.q: What does the sequence `\x1b[5;10H` do?
cards.a:
Moves the cursor to row 5, column 10

`H` positions the cursor; escape-sequence rows and columns start at 1.

cards.q: How do you avoid flicker when redrawing a text-mode game screen?
cards.a:
Build the whole frame as one string and write it once

The console then shows complete frames only.

cards.q: Why use `ReadConsoleInputW` instead of `std::cin` for a text-mode game?
cards.a:
It gives single key events without waiting for Enter

Games need each key press as it happens.

cards.q: What is the difference between a program, a process and a module?
cards.a:
A file; a running instance with its own memory; an exe or DLL mapped into one

Two copies of the same game are one program file and two processes, each with its own modules mapped in.

cards.q: What does `CreateProcessW` give back, and what must you do with it?
cards.a:
Process and thread handles plus ids; both handles must be closed

Forgetting to close the two handles keeps the kernel objects alive even after the child exits.

cards.q: Why must arguments containing spaces be quoted?
cards.a:
The new process splits its one command-line string on spaces

`game.exe C:\My Games\save.dat` arrives as two arguments unless the path is in quotes.

cards.q: Two copies of the same game are running. How many processes and how many program files are there?
cards.a:
Two processes, one program file

Each running instance is its own process with its own address space.

cards.q: How do you wait for a child process to finish?
cards.a:
`WaitForSingleObject` on its process handle

Process handles are waitable kernel objects.

cards.q: A child process's exit code is 3221225477 (`0xC0000005`). What happened?
cards.a:
It crashed with an access violation

`0xC0000005` is the status code for an access violation.

cards.q: What is the difference between a process id and a process handle?
cards.a:
An id is a system-wide number; a handle is a reference with rights

Windows checks rights when the handle is opened. Handles come from `OpenProcess` or `CreateProcessW` and must be closed.

cards.q: How many bytes is a page on x64 Windows, and how many bits of an address are the offset within it?
cards.a:
4,096 bytes; the low 12 bits

2 to the power of 12 is 4,096, so 12 bits are needed to pick a byte within a page. 64 KB is the allocation granularity, not the page size.

cards.q: What is a canonical address?
cards.a:
One whose bits 48 to 63 all copy bit 47

Only canonical addresses are valid, which is why user-mode pointers on x64 start with `0000`. User-mode addresses are in the lower half, kernel ones in the upper half.

cards.q: What happens when a program touches a page that was paged out to disk?
cards.a:
A page fault: the kernel reads it back and resumes the program

The program only notices a delay; to it the memory was always there.

cards.q: What does the MMU replace when it translates an address?
cards.a:
The page number, with a physical frame number

Translation works page by page.

cards.q: Why does every user-mode pointer on x64 Windows start with `0000`?
cards.a:
User addresses are low, so the top 16 bits are zero

Canonical user-mode addresses have bits 48 to 63 equal to bit 47, which is 0.

cards.q: What is a demand-zero page fault?
cards.a:
A first touch of committed memory, given a zeroed page

It is invisible to the program, apart from a tiny delay.

cards.q: Why are page tables a tree rather than one flat array?
cards.a:
So only the parts of the address space in use need tables

A flat table for 48-bit addresses would need billions of entries per process.

cards.q: What are the three states a page can be in?
cards.a:
Free, reserved and committed

Read, write and execute are protections, which only apply to committed pages.

cards.q: What is a guard page used for?
cards.a:
An inaccessible page after a buffer or stack, so overruns fault at once

Faulting at the exact moment of the overrun shows where the bug is instead of letting it corrupt other data.

cards.q: Why reserve a large region and commit it gradually?
cards.a:
The data never moves as it grows, and unused space costs nothing

Reserving only sets addresses aside; memory is used only for the pages actually committed.

cards.q: What is the difference between reserving and committing memory?
cards.a:
Reserving sets addresses aside; committing backs them with memory

Reserved pages still fault on access; committed pages are usable.

cards.q: A 1 GB region is reserved and two pages committed. Roughly how much memory does the program use for it?
cards.a:
About 8 KB, once those pages are touched

Only committed pages are backed, and only touched pages take RAM.

cards.q: Why are code pages not writable?
cards.a:
So bugs or attacks cannot change or plant code

Keeping writable and executable apart is a basic defence.

cards.q: What happens when a program writes to a `PAGE_NOACCESS` page?
cards.a:
An access violation, at the exact instruction that tried

That is what makes no-access guard pages useful for catching overruns.

cards.q: What three memory types does `VirtualQuery` report, and what is each?
cards.a:
`MEM_IMAGE` (a loaded exe or DLL), `MEM_MAPPED` (a mapped file) and `MEM_PRIVATE` (heaps, stacks, `VirtualAlloc`)

Free, reserved and committed are the page states, reported separately; the type says what backs the memory.
cards.lessonTitle: Exploring Your Own Process with VirtualQuery

cards.q: Why does one DLL show up as several regions?
cards.a:
Its sections have different protections, and regions share one

Code is execute-read, constants read-only and data read-write, so the DLL splits into a region for each.
cards.lessonTitle: Exploring Your Own Process with VirtualQuery

cards.q: How can a tool tell which module a code address belongs to?
cards.a:
Query it; a `MEM_IMAGE` region's `AllocationBase` is the module

The allocation base of an image region is where the module was loaded, and that is exactly its `HMODULE`.
cards.lessonTitle: Exploring Your Own Process with VirtualQuery

cards.q: What does `VirtualQuery` describe?
cards.a:
The run of pages with the same attributes around the address

A region is a run of pages with identical attributes.
cards.lessonTitle: Exploring Your Own Process with VirtualQuery

cards.q: A pointer's region has type `MEM_IMAGE` and protection `PAGE_EXECUTE_READ`. What does it point at?
cards.a:
Code inside a loaded exe or DLL

Image regions are modules; execute permission means the code section.
cards.lessonTitle: Exploring Your Own Process with VirtualQuery

cards.q: How do you get from one region to the next when walking the address space?
cards.a:
Query at `BaseAddress + RegionSize` of the current region

Regions are consecutive and cover the whole space, free parts included.
cards.lessonTitle: Exploring Your Own Process with VirtualQuery

cards.q: What is a context switch?
cards.a:
Saving one thread's registers and loading another's on a core

Each thread's own state is its registers and stack, so switching threads means swapping register sets.

cards.q: Why do games use a fixed set of worker threads instead of creating a thread per task?
cards.a:
Creating threads is slow and costly; reused workers avoid that

Tasks are small and frequent, so paying thread creation for each would cost more than the work.

cards.q: What must happen to a `std::thread` before it is destroyed?
cards.a:
It must be joined or detached, or the program terminates

A `std::thread` that is still joinable when destroyed calls `std::terminate`. (`std::jthread` is the one that joins in its destructor.)

cards.q: What does each thread have that is not shared with the other threads of its process?
cards.a:
Its registers and its stack

Heap, globals, code and handles are shared; registers and stack are per thread.

cards.q: Why does the summing example give each thread its own slot in `partial`?
cards.a:
So no two threads write the same memory

Separate outputs, combined after `join`, is the simplest safe pattern.

cards.q: A thread calls `Sleep(5)`. What happens on its core?
cards.a:
The scheduler runs another ready thread there

A waiting thread gives up the core immediately.

cards.q: What does `std::thread::hardware_concurrency()` tell you?
cards.a:
How many threads the processor can run truly in parallel

More CPU-bound threads than this only take turns.

cards.q: What is a data race?
cards.a:
Unsynchronised access to the same memory, at least one a write

In C++ a data race is undefined behaviour. Two threads waiting for each other is a deadlock.

cards.q: Why should a mutex always be locked through an RAII guard?
cards.a:
So it is released on every path out, including exceptions

A forgotten unlock freezes every other thread that needs the mutex.

cards.q: How do you prevent deadlocks between two mutexes?
cards.a:
Lock them in the same order everywhere, or with `std::scoped_lock`

Deadlock needs two threads taking the locks in opposite orders, so a consistent order makes it impossible.

cards.q: Why can two threads doing `++score` lose updates?
cards.a:
Both can read the same old value before writing

Without synchronisation, the steps of the two threads interleave.

cards.q: When is `std::atomic` enough on its own?
cards.a:
For one value changed by indivisible operations, like a counter

Changes involving several values need a mutex around all of them.

cards.q: Thread 1 holds mutex A and waits for B; thread 2 holds B and waits for A. What is this?
cards.a:
A deadlock

Taking locks in a consistent order, or with `std::scoped_lock`, prevents it.

cards.q: What is the difference between a manual-reset and an auto-reset event?
cards.a:
Manual-reset releases every waiter until reset; auto-reset releases one

Choose by whether one or all waiting threads should proceed.

cards.q: What two steps does the Tool Help API use?
cards.a:
Take a snapshot with `CreateToolhelp32Snapshot`, then walk it with the matching First and Next functions

The snapshot is a copy taken at one moment, so it does not change while you walk it.

cards.q: What does a module entry tell you?
cards.a:
The module's name, path, base address and size

Base and size are what turn a raw crash address into "module + offset".

cards.q: Why can holding only a process id be risky?
cards.a:
When the process ends its id can be reused, so the id might later refer to a different process

A handle keeps the process object alive and always refers to the same process; an id is only a number.

cards.q: What does `CreateToolhelp32Snapshot` capture?
cards.a:
A copy of the chosen information (processes, threads or modules) at one moment

You walk the copy; later changes are not reflected.

cards.q: Two processes are both called `game.exe`. How do you tell them apart?
cards.a:
By their process ids, and if needed their full paths

File names are not unique; ids are unique among running processes.

cards.q: Why is "module + offset" more useful in a crash report than a raw address?
cards.a:
Load addresses vary, but offsets match the symbols

The offset can be looked up in the matching `.pdb` to find the source line.

cards.q: What three things does the access check compare?
cards.a:
The process's token, the object's security descriptor, and the rights requested

The token says who the process is, the descriptor says who may do what, and the request says what is wanted now.
cards.lessonTitle: Access Rights, Tokens and Why Windows Says No

cards.q: What is the principle of least privilege?
cards.a:
Requesting and holding only the rights the code actually needs

Asking for less means requests succeed for ordinary users, and a compromised program can do less harm.
cards.lessonTitle: Access Rights, Tokens and Why Windows Says No

cards.q: What is a protected process?
cards.a:
One the kernel shields even from administrators

Anti-cheat and DRM components often run this way. The protection comes from the kernel, not from rights on the object. Its memory cannot be read, injected into or debugged by other processes.
cards.lessonTitle: Access Rights, Tokens and Why Windows Says No

cards.q: When does Windows check whether you may write to a file?
cards.a:
When the handle is opened with write access requested

The access check happens at open time.
cards.lessonTitle: Access Rights, Tokens and Why Windows Says No

cards.q: A program running as a normal user asks for `GENERIC_ALL` on a file it may only read. What happens?
cards.a:
The open fails with access denied

Windows grants all of the requested rights or none.
cards.lessonTitle: Access Rights, Tokens and Why Windows Says No

cards.q: What does UAC elevation change?
cards.a:
The process gets the full administrator token

Without elevation, an administrator's programs run with the administrator group disabled.
cards.lessonTitle: Access Rights, Tokens and Why Windows Says No

cards.q: Why can even an administrator not read the memory of a protected process?
cards.a:
The kernel enforces it whatever the caller's token

Protected Process Light shields security components from tampering.
cards.lessonTitle: Access Rights, Tokens and Why Windows Says No

cards.q: What is ASLR and why does it exist?
cards.a:
Loading modules, heaps and stacks at different addresses each run, so attackers cannot rely on knowing where code or data is

Addresses differ between runs but stay fixed for the life of one run.
cards.lessonTitle: Address Space Layout Randomisation and Base Addresses

cards.q: What is an RVA?
cards.a:
An offset from a module's start, the same wherever it loads

Address minus module base gives the RVA, which is why crash reports use "module + offset".
cards.lessonTitle: Address Space Layout Randomisation and Base Addresses

cards.q: What do relocations do?
cards.a:
They list absolute addresses inside a module, for the loader to adjust

Most x64 code uses addresses relative to the instruction pointer and needs no relocation; only stored absolute addresses do.
cards.lessonTitle: Address Space Layout Randomisation and Base Addresses

cards.q: What stays the same between two runs of a program with ASLR?
cards.a:
Each function's offset from its module's start

Modules move as a whole; everything inside keeps its offset.
cards.lessonTitle: Address Space Layout Randomisation and Base Addresses

cards.q: Why does most x64 code not need relocating when it is loaded at a new address?
cards.a:
It uses RIP-relative offsets, which do not change when it moves

Only stored absolute addresses, listed in the relocation table, need fixing up.
cards.lessonTitle: Address Space Layout Randomisation and Base Addresses

cards.q: `game.exe` is loaded at `0x00007FF600000000` and a crash is at `0x00007FF600012345`. What is the RVA?
cards.a:
`0x12345`

RVA = address − module base.
cards.lessonTitle: Address Space Layout Randomisation and Base Addresses

cards.q: Why must save files not contain raw pointers?
cards.a:
Addresses change between runs, so they mean nothing

Save ids or indices and rebuild pointers after loading.
cards.lessonTitle: Address Space Layout Randomisation and Base Addresses

cards.q: What is a register?
cards.a:
A small, fixed storage slot inside the processor itself

x64 has sixteen general-purpose 64-bit registers. Reading one needs no memory access at all, which is why arithmetic happens in them.
cards.lessonTitle: Registers and the Shape of an Instruction

cards.q: What are `eax`, `ax` and `al`?
cards.a:
The low 32, 16 and 8 bits of `rax`, usable as registers in their own right

Writing to `eax` also zeroes the top half of `rax`, which is why `mov eax, 2` leaves `rax` holding 2.
cards.lessonTitle: Registers and the Shape of an Instruction

cards.q: What three kinds of operand can an instruction have?
cards.a:
A register, an immediate constant, or a memory location

`byte`, `word` and `dword` describe operand sizes, not kinds of operand.
cards.lessonTitle: Registers and the Shape of an Instruction

cards.q: Which register holds a function's return value on x64 Windows?
cards.a:
`rax`

`rcx`, `rdx`, `r8` and `r9` bring arguments in; `rax` carries the result out.
cards.lessonTitle: Registers and the Shape of an Instruction

cards.q: `rax` holds -1 (all bits set). After `mov eax, 2`, what is in `rax`?
cards.a:
2

Writing a 32-bit register clears the upper 32 bits.
cards.lessonTitle: Registers and the Shape of an Instruction

cards.q: In `sub ecx, 10`, which operand receives the result?
cards.a:
`ecx`, the first operand

Intel syntax puts the destination first.
cards.lessonTitle: Registers and the Shape of an Instruction

cards.q: Which of these is a memory operand?
cards.a:
`qword ptr [rdx+16]`

Square brackets mean "the value at this address".
cards.lessonTitle: Registers and the Shape of an Instruction

cards.q: What four parts can a memory operand's address have?
cards.a:
A base register, an index register multiplied by 1, 2, 4 or 8, and a constant displacement

`[rcx+rdx*8+10h]` uses all of them: base `rcx`, index `rdx` scaled by 8, displacement `10h`.
cards.lessonTitle: Moving Data: mov, lea and Addressing Modes

cards.q: What is the difference between `movzx` and `movsx`?
cards.a:
Both widen; `movzx` fills with zeros, `movsx` with the sign bit

So the byte `0xFE` becomes 254 with `movzx` and -2 with `movsx`.
cards.lessonTitle: Moving Data: mov, lea and Addressing Modes

cards.q: What does `lea` do?
cards.a:
It computes a memory operand's address without reading memory

Because it only computes, compilers also use it for fast arithmetic such as `lea eax, [rcx+rcx*2]` for `x * 3`.
cards.lessonTitle: Moving Data: mov, lea and Addressing Modes

cards.q: What does `mov eax, dword ptr [rcx+8]` do?
cards.a:
Copies the 4 bytes at address rcx+8 into eax

The brackets read memory; `lea` would compute the address instead.
cards.lessonTitle: Moving Data: mov, lea and Addressing Modes

cards.q: The byte at `[rdx]` is `0xFE`. What does `movsx eax, byte ptr [rdx]` put in eax?
cards.a:
-2

Sign extension copies the top bit, so `0xFE` as a signed byte, -2, stays -2.
cards.lessonTitle: Moving Data: mov, lea and Addressing Modes

cards.q: Which C++ expression is `[rcx+rdx*8]` most likely to come from?
cards.a:
`p[i]` where `p` points at 8-byte values

Base, index and a scale equal to the element size: array indexing.
cards.lessonTitle: Moving Data: mov, lea and Addressing Modes

cards.q: Why might a compiler emit `lea eax, [rcx+rcx*2]`?
cards.a:
To compute `x * 3` in one instruction

`lea` does arithmetic with the address hardware and never touches memory.
cards.lessonTitle: Moving Data: mov, lea and Addressing Modes

cards.q: What is the difference between the carry flag and the overflow flag?
cards.a:
CF: the result does not fit unsigned; OF: it does not fit signed

The CPU does not know whether the bits are signed, so it reports both and the code picks the one it needs.

cards.q: Why do compilers avoid `div`?
cards.a:
Division is very slow, so it is replaced by faster operations

The replacement gives the same result, only faster. Division by a constant becomes shifts, masks or a multiply by a precomputed constant.

cards.q: How is `x % 8` computed for unsigned `x`?
cards.a:
With `and x, 7`

Keeping the low three bits gives the remainder after dividing by 8. `shr x, 3` would give the quotient, `x / 8`.

cards.q: After `mov al, 200` then `add al, 100`, which flag tells you the unsigned result did not fit?
cards.a:
CF

300 does not fit in a byte; the carry out of the top bit sets CF.

cards.q: What does `xor ecx, ecx` do?
cards.a:
Sets ecx to zero

Any value XOR itself is 0. It is the usual way to zero a register.

cards.q: A compiler turned `n / 16` into `shr eax, 4`. What does that tell you about `n`?
cards.a:
It is unsigned

A logical right shift divides an unsigned number by a power of two. A signed value would need a correction for negative numbers.

cards.q: Which instruction shifts right while keeping the sign of a negative number?
cards.a:
`sar`

Arithmetic shift right copies the sign bit into the new top bits.

cards.q: What do `cmp` and `test` compute, and what do they keep?
cards.a:
`cmp` subtracts and `test` ANDs their operands; both keep only the flags and throw the result away

That is why a conditional jump comes after them: it reads the flags they set.

cards.q: How can you tell from compiled code whether a comparison was signed or unsigned?
cards.a:
From the jump or set instruction that reads the flags: `l`/`g` are signed, `b`/`a` are unsigned

`cmp` is the same either way; the choice of `jl` or `jb` (and so on) shows how the bits were meant.

cards.q: What do `setcc` and `cmovcc` do?
cards.a:
`setcc` writes 1 or 0 by a condition; `cmovcc` copies only if it holds

Both avoid a branch, which can be faster when the condition is hard to predict.

cards.q: What does `test eax, eax` followed by `jz done` do?
cards.a:
Jumps to `done` if eax is zero

AND of a value with itself is zero only when the value is zero, setting ZF.

cards.q: After `cmp ecx, edx`, the compiler uses `ja`. What does that suggest about ecx and edx?
cards.a:
They are being compared as unsigned values

`ja`/`jb` are the unsigned conditions; `jg`/`jl` the signed ones.

cards.q: The C++ says `if (x == 0) { ... }`. Which jump is the compiler most likely to emit before the body?
cards.a:
`jne`, to skip the body

The jump goes around the body, so its condition is inverted.

cards.q: Why do compilers sometimes use `cmov` instead of a jump?
cards.a:
To avoid a branch that might be mispredicted

A mispredicted branch costs many cycles; a conditional move never mispredicts.

cards.q: What do `push` and `pop` do to `rsp`?
cards.a:
`push` subtracts 8 then stores; `pop` loads then adds 8

The stack grows towards lower addresses, so pushing moves `rsp` down.
cards.lessonTitle: The Stack, push, pop, call and ret

cards.q: What are a function's prologue and epilogue?
cards.a:
The code that saves registers and sets up the frame, and that undoes it

The epilogue undoes the prologue in reverse order.
cards.lessonTitle: The Stack, push, pop, call and ret

cards.q: Why can a stack buffer overrun make a program jump to a random address?
cards.a:
The overrun can overwrite the return address above the locals, and `ret` then jumps to whatever is there

`ret` trusts whatever value is at the top of the stack. Stack cookies exist to detect this before `ret` runs.
cards.lessonTitle: The Stack, push, pop, call and ret

cards.q: What does `call square` push onto the stack?
cards.a:
The address of the instruction after the call

`ret` later pops it to continue after the call.
cards.lessonTitle: The Stack, push, pop, call and ret

cards.q: A function's prologue is `push rbx` then `push rsi`. In what order must its epilogue restore them?
cards.a:
`pop rsi`, then `pop rbx`

The stack is last in, first out.
cards.lessonTitle: The Stack, push, pop, call and ret

cards.q: What does a stack cookie protect?
cards.a:
The return address, from stack overruns

The epilogue checks the cookie and stops the program if it changed.
cards.lessonTitle: The Stack, push, pop, call and ret

cards.q: In `square` above, why does the function push and pop `rbx`?
cards.a:
`rbx` is non-volatile, so it must be preserved

Functions may use non-volatile registers only if they restore them.
cards.lessonTitle: The Stack, push, pop, call and ret

cards.q: Which registers carry the first four arguments?
cards.a:
`rcx`, `rdx`, `r8`, `r9` for integers and pointers; `xmm0` to `xmm3` for floating point, by position

"By position" means a `double` as the second argument goes in `xmm1`, and `rdx` is then left unused. `rdi`, `rsi` first is the Linux convention.

cards.q: What is shadow space?
cards.a:
32 bytes the caller reserves on the stack above the return address, where the callee may store its four register arguments

The caller always reserves it, even if the called function takes fewer than four arguments.

cards.q: What is the difference between volatile and non-volatile registers?
cards.a:
A callee may overwrite volatile ones but must preserve non-volatile ones

So a caller that needs a value across a call keeps it in a non-volatile register such as `rbx`, or saves it itself.

cards.q: Where is the third argument of `void f(int a, int b, int c, int d, int e)`?
cards.a:
`r8`

rcx, rdx, r8, r9 for the first four; the fifth goes on the stack.

cards.q: Where is `y` in `void g(int x, double y)`?
cards.a:
`xmm1`, because it is the second argument

The position decides the register.

cards.q: In `player.heal(25)`, which register holds 25?
cards.a:
`rdx`, as `this` is in `rcx`

The hidden `this` is the first argument.

cards.q: A function changes `rbx` and `r10`. Which must it restore before returning?
cards.a:
Only `rbx`

`rbx` is non-volatile; `r10` is volatile and may be destroyed.

cards.q: What is a basic block?
cards.a:
Straight-line code with one entry at the top and one exit

Nothing jumps into the middle or out of the middle of a basic block, which makes blocks the boxes of a control-flow graph.
cards.lessonTitle: Reading Compiler Output: if, Loops and switch

cards.q: How does a compiler implement `a && b`?
cards.a:
With jumps: if `a` is false, skip straight past `b` and the body

`&&` must not evaluate `b` when `a` is false, so the code jumps over it.
cards.lessonTitle: Reading Compiler Output: if, Loops and switch

cards.q: What three parts make up a jump table's code?
cards.a:
A range check, a load from a table, and an indirect jump

The range check is one unsigned compare and jump to the default case, which also catches negative values.
cards.lessonTitle: Reading Compiler Output: if, Loops and switch

cards.q: What is the signature of a loop in disassembly?
cards.a:
A conditional jump backwards

Looping means going back to code that already ran.
cards.lessonTitle: Reading Compiler Output: if, Loops and switch

cards.q: Why does a rotated loop have a test before the loop as well as at the bottom?
cards.a:
To skip the loop entirely when it should run zero times

The bottom test decides whether to go round again; the guard handles the zero-iteration case.
cards.lessonTitle: Reading Compiler Output: if, Loops and switch

cards.q: Two conditional jumps lead to the same label just before a `call`. What C++ is this likely to be?
cards.a:
`if (a && b) call();`

Either condition failing skips the call.
cards.lessonTitle: Reading Compiler Output: if, Loops and switch

cards.q: Why does a jump table's range check use `ja` instead of `jg`?
cards.a:
Unsigned, it also sends negatives to default

Negative numbers read as unsigned are larger than any case.
cards.lessonTitle: Reading Compiler Output: if, Loops and switch

cards.q: How does a member access appear in assembly?
cards.a:
As `[pointer + offset]` with a size such as `dword ptr`

The size tells you the member's type width, and the offset tells you where in the struct it is.
cards.lessonTitle: Structs, Arrays and Pointers in Assembly

cards.q: How do you find the element size of an array of structs from compiled code?
cards.a:
From how the index is scaled before it is added

`lea rax, [rax+rax*2]` then `[rcx+rax*8]` scales the index by 3 × 8, so each element is 24 bytes. The multiply or `lea` combination, times the addressing-mode scale, gives the struct size.
cards.lessonTitle: Structs, Arrays and Pointers in Assembly

cards.q: What does a chain of dependent 8-byte loads represent?
cards.a:
Following pointers: each load gives the next address

Each load needs the previous one's result, which is why pointer chasing is slow.
cards.lessonTitle: Structs, Arrays and Pointers in Assembly

cards.q: `mov eax, dword ptr [rcx+0Ch]` with `rcx` holding a struct pointer. What is being read?
cards.a:
A 4-byte member at offset 12

`dword ptr` is 4 bytes; `+0Ch` is the member's offset.
cards.lessonTitle: Structs, Arrays and Pointers in Assembly

cards.q: Code computes `lea rax, [rax+rax*2]` and then reads `[rcx+rax*8]`. What is the element size?
cards.a:
24 bytes

The index is multiplied by 3, then scaled by 8.
cards.lessonTitle: Structs, Arrays and Pointers in Assembly

cards.q: What does `mov rax, [rcx]` followed by `call qword ptr [rax+10h]` indicate?
cards.a:
A virtual call to slot 2 of the object's vtable

The first load fetches the vptr; 0x10 / 8 = slot 2.
cards.lessonTitle: Structs, Arrays and Pointers in Assembly

cards.q: What do the suffixes `ss`, `sd`, `ps` and `pd` mean?
cards.a:
Scalar single, scalar double, packed single (four floats), packed double (two doubles)

`addss` adds one float; `addps` adds four floats at once.

cards.q: Where do a function's float arguments and float result go on x64 Windows?
cards.a:
The first four arguments in `xmm0` to `xmm3` by position; the result in `xmm0`

Integer results come back in `rax`; float and double results come back in `xmm0`.

cards.q: What does a loop need for the compiler to vectorise it?
cards.a:
Independent iterations, a simple body and contiguous data

Then several elements can be processed per instruction, four floats at a time with SSE.

cards.q: What does `mulss xmm0, xmm1` do?
cards.a:
Multiplies the lowest float of xmm0 by xmm1's

`ss` means scalar single precision.

cards.q: Why does compiled float code load constants from memory?
cards.a:
x64 instructions cannot hold floating-point immediates

They are stored in read-only data, often named after their bit pattern.

cards.q: What is the advantage of `addps` over `addss`?
cards.a:
It adds four pairs of floats in one instruction

Packed instructions operate on every lane at once: SIMD.

cards.q: After `comiss xmm0, xmm1`, which jump means "xmm0 is greater"?
cards.a:
`ja`

Float compares set the flags like an unsigned comparison.

cards.q: How do you add an assembly file to a Visual Studio C++ project?
cards.a:
Enable the masm build customisation, then add a `.asm` file

MSVC does not support inline `__asm` blocks for x64, which is why separate `.asm` files are used. Check that the file's item type is Microsoft Macro Assembler.

cards.q: What does an assembly function have to do with non-volatile registers?
cards.a:
Save any it uses (for example with `push`) and restore them before returning

The caller relies on non-volatile registers such as `rbx` keeping their values across the call.

cards.q: How do you check the stack is aligned at a call?
cards.a:
Add up pushes and `sub rsp` from entry; `rsp` must end a multiple of 16

The return address pushed by your own caller is what makes `rsp` 8 off at entry. At entry `rsp` is 8 off a multiple of 16, and 32 bytes of shadow space must be reserved too.

cards.q: Why must the C++ declaration of an assembly function be `extern "C"`?
cards.a:
So C++ looks for the plain, unmangled name

Otherwise the linker searches for a mangled symbol that does not exist.

cards.q: Inside `logTwice`, why is the value kept in `ebx` between the two calls?
cards.a:
`rbx` is non-volatile, so calls leave it alone

Anything needed after a call must be in a non-volatile register or memory.

cards.q: What two conditions must hold at every `call` instruction in your assembly?
cards.a:
`rsp` is a multiple of 16, with 32 bytes of shadow space reserved

Both come from the Microsoft x64 calling convention.

cards.q: Name five transformations an optimiser applies.
cards.a:
Inlining, unrolling, vectorisation, branch removal with setcc/cmov, constant folding (also strength reduction, tail calls, dead code removal)

The first group is what a Debug build does; optimisation removes overhead rather than adding it.

cards.q: Why can a breakpoint in a function fail to hit in a Release build?
cards.a:
The function may have been inlined into its callers or removed, so there is no separate code there to stop in

Release builds can have a `.pdb`; the problem is that the code you set the breakpoint on was folded into other code.

cards.q: What is the best first step when reading an unfamiliar optimised function?
cards.a:
Find its loops, calls and returns before the arithmetic tricks

The shape tells you what the function does; the tricks only make it faster.

cards.q: A small getter function has no `call` to it anywhere in an optimised build. Why?
cards.a:
It was inlined: its body was copied into each caller

Inlining removes the call entirely.

cards.q: Why might an `if` inside a loop compile to `setg` and `add` instead of a jump?
cards.a:
To avoid mispredicted branches

Branchless code costs the same every iteration.

cards.q: A function ends with `jmp otherFunction` instead of `call` and `ret`. What is this?
cards.a:
A tail call into `otherFunction`

The current function has no more work after the call, so it jumps instead.

cards.q: What usually accompanies a vectorised loop?
cards.a:
A scalar loop handling the leftover elements

The number of elements is rarely a multiple of the vector width.

cards.q: What are the steps of the debugging loop?
cards.a:
Reproduce, observe, form one testable hypothesis, test it, repeat

The fix is checked against the original reproduction, which is why reproducing comes first. Then fix it and check the fix against the original reproduction.

cards.q: What is bisecting, and why is it so effective?
cards.a:
Halving the search space each step, so steps grow only logarithmically

512 commits need at most 9 tests, because each test halves what is left.

cards.q: Why make a minimal reproduction?
cards.a:
It is easier to reason about, and shrinking it often shows the cause

Every piece you remove without losing the bug rules something out.

cards.q: Why is reproducing a bug reliably the first step?
cards.a:
Without it, you cannot tell whether an experiment or fix made any difference

Every later step depends on being able to trigger the bug on demand.

cards.q: A bug appeared somewhere in the last 512 commits. How many tests does bisecting need, at most?
cards.a:
About 9

Each test halves the range: 2⁹ = 512.

cards.q: What makes a good hypothesis?
cards.a:
A specific cause that a quick experiment could disprove

Specific and testable is what makes progress possible.

cards.q: What does a PDB contain?
cards.a:
Function names, line tables, types and locals for the build

The source itself is not in the PDB; the debugger finds the source files separately using the paths and line tables it holds.

cards.q: Why must you keep the PDB of every build you release?
cards.a:
Only its own PDB can turn a build's crash reports into names

A PDB from a later build of the same source does not match, because addresses and the build signature differ.

cards.q: What is a symbol server?
cards.a:
A service that hands out the PDB matching a module's signature

A studio can run its own for its builds, so crash dumps from players resolve automatically.

cards.q: Why does a call stack show `game.exe!00007ff6a1235f10()` instead of a function name?
cards.a:
The debugger could not load a matching PDB for game.exe

Without symbols, only addresses are known. Check the Modules window.

cards.q: How does the debugger know a PDB belongs to a particular exe?
cards.a:
By a signature (GUID and age) both must share

Each build gets a new signature, so only that build's PDB fits.

cards.q: How can a debugger walk an x64 stack when functions do not use a frame pointer?
cards.a:
From the unwind information in `.pdata` and `.xdata`

The same data drives exception unwinding.

cards.q: What does `srv*C:\Symbols*https://msdl.microsoft.com/download/symbols` in a symbol path do?
cards.a:
Fetches Microsoft's symbols and caches them in C:\Symbols

Public symbols turn Windows frames into names.

cards.q: What is the difference between an assert and error handling?
cards.a:
An assert catches bugs; error handling copes with expected failures

A missing file is not a bug in your code, so it needs real handling that stays in Release, not an assert. A missing file can legitimately happen; it needs real handling that stays in Release.

cards.q: Why wrap a macro's body in `do { ... } while (false)`?
cards.a:
So the macro acts as one statement, even after a braceless `if`

Without it, a multi-statement macro after an unbraced `if` would only have its first statement controlled by the `if`.

cards.q: What makes a log line useful?
cards.a:
A level, a time or frame, a category, and the values involved

"Loading failed" says little; "level 3: failed to open textures/rock.png, error 2" tells you what to check.

cards.q: What happens to `assert(x > 0)` in a Release build?
cards.a:
Nothing is checked: the line compiles to nothing

`NDEBUG` disables it.

cards.q: Which kind of check is right for "this struct must be exactly 16 bytes"?
cards.a:
`static_assert(sizeof(T) == 16)`

Sizes are known at compile time, so the compiler can check them.

cards.q: Why use `__debugbreak()` in a custom assert?
cards.a:
It stops the debugger right at the failing line

It is the `int 3` breakpoint instruction.

cards.q: What is a ring buffer of log messages good for?
cards.a:
Keeping recent messages to write out on a crash

The oldest messages are overwritten, so memory use stays fixed.

cards.q: What is a crash dump?
cards.a:
A file of a process's threads, stacks and memory, for later debugging

Opening the dump is like being paused at the crash, though the program can no longer run on.

cards.q: How does a program write its own minidump when it crashes?
cards.a:
It installs an unhandled exception filter with `SetUnhandledExceptionFilter`, and calls `MiniDumpWriteDump` in it

An access violation is a structured exception, not a C++ exception, so `try`/`catch` does not see it.

cards.q: What do you need to turn a dump from a player into a readable call stack?
cards.a:
The exact PDB files of the build the player was running

Windows' own PDBs come from Microsoft's symbol server; your game's must be the ones you kept for that build.

cards.q: A crash report shows exception code `0xC0000005`. What kind of error is it?
cards.a:
An access violation on memory

Look at the access type and address in the exception record next.

cards.q: What does a small minidump contain?
cards.a:
Modules, each thread's registers and stack

Enough for call stacks and stack locals when symbols are available.

cards.q: Why might a crash reporter write the dump from a separate process?
cards.a:
The crashed process may be too damaged to run much code safely

A healthy watchdog process can capture the crashed one from outside.

cards.q: What does `0xE06D7363` mean?
cards.a:
An uncaught C++ exception

The low bytes spell "msc", for Microsoft C++.

cards.q: Why learn WinDbg when Visual Studio has a debugger?
cards.a:
It is quick with dumps, needs no Visual Studio, and debugs the kernel

Visual Studio can open dumps too, but WinDbg is lighter and goes deeper into Windows itself.

cards.q: What is the difference between commands starting with `.` and with `!`?
cards.a:
`.` commands control the debugger itself; `!` commands are extensions provided by debugger DLLs

`.symfix` sets up the symbol path (debugger control); `!analyze` comes from an extension DLL.

cards.q: Which commands show locals, a typed structure and raw memory?
cards.a:
`dv` for locals, `dt` for a typed structure, and `db`/`dd`/`dq` for memory

`db`, `dd` and `dq` show memory as bytes, dwords or qwords; `k` is the call stack and `lm` lists modules.

cards.q: Which WinDbg command shows the call stack?
cards.a:
`k`

`kp` adds parameters, `kn` frame numbers.

cards.q: What does `!analyze -v` do?
cards.a:
Summarises the likely cause of a crash

It is the usual first command on a crash dump.

cards.q: How do you look at the 4-byte values at an address?
cards.a:
`dd address`

`db` shows bytes, `dd` double words (4 bytes), `dq` quad words, `du` UTF-16 text.

cards.q: What does `.symfix` do?
cards.a:
Points the symbol path at Microsoft's server

Follow it with `.reload`.

cards.q: Which settings make a Release build debuggable without slowing it down?
cards.a:
A full PDB (`/Zi`, linker `/DEBUG`) plus `/Zo`

Debug information does not change the generated code, so the build stays as fast as before.

cards.q: How do you see a value the debugger reports as optimised away?
cards.a:
Find its register or stack slot in the disassembly and read that

The value still exists somewhere while it is in use; the PDB just cannot say where.

cards.q: Name three common causes of bugs that only appear in Release builds.
cards.a:
Uninitialised variables, out-of-bounds accesses and data races

Debug builds fill memory, run slower and keep asserts, which can hide all of these. Side effects in asserts, timing differences and other undefined behaviour are common too.

cards.q: The debugger says a local is "optimised away". What should you try?
cards.a:
Find the register that holds it in the disassembly

Optimised code keeps most values in registers.

cards.q: A bug disappears when one file is compiled with `/Od`. What does that suggest?
cards.a:
Undefined behaviour near that code, exposed by the optimiser

UB behaves differently under optimisation; find and fix it.

cards.q: Where are a function's first four arguments most reliably found in optimised code?
cards.a:
In `rcx`, `rdx`, `r8`, `r9` on entry

Optimised code soon moves or overwrites them.

cards.q: How do you find the threads involved in a deadlock?
cards.a:
Break All and match what each thread waits for with what it holds

A deadlock uses almost no CPU: the threads are all waiting, so their stacks show exactly where.

cards.q: What is the Parallel Stacks window good for?
cards.a:
Seeing all threads' stacks at once to spot the odd one out

Twenty identical worker stacks collapse into one, and the odd one out stands out.

cards.q: Why do races often disappear when you add logging?
cards.a:
Logging changes the timing, so the accesses may no longer overlap

The race is still there; it has only become less likely to show, which is why races need tools and reasoning, not just prints.

cards.q: The game freezes with almost no CPU use. What is most likely?
cards.a:
A deadlock: threads waiting on each other

An infinite loop would keep a core busy.

cards.q: What does freezing a thread in the Threads window let you do?
cards.a:
Hold it while others run, to force an order

Forced interleavings make rare races reproducible.

cards.q: Why is `SetThreadDescription` worth calling?
cards.a:
Tools then show each thread's name

Named threads make every multithreaded investigation faster.

cards.q: What is the difference between sampling and instrumenting profilers?
cards.a:
Sampling records stacks statistically; instrumenting times marked sections

Sampling needs no code changes; instrumenting gives exact per-frame timelines of the sections you mark.
cards.lessonTitle: Profiling: Finding Where the Time Goes

cards.q: What is the difference between self and total time?
cards.a:
Self time is spent in the function's own instructions; total time includes everything it calls

90% total and 1% self means the function itself is cheap, and the time is in something it calls.
cards.lessonTitle: Profiling: Finding Where the Time Goes

cards.q: How long is a frame at 60 frames per second?
cards.a:
About 16.7 milliseconds

1000 ms divided by 60 is about 16.7 ms. 33.3 ms is a frame at 30 fps.
cards.lessonTitle: Profiling: Finding Where the Time Goes

cards.q: What does a sampling profiler do?
cards.a:
Records the call stack at intervals to show where time goes

It needs no code changes and has low overhead.
cards.lessonTitle: Profiling: Finding Where the Time Goes

cards.q: A function shows 90% total CPU but 1% self CPU. What does that mean?
cards.a:
It is not slow itself; functions it calls account for the time

Follow the hot path into its callees.
cards.lessonTitle: Profiling: Finding Where the Time Goes

cards.q: Why think in milliseconds per frame rather than frames per second?
cards.a:
Milliseconds of each system add up; frame rates do not

60 fps means a budget of 16.7 ms shared by everything.
cards.lessonTitle: Profiling: Finding Where the Time Goes

cards.q: A game averages 60 fps but stutters. What should you look at?
cards.a:
The worst frame times, and what happened then

Occasional spikes cause stutter.
cards.lessonTitle: Profiling: Finding Where the Time Goes

cards.q: Name four legitimate uses of reverse engineering.
cards.a:
Security research, malware analysis, interoperability with file formats and protocols, and preserving old software

Debugging third-party code and learning are also legitimate. The ground rules of the course rule out piracy and cheating in online games.
cards.lessonTitle: What Reverse Engineering Is, and Its Ground Rules

cards.q: What do reverse engineers recover, and what can they not recover?
cards.a:
Logic, strings and imports, but not comments, local names or source

Compiling throws away comments and local names for good; the behaviour remains in the machine code.
cards.lessonTitle: What Reverse Engineering Is, and Its Ground Rules

cards.q: What should you do if you find a security vulnerability?
cards.a:
Report it privately to the vendor and give them time to fix it before discussing it publicly

This is responsible disclosure: users get a fix before attackers learn the details.
cards.lessonTitle: What Reverse Engineering Is, and Its Ground Rules

cards.q: What is the difference between static and dynamic analysis?
cards.a:
Static examines the program unrun; dynamic runs and observes it

Each reveals things the other cannot; real work uses both.
cards.lessonTitle: What Reverse Engineering Is, and Its Ground Rules

cards.q: Which of these is lost when a program is compiled without a PDB?
cards.a:
Local variable names

Locals become registers and stack offsets.
cards.lessonTitle: What Reverse Engineering Is, and Its Ground Rules

cards.q: Which practice targets does this course use?
cards.a:
Programs you build yourself, and open source

These are targets you clearly have the right to analyse.
cards.lessonTitle: What Reverse Engineering Is, and Its Ground Rules

cards.q: In what order do the parts of a PE file come?
cards.a:
DOS header, PE signature, file header, optional header, sections

`e_lfanew` in the DOS header gives the offset of the PE signature, where the NT headers start. The optional header ends with the data directories, and the section table comes just before the sections.

cards.q: What does the section table tell you for each section?
cards.a:
Its name, memory and file positions and sizes, and its flags

The memory and file positions differ, which is why converting an RVA to a file offset needs the section table.

cards.q: Why should a PE parser check offsets against the file size?
cards.a:
Because malformed or malicious files can contain offsets and counts pointing outside the file

Using them unchecked reads out of bounds, which can crash the parser or worse.

cards.q: Which two bytes start every PE file?
cards.a:
`4D 5A` ("MZ")

"MZ" is the DOS header's signature; the PE signature comes later, at e_lfanew.

cards.q: What does `e_lfanew` hold?
cards.a:
The file offset of the PE signature

It is at offset 0x3C of the DOS header.

cards.q: What is the value of `FileHeader.Machine` for a 64-bit x86 program?
cards.a:
`0x8664`

`0x20B` is the optional header's magic for PE32+.

cards.q: What are the data directories?
cards.a:
RVAs and sizes of key tables such as imports and exports

They are the index of the file's important tables.

cards.q: What three things does an import descriptor point to?
cards.a:
The DLL's name, its lookup table, and its import address table

Functions are named by name or ordinal in the lookup table; calls in the program go through the address table. The lookup table says which functions; the address table is where the loader writes their addresses.

cards.q: How does `GetProcAddress` find a function by name?
cards.a:
It binary-searches the sorted export names and returns base + RVA

Export names are stored sorted precisely so this search is fast.

cards.q: How do you convert an RVA to a file offset?
cards.a:
RVA − the section's VirtualAddress + its PointerToRawData

Sections are laid out differently in memory and in the file, so the offset depends on which section holds the RVA.

cards.q: What does the loader write into the import address table?
cards.a:
The real addresses of the imported functions

Calls to imports go through these slots.

cards.q: How does a call to an imported function look in disassembly?
cards.a:
An indirect call through a slot, `call [__imp_X]`

The code reads the address from the IAT at run time.

cards.q: A section has VirtualAddress 0x5000 and PointerToRawData 0x3400. What is the file offset of RVA 0x5120?
What is a forwarded export?
cards.a:
An export that redirects to another DLL's function

Many kernel32 exports forward to ntdll.

cards.q: What does Ghidra's automatic analysis do?
cards.a:
It disassembles, finds functions, follows xrefs and decompiles

All of this is static: the program is never run.

cards.q: Why does `main` not start at the entry point?
cards.a:
The entry point is C runtime start-up code that later calls `main`

Finding `main` means following the start-up code to the call that passes `argc` and `argv`.

cards.q: What does annotating a program in a disassembler involve?
cards.a:
Renaming things, applying struct types, and adding comments

Each name you add makes every other function that uses it easier to read.

cards.q: What does a decompiler produce?
cards.a:
C-like pseudocode from the machine code

It is a readable approximation, not the original source.

cards.q: What is the quickest way to find the function that prints a particular message?
cards.a:
Find the string, then follow its cross-reference

Strings and their cross-references are the usual way in.

cards.q: Why does creating a struct type and applying it to a parameter help so much?
cards.a:
The decompiler shows member names instead of offsets

Annotations propagate across the program.

cards.q: What are signs that an address is the start of a function?
cards.a:
Calls target it, it has a prologue, or `.pdata` lists it

Several of these signs together make it almost certain.

cards.q: What is an induction variable?
cards.a:
The variable that changes by a fixed step each time round a loop and is compared with the limit

It shows what the loop iterates over, such as an index into an array.

cards.q: What is the most useful first step when reading an unknown function?
cards.a:
Work out its arguments, its return value and its calls

Arguments and calls frame everything else in the function.

cards.q: How can you tell which registers are a function's arguments?
cards.a:
Argument registers that are read before being written

Unused argument registers are simply never read.

cards.q: What marks a loop in a function graph?
cards.a:
A back edge to an earlier block

The target of the back edge is the loop's head.

cards.q: `test rax, rax` / `je error` straight after a call. What is it probably?
cards.a:
A null check of the result

Functions returning pointers use null to signal failure.

cards.q: What can vtables tell you about an unknown program?
cards.a:
Which classes exist, their virtual functions, and overrides

Vtables sit in read-only data and are written into objects by constructors, so they are a map of the class design. Through the constructors that reference them, vtables also show which code creates each class.

cards.q: What does RTTI provide to a reverse engineer?
cards.a:
Class names and inheritance, linked from each vtable

A string such as `.?AVGoblin@@` names the class `Goblin`. Building with `/GR-` removes RTTI and makes analysis harder.

cards.q: How does a `strings`-style tool work?
cards.a:
It scans bytes for runs of printable characters, ASCII and UTF-16

Searching UTF-16 too matters on Windows, where much text is stored that way.

cards.q: Where is a class's vtable stored?
cards.a:
In read-only data, once per class

Objects hold only a pointer to it.

cards.q: How can you recognise a constructor without symbols?
cards.a:
It writes a vtable address into offset 0 of the object

Every write of a vtable address into an object marks a constructor or destructor.

cards.q: What is `.?AVGoblin@@`?
cards.a:
The RTTI decorated name of `Goblin`

`.?AV` introduces a class's decorated name.

cards.q: Why search for UTF-16 strings as well as ASCII?
cards.a:
Windows programs often store text as UTF-16

Wide strings appear with a zero byte between ASCII letters.

cards.q: What does dynamic analysis add to static analysis?
cards.a:
Real values, real call targets, and which branches run

A `call qword ptr [rax+18h]` has no fixed target in the listing; running it shows where it really goes.

cards.q: Why are API calls good breakpoints in an unknown program?
cards.a:
They mark key actions, and their arguments show what is happening

Breaking on `CreateFileW` shows the file name in `rcx`; stepping out lands in the code that opened it.

cards.q: Where can you see whether a conditional jump will be taken, before stepping it?
cards.a:
From the flags, or the debugger's mark on the jump

x64dbg marks the jump as taken or not taken based on the current flags.

cards.q: You break on `CreateFileW`. Where is the file name?
cards.a:
Pointed to by `rcx`, as a UTF-16 string

It is the first argument.

cards.q: How do you find the program's own function that opens a particular file?
cards.a:
Break on `CreateFileW`, check the name, step out

Stepping out lands in the code that made the call.

cards.q: What is the advantage of dynamic analysis for `call qword ptr [rax+18h]`?
cards.a:
Stepping into it shows the actual target at run time

Static analysis may not know which object `rax` points to.

cards.q: What is a cross-reference?
cards.a:
A recorded reference from one place to another, such as a call

Listing the xrefs to a string or function shows every place that uses it.
cards.lessonTitle: Cross-References: Finding Where Data Is Used

cards.q: How is the target of an `E8` call computed?
cards.a:
The next instruction's address plus the signed displacement

The displacement is relative to the next instruction, not to the call itself. `F0 FF FF FF` is -16.
cards.lessonTitle: Cross-References: Finding Where Data Is Used

cards.q: Why might static analysis miss a reference?
cards.a:
The address may only be computed or looked up at run time

These are exactly the cases where running the program fills the gaps.
cards.lessonTitle: Cross-References: Finding Where Data Is Used

cards.q: A `call` at 0x140002000 is encoded `E8 F0 FF FF FF`. Where does it call?
cards.a:
0x140001FF5

rel32 = 0xFFFFFFF0 = -16; next instruction at 0x140002005; 0x140002005 - 16 = 0x140001FF5.
cards.lessonTitle: Cross-References: Finding Where Data Is Used

cards.q: What do the xrefs to a vtable usually point to?
cards.a:
The constructors and destructors

Virtual calls read the vptr from the object, not the vtable's address directly.
cards.lessonTitle: Cross-References: Finding Where Data Is Used

cards.q: How can you find every place a program opens a file?
cards.a:
List the cross-references to the imported `CreateFileW`

Every call to an import goes through its IAT slot, and each is an xref.
cards.lessonTitle: Cross-References: Finding Where Data Is Used

cards.q: What three pieces of evidence does each member access give?
cards.a:
The member's offset, its size, and clues to its type

A `movss` read suggests a `float`; an 8-byte value used as an address is a pointer.

cards.q: Why look at the code that creates the struct?
cards.a:
The allocation gives the size; the constructor shows members

A `new` of 0x40 bytes says the struct is 64 bytes, and stores in the constructor reveal members you have not seen used yet.

cards.q: What should you do with members you are unsure about?
cards.a:
Mark them as guesses, with evidence, until confirmed

Wrong guesses written down as facts spread through every function that uses the struct.

cards.q: A member is read with `movss` at offset 0x8. What type is it most likely?
cards.a:
`float`

`movss` moves a single-precision float.

cards.q: How can you find a struct's total size?
cards.a:
From the size passed to its allocation

Creators reveal sizes directly.

cards.q: An 8-byte member is loaded and then used as an address. What is it?
cards.a:
A pointer to another object

Following it leads to the next struct.

cards.q: What is the routine for a practice target?
cards.a:
Build it optimised without symbols, analyse it, then check the source

Checking against your own source is what makes self-built targets so valuable: you find out exactly where you were wrong. Write down conclusions before checking, then compare again with the PDB loaded.

cards.q: How can you make a practice target easier or harder?
cards.a:
Easier unoptimised; harder with more inlining and no RTTI

Unoptimised code follows the source closely; inlining and missing RTTI hide structure.

cards.q: Why do level 5 targets include a file the program wrote?
cards.a:
Documenting a file format is core interoperability work

Interoperability is one of the main legitimate reasons for reverse engineering.

cards.q: Why read values from `std::cin` in a practice target?
cards.a:
So the optimiser cannot precompute the results

With constant inputs, an optimising compiler may fold everything into a few printed constants.

cards.q: What does building with `/GR-` change for a reverse engineer?
cards.a:
RTTI, and so class names, are removed

Vtables remain, but nameless.

cards.q: What is the most valuable part of a self-built target?
cards.a:
The source, which lets you check every conclusion

Checking answers is how you calibrate your judgement.

cards.q: What is a frame?
cards.a:
One pass of the loop: input, one update, one image

Frames are not tied to a fixed length of time; how long one takes depends on the work in it.

cards.q: Why keep input, update and render separate?
cards.a:
So each can run at its own rate, and rendering never changes the world

If rendering changed game state, the game would behave differently depending on the frame rate. Separating them also lets input be recorded and replayed.

cards.q: Why does the order of systems in the update matter?
cards.a:
Later systems use earlier ones' results, or see stale data

Running collision before movement, for example, checks positions from the previous frame.

cards.q: What are the three phases of the game loop?
cards.a:
Input, update, render

They repeat every frame for as long as the game runs.

cards.q: Why should rendering never change the game state?
cards.a:
The state would depend on how many frames get drawn

Updates belong in the update phase, driven by time.

cards.q: Why multiply speeds by `dt`?
cards.a:
So movement per second is the same at any frame rate

A fixed step per frame makes speed depend on frame rate.

cards.q: What is the difference between a variable and a fixed time step?
cards.a:
Variable steps by the last frame's time; fixed always steps the same amount

The fixed step makes the simulation repeatable, which is what replays and networking need.

cards.q: How does the accumulator work?
cards.a:
It gains real time each frame and runs one update per whole step held

A 50 ms frame with 1/60 s steps runs three updates and carries the leftover into the next frame. Each update subtracts one step; whatever is left carries over to the next frame.

cards.q: Why interpolate when rendering?
cards.a:
To draw smooth motion between fixed steps

`alpha` is how far the leftover time is into the next step, so positions are blended between the last two steps.

cards.q: With a fixed step of 1/60 s, how many updates does a 50 ms frame run (starting with an empty accumulator)?
cards.a:
3

50 ms holds three 16.7 ms steps, with a small remainder carried to the next frame.

cards.q: Why does a fixed time step make replays possible?
cards.a:
The same inputs always give the same updates

A variable step makes results depend on frame timings.

cards.q: What does `alpha` in the fixed-step loop represent?
cards.a:
How far time has got into the next step

It is the leftover accumulator divided by the step. It is used to blend the previous and current states when drawing.

cards.q: What problem does capping the accumulator solve?
cards.a:
The spiral of death

Under extreme load the game slows down instead of freezing.

cards.q: What are entities, components and systems?
cards.a:
Entities are ids; components are plain data attached to entities; systems are functions processing every entity with a given set of components

An entity has no behaviour of its own: what it is comes from which components it has.

cards.q: What problem with deep inheritance does ECS solve?
cards.a:
Rigid hierarchies, and scattered virtual-heavy memory

Composition lets any entity have any mix of components, and systems loop over tightly packed arrays.

cards.q: What does a sparse set store, and why?
cards.a:
An id-to-index array plus dense arrays, for O(1) changes and fast loops

Removal swaps the last dense element into the gap and fixes the sparse entry, which keeps it constant time.

cards.q: In ECS, what is an entity?
cards.a:
Just an id that components are attached to

All its data lives in components; all behaviour in systems.

cards.q: Why are ECS systems often faster than looping over objects with virtual `update` functions?
cards.a:
They walk contiguous plain data with no virtual calls

Data-oriented layout suits caches and vectorisation.

cards.q: In a sparse set, how is a component removed in constant time?
cards.a:
Swap-and-pop, then fix the moved entity's entry

The dense arrays stay dense.

cards.q: What are the main stages a triangle goes through on the GPU?
cards.a:
Vertex shader, rasterisation, pixel shader, then output merging

The depth test in output merging decides which surface is in front at each pixel.
cards.lessonTitle: A Tour of the Rendering Pipeline

cards.q: What coordinate spaces does a vertex pass through?
cards.a:
Model, world, view, clip and screen space

Each step is a transform: placing the model in the world, seeing it from the camera, projecting it, then mapping to pixels.
cards.lessonTitle: A Tour of the Rendering Pipeline

cards.q: What is the difference between being CPU-bound and GPU-bound in rendering?
cards.a:
CPU-bound: submitting work is too slow; GPU-bound: drawing it is

Too many draw calls is a typical cause of being CPU-bound, which is why batching helps.
cards.lessonTitle: A Tour of the Rendering Pipeline

cards.q: What does a vertex shader do?
cards.a:
Transforms each vertex's position for rasterisation

Pixel shaders compute colours; vertex shaders place vertices.
cards.lessonTitle: A Tour of the Rendering Pipeline

cards.q: Why batch many sprites into one draw call?
cards.a:
Each draw call costs CPU time, so fewer is faster

Submission overhead adds up with thousands of calls.
cards.lessonTitle: A Tour of the Rendering Pipeline

cards.q: What does the depth test do?
cards.a:
Discards pixels that are behind something already drawn at that position

It uses the depth buffer, one depth value per pixel.
cards.lessonTitle: A Tour of the Rendering Pipeline

cards.q: What is culling?
cards.a:
Skipping objects that cannot be seen

Cheap tests save expensive drawing.
cards.lessonTitle: A Tour of the Rendering Pipeline

cards.q: Why should game code use actions rather than keys?
cards.a:
So controls can be rebound and gamepads work unchanged

Game code asks "is Jump pressed?", and the binding table decides which keys or buttons mean Jump.

cards.q: How are pressed and released worked out?
cards.a:
By comparing this frame's state with last frame's

Keeping last frame's snapshot is all it takes; "held" is simply down in this frame.

cards.q: Why apply a 2D stick's dead zone to its length rather than to each axis?
cards.a:
Because per-axis dead zones distort diagonal directions and make movement snap to the axes

A radial dead zone ignores small movements in every direction equally.

cards.q: An action was up last frame and is down now. Which queries are true?
cards.a:
`pressed` and `held`

Pressed is the transition; held is the current state.

cards.q: Why take one input snapshot per frame?
cards.a:
So every system in that frame sees the same input state

Mixing live reads makes systems disagree.

cards.q: What is a dead zone for?
cards.a:
Ignoring a resting stick's small readings

Without it, characters creep around on their own.

cards.q: What does input buffering do?
cards.a:
Remembers a press until the action is possible

It forgives presses that come slightly early.

cards.q: Why hand out handles instead of raw pointers to resources?
cards.a:
Handles stay safe when resources unload or reload

A pointer to an unloaded texture dangles; a handle can be checked or pointed at the reloaded version.

cards.q: How does reference counting decide when to unload?
cards.a:
Acquire adds one, release subtracts; at zero it may unload

This is what `std::shared_ptr` does internally, and why the cache in the lesson holds `weak_ptr`s that do not count.

cards.q: How can a game load resources without freezing?
cards.a:
Load on worker threads and show placeholders until ready

The main thread keeps running frames while workers do the slow reading and decoding.

cards.q: What problem does a resource manager solve first?
cards.a:
Loading each resource only once

Loading the same texture several times wastes time and memory.

cards.q: Why does the cache in the example hold `weak_ptr`s?
cards.a:
To find resources still in use without keeping them alive itself

When the last user lets go, the texture is freed even though the cache remembers its name.

cards.q: What is an asset pipeline?
cards.a:
Build tools converting assets into fast formats

Games load preprocessed data, not artists' source files.

cards.q: What should a save contain, and what should be rebuilt?
cards.a:
Only state that cannot be derived; the rest is rebuilt on load

Saving derived data wastes space and risks it disagreeing with what it was derived from.

cards.q: What goes in a save file's header?
cards.a:
A magic number, a version, a length and a checksum

The magic number and version say how to read the rest; the length and checksum detect truncated or damaged files.

cards.q: How do old saves keep working after the format changes?
cards.a:
Each version is migrated step by step up to the current one

Each migration step only needs to know about two neighbouring versions.

cards.q: Why are references between saved objects stored as ids rather than pointers?
cards.a:
Addresses differ the next time the game runs

ASLR and new allocations change every address between runs.

cards.q: What is a save file's version number for?
cards.a:
Telling the loader which format the file uses

Each format change gets a new version and a migration from the old one.

cards.q: What does a CRC-32 checksum detect?
cards.a:
Accidental damage to the data, such as truncation or flipped bits

Anyone can recompute it after editing, so it is not tamper protection.

cards.q: What belongs in C++ and what in data or scripts?
cards.a:
Engine and hot code in C++; content and balance in data

Designers can then change content and balance without rebuilding the engine.

cards.q: Why validate data files when loading?
cards.a:
So mistakes are reported at once, naming the file and line

A misspelled key found at load time costs seconds; found as a strange bug in play it can cost hours.

cards.q: What does registering a function with Lua do?
cards.a:
It makes a C++ function callable from scripts by name

Scripts can only do what the engine has chosen to expose this way.

cards.q: What is the main advantage of data-driven design?
cards.a:
Content can change without recompiling

Designers iterate on data files directly.

cards.q: When is an embedded scripting language more appropriate than a data file?
cards.a:
When content needs logic, like a boss's attacks
