Data describes what; scripts describe how and when.

cards.q: How does a Lua script call into the engine?
cards.a:
Through C++ functions the engine registered with the Lua state

The registered set defines what scripts are allowed to do.

cards.q: What steps does the method follow?
cards.a:
Build it, map folders, find the loop, trace one feature, write it down

Running it first means you can always check your reading against what really happens.
cards.lessonTitle: Reading the Source of an Open-Source Game

cards.q: How do you find the main loop?
cards.a:
Step from the entry point until the once-per-frame loop

The debugger follows the real path, which is more reliable than guessing from file names.
cards.lessonTitle: Reading the Source of an Open-Source Game

cards.q: What should you check before reusing code from an open-source game?
cards.a:
Its licence, and that your use follows the licence's terms

Open source does not mean free of conditions: many licences require attribution or that your code uses the same licence.
cards.lessonTitle: Reading the Source of an Open-Source Game

cards.q: What is the best first step with an unfamiliar game codebase?
cards.a:
Build it and run it under a debugger

Being able to step through it makes everything else faster.
cards.lessonTitle: Reading the Source of an Open-Source Game

cards.q: How do you find the code behind a visible feature?
cards.a:
Search for the strings it shows

Follow execution from something you can see.
cards.lessonTitle: Reading the Source of an Open-Source Game

cards.q: Why trace one feature end to end?
cards.a:
It crosses most major systems on one real path

Input, logic, entities, rendering and audio all appear along the way.
cards.lessonTitle: Reading the Source of an Open-Source Game

cards.q: What three things happen each time round Delve's main loop?
cards.a:
Waiting events are processed, the game is updated in fixed steps for the elapsed time, and the frame is rendered and presented

Fixed steps keep the rules independent of the frame rate, and every waiting event is handled before updating.

cards.q: What does `SDL_RenderPresent` do?
cards.a:
It shows the frame drawn in the back buffer

Drawing happens off-screen first, so the player never sees a half-drawn frame.

cards.q: Why does `main.cpp` own only the window, loop and timing?
cards.a:
So the rules live in `Game`, apart from platform code and testable

`Game::update` never touches SDL, so it can be tested without a window.

cards.q: Why use SDL2 instead of the raw Windows API from chapter 5?
cards.a:
It handles windows, input and drawing portably

Underneath, it does on Windows what chapter 5 did by hand.

cards.q: What does `SDL_PollEvent` correspond to in chapter 5?
cards.a:
The `PeekMessage` loop

It returns immediately when no events are waiting.

cards.q: Why keep SDL out of `Game::update`?
cards.a:
So the game rules can run and be tested without a window

Logic separated from the platform is testable and portable.

cards.q: How is the map stored in memory?
cards.a:
As one flat vector of tiles in row-major order, with (x, y) at index y × width + x

One flat block keeps the tiles together in memory and makes the index calculation trivial.

cards.q: What does the level loader need to check?
cards.a:
Equal row widths, known characters, exactly one player start

A clear message naming the line beats a strange crash in play. It should report each problem with its line number.

cards.q: How does a tile sheet make drawing more efficient?
cards.a:
All tiles share one texture, so they can be batched

Switching textures between draws prevents batching, which is costly.

cards.q: Why does `TileMap::at` return `Wall` for positions outside the map?
cards.a:
So movement and AI code never read out of bounds and treat the edge as solid

A safe default removes a class of out-of-bounds bugs.

cards.q: A level is 40 tiles wide. Which index holds the tile at x = 5, y = 3?
How does the renderer avoid drawing off-screen tiles?
cards.a:
It loops only over the tiles the camera can see

Culling by range is cheap and exact for a grid.

cards.q: What does "turn-based on a real-time loop" mean for Delve?
cards.a:
The loop runs every frame, but rules advance only when the player acts

The window stays responsive and animated even while the world waits for the player.

cards.q: Which moves cost a turn?
cards.a:
Moving, opening a door and attacking; not bumping a wall

A wasted bump that let monsters act would feel unfair.

cards.q: How does the renderer make tile-by-tile movement look smooth?
cards.a:
It slides the player's picture from the old tile to the new

The sliding position is only used for drawing; the rules still see the player on whole tiles.

cards.q: The player walks into a wall. What should happen?
cards.a:
Nothing, and no turn passes

Bumps should be free, so mistakes do not let monsters act.

cards.q: What does walking into a closed door do in Delve?
cards.a:
Opens it, using the turn

Opening and passing are separate actions.

cards.q: Why is the sliding position used only for drawing?
cards.a:
The rules stay exact on whole tiles

It is interpolation for presentation only.

cards.q: What are a Delve monster's states, and what moves it between them?
cards.a:
Idle, Chasing and Attacking, moved by seeing and reaching the player

A state machine keeps each monster's behaviour simple and easy to follow. Noticing the player starts a chase, being adjacent starts attacking, and losing the player for a while returns to idle.

cards.q: What is a distance map?
cards.a:
Steps from every tile to a goal, from one breadth-first search

Each monster steps to a neighbouring tile with a smaller number, so one search serves all monsters.

cards.q: How do monsters avoid moving onto the same tile?
cards.a:
They move one at a time, checking the tile is free

Acting in turn means each monster sees the moves of those before it.

cards.q: How does a monster use the distance map to chase the player?
cards.a:
It steps to whichever neighbouring tile has the smallest distance value

Walking downhill on the distance map follows a shortest path around walls.

cards.q: Why build the distance map from the player rather than from each monster?
cards.a:
One search serves every monster

The work is shared instead of repeated.

cards.q: How can a frightened monster flee using the same map?
cards.a:
Step to a larger distance value

Uphill on the map leads away from the player.

cards.q: What are the steps of the damage formula?
cards.a:
Roll to hit, then power minus half armour plus spread, at least 1

Clamping to at least 1 means a hit always does something, however strong the armour.

cards.q: What is the difference between an item definition and an item in the inventory?
cards.a:
A definition is shared data; a slot holds just its id and count

Sharing one definition means changing a potion in the data file changes every potion.

cards.q: In what order does picking up fill the inventory?
cards.a:
Top up matching stacks, then use empty slots

Topping up stacks first keeps empty slots free for as long as possible; whatever does not fit stays on the floor.

cards.q: Why clamp damage to at least 1 on a hit?
cards.a:
So every hit matters, and never heals

Without it, high armour makes damage zero or negative.

cards.q: Why pass a random generator object around instead of calling `rand()`?
cards.a:
It can be seeded, so tests and replays repeat

Determinism needs control over the random numbers.

cards.q: An inventory has [potion 4] and one empty slot; potions stack to 5. Seven potions are picked up. What happens?
cards.a:
Slots become 5 and 5; 1 stays on the floor

Top up existing stacks first, then fill empty slots, and leave the rest.

cards.q: How does Delve divide its state for level transitions and saving?
cards.a:
Player state, which persists, and floor state, which is rebuilt

Saving only the changes keeps saves small and lets the level file supply the rest. Floor state is rebuilt from the level file plus a record of changes.

cards.q: What does a Delve save contain?
cards.a:
The floor's changes, the player, and the random generator's state

Saving the generator's state makes a loaded game continue exactly as it would have. That means opened doors, surviving monsters, floor items, and the player's position, stats and inventory.

cards.q: How is the save written so a crash cannot destroy it?
cards.a:
Written to a temporary file, flushed, then swapped in atomically

At every moment either the old or the new save is complete on disk.

cards.q: What survives a transition to the next floor?
cards.a:
The player's state: health, inventory, stats

Everything belonging to the floor is discarded and rebuilt from the next level file.

cards.q: Why save the random generator's state?
cards.a:
So play continues exactly as before

Without it, the reloaded game takes different random outcomes.

cards.q: Why start each line of the save body with a keyword?
cards.a:
Loading is a simple loop; missing keys get defaults

Keyword lines are easy to extend across versions.

cards.q: What does the console's registry store for each command?
cards.a:
Its name, a help line, and a handler function

The help text lets a `help` command list everything automatically.

cards.q: What should the game do with key presses while the console is open?
cards.a:
Send them only to the console (text, editing keys, history), not to the game's controls

Typing "go" should not make the player walk.

cards.q: How does command history recall work?
cards.a:
Up goes back, Down goes forward, past the newest is the current line

Returning to the line being typed means nothing half-written is lost.

cards.q: Why does each command carry a help text?
cards.a:
So `help` can list every command

A console nobody remembers how to use is not much use.

cards.q: Why use SDL's text input events rather than key-down events for typing?
cards.a:
They give the actual characters typed

Like `WM_CHAR` in lesson 5.07.

cards.q: How do you keep cheat commands out of the released game?
cards.a:
Register them only in development builds

Code that is not compiled cannot be used.

cards.q: What makes an action feel good to perform?
cards.a:
Immediate feedback in effects and sound, not in the rules

Feedback belongs to presentation, so it never changes how the game plays.

cards.q: What goes into a Delve release folder?
cards.a:
The exe, its DLLs, the data, a readme and licences

PDBs are kept by you, not shipped; the libraries' licences usually require including their notices.

cards.q: What are the two ways to handle the Visual C++ runtime?
cards.a:
Ship the Redistributable, or link it in with `/MT`

Debug runtime DLLs may not be redistributed, and `/MDd` is the Debug DLL runtime.

cards.q: Why should screen shake use a different random generator from the gameplay?
cards.a:
So effects cannot change gameplay outcomes

Presentation must never affect game state.

cards.q: Why test the packaged game on a clean virtual machine?
cards.a:
It reveals missing DLLs and runtimes

Your development PC hides missing dependencies.

cards.q: What must you keep for every build you release?
cards.a:
Its PDB files

Symbols match exactly one build.

cards.q: Name three documented ways for a tool to get data from a game.
cards.a:
Shared memory, named pipes or sockets, and log files

These work because the game takes part, or because Windows documents them for exactly this purpose. ETW events, the debugging API and crash dumps are documented routes too.
cards.lessonTitle: Looking at Another Process with Documented APIs

cards.q: Why is it best for the game to publish data deliberately?
cards.a:
An agreed, versioned layout keeps working as the game changes

Guessed memory layouts break with every new build; an agreed layout does not.
cards.lessonTitle: Looking at Another Process with Documented APIs

cards.q: What may and may not go into a shared-memory block?
cards.a:
Fixed-size plain data; never pointers or heap-owning types

A pointer means nothing in another process's address space, and `std::string` holds one internally.
cards.lessonTitle: Looking at Another Process with Documented APIs

cards.q: Why can a tool not simply follow a pointer it got from the game?
cards.a:
It is an address in the game's own space

Each process has its own private address space (lesson 6.02).
cards.lessonTitle: Looking at Another Process with Documented APIs

cards.q: What makes shared memory work between two processes?
cards.a:
Both map the same named file-mapping object

Each sees it at its own address, but it is the same memory.
cards.lessonTitle: Looking at Another Process with Documented APIs

cards.q: Which channel suits sending a command such as "load level 3" from an editor to the game?
cards.a:
A named pipe (or socket) carrying messages

Pipes carry streams of messages; shared memory holds current state.
cards.lessonTitle: Looking at Another Process with Documented APIs

cards.q: What are the three columns of a hex view?
cards.a:
The address, the bytes in hex, and the same bytes as text

This classic layout is the same in Visual Studio's Memory window and most hex editors.

cards.q: What rights does a tool need to read another process's memory?
cards.a:
`PROCESS_VM_READ`, plus query rights to list regions

Ask for only what you need. A process the tool created itself already comes with a full-access handle.

cards.q: How does `ReadProcessMemory` report a partial read?
cards.a:
It fails and reports how many bytes it did copy

Reading page by page avoids losing a whole range because one page in it is not readable.

cards.q: What does a viewer show for bytes it could not read?
cards.a:
A marker such as `??`, never a made-up value like 0

Showing zeros would mislead whoever reads the dump.

cards.q: Why read another process's memory one page at a time?
cards.a:
An unreadable page then blanks only its own bytes

Protection and commitment are per page.

cards.q: Why keep the formatting separate from the reading?
cards.a:
Formatting is pure logic, testable without a process

Testable logic, thin platform layer.

cards.q: What is the shape of a debugger's main loop?
cards.a:
Wait for a debug event, handle it, continue, until exit

While the debugger handles an event, every thread of the debuggee is stopped.
cards.lessonTitle: A Minimal Debugger of Your Own

cards.q: Name five kinds of debug event.
cards.a:
Process and thread start and exit, DLL loads, exceptions, debug output

Process exit is another. Windows sends these to the debugger, not to the program.
cards.lessonTitle: A Minimal Debugger of Your Own

cards.q: Why are out-of-process crash reporters built as debuggers?
cards.a:
As debugger they get the crash with it frozen, and dump from outside

Writing a dump from inside a crashing process is risky; a separate healthy process is reliable.
cards.lessonTitle: A Minimal Debugger of Your Own

cards.q: What happens to the debuggee while the debugger handles an event?
cards.a:
It is suspended until `ContinueDebugEvent`

Every thread waits while the debugger inspects it.
cards.lessonTitle: A Minimal Debugger of Your Own

cards.q: What is a second-chance exception?
cards.a:
One the program did not handle, so it will crash

The debugger saw it first-chance, passed it on, and nothing handled it.
cards.lessonTitle: A Minimal Debugger of Your Own

cards.q: How does a software breakpoint work?
cards.a:
`0xCC` over an instruction raises an exception for the debugger

Hardware breakpoints use debug registers instead (lesson 4.09).
cards.lessonTitle: A Minimal Debugger of Your Own

cards.q: What is a sequence lock's writer protocol?
cards.a:
Increment the sequence, write the data, increment it again

An odd number means a write is in progress; the writer never waits for readers.
cards.lessonTitle: A Telemetry Channel: Letting the Game Publish Its State

cards.q: How does a reader know its copy is consistent?
cards.a:
The sequence number was even before copying and unchanged after

If the number was odd or changed, the reader copies again.
cards.lessonTitle: A Telemetry Channel: Letting the Game Publish Its State

cards.q: Why does the telemetry block start with magic, version and size?
cards.a:
So a tool can check what it is reading before trusting any field

Wrong data, or the right data in a newer layout, would otherwise be read as garbage.
cards.lessonTitle: A Telemetry Channel: Letting the Game Publish Its State

cards.q: What does an odd sequence number mean?
cards.a:
A write is in progress; do not trust the copy

The writer increments once before and once after writing.
cards.lessonTitle: A Telemetry Channel: Letting the Game Publish Its State

cards.q: A reader copies the fields and then finds the sequence number has changed. What should it do?
cards.a:
Discard its copy and try again

The writer updated during the copy, so it may be torn.
cards.lessonTitle: A Telemetry Channel: Letting the Game Publish Its State

cards.q: Why is a seqlock better than a shared mutex here?
cards.a:
The game never waits for a slow tool

Only readers retry; the writer always proceeds.
cards.lessonTitle: A Telemetry Channel: Letting the Game Publish Its State

cards.q: What three connection states should a monitoring tool show?
cards.a:
Live, stale (paused or frozen), and not connected

Stale and not connected look similar in the numbers but mean very different things to the person watching.
cards.lessonTitle: A Live Stats Panel for Your Game

cards.q: How does the tool find the game's telemetry?
cards.a:
It opens the mapping named with each `delve.exe`'s process id

Naming the mapping with the process id keeps two running copies of the game apart. It opens it read-only and checks the header before trusting it.
cards.lessonTitle: A Live Stats Panel for Your Game

cards.q: How does the panel draw without flickering?
cards.a:
It writes the whole screen as one string, once

Clearing and redrawing line by line is what causes flicker.
cards.lessonTitle: A Live Stats Panel for Your Game

cards.q: How does the tool tell "the game is paused" from "the game has exited"?
cards.a:
By whether its process handle is signalled

The mapping outlives the game while the tool holds it open.
cards.lessonTitle: A Live Stats Panel for Your Game

cards.q: Why does the tool include the process id when opening the mapping?
cards.a:
Each running copy uses a name with its id

It lets several copies run side by side.
cards.lessonTitle: A Live Stats Panel for Your Game

cards.q: How often should a stats panel read snapshots?
cards.a:
About 10 to 30 times a second

Faster than people can read wastes CPU for nothing.
cards.lessonTitle: A Live Stats Panel for Your Game

cards.q: What does "append-only" mean for a shared layout?
cards.a:
New fields go only at the end; old ones never move or change

Old readers then keep finding every field they know at the same offset.
cards.lessonTitle: Versioning the Interface Between a Game and Its Tools

cards.q: How does a reader use the size field?
cards.a:
A field exists only if it lies within the writer's size

A newer tool reading an older game sees the new fields as missing instead of reading garbage. The reader copies the smaller of the two sizes and treats the rest as unavailable.
cards.lessonTitle: Versioning the Interface Between a Game and Its Tools

cards.q: What are feature flags for?
cards.a:
Saying which optional parts the writer provides now

A field can exist in the layout but be unused right now; the flag says whether to trust it.
cards.lessonTitle: Versioning the Interface Between a Game and Its Tools

cards.q: Where must new fields go in a shared structure?
cards.a:
At the end, so old offsets stay

Inserting moves later fields and breaks older readers.
cards.lessonTitle: Versioning the Interface Between a Game and Its Tools

cards.q: A tool's struct is 64 bytes; the game's header says size 48. What does that mean?
cards.a:
The game is older; fields past 48 are missing

The size field tells the reader what the writer provided.
cards.lessonTitle: Versioning the Interface Between a Game and Its Tools

cards.q: When must the major version change?
cards.a:
When existing data changes meaning or layout

Additions at the end only need a minor version.
cards.lessonTitle: Versioning the Interface Between a Game and Its Tools

cards.q: Why treat data from another process as untrusted?
cards.a:
It may be another version, half written or corrupt

A count of 3 billion monsters is more likely a bug or a layout mismatch than a real number.

cards.q: Which waits in a tool need limits?
cards.a:
All of them, including retries and pipe reads

A tool that hangs because the game froze is no help in finding why the game froze.

cards.q: What does "garbage testing" mean for a tool?
cards.a:
Feeding its logic random and broken data to check it copes

Keeping the logic free of Windows calls is what makes it easy to feed it such data in tests.

cards.q: A telemetry snapshot says 3 billion monsters are alive. What should the tool do?
cards.a:
Reject the snapshot as invalid and report it

Implausible values mean corruption or a version mismatch.

cards.q: Why keep a tool's logic free of Windows calls?
cards.a:
So it can be unit-tested without a game

A thin platform layer around pure logic is easy to test.

cards.q: What rights does a read-only stats tool need on the game's process?
cards.a:
Limited query information and synchronize

Least privilege: nothing more than its job needs.

cards.q: Name the layers through which a game can support mods.
cards.a:
Data overrides, assets, scripting, native plugins and official tools

Each layer gives modders more power and the game more risk; data overrides are the safest.

cards.q: What is a mod conflict?
cards.a:
Two mods changing the same entry, so only the later one counts

Load order decides which change wins, which is why games let players order their mods.

cards.q: What responsibilities come with supporting mods?
cards.a:
Failing safely, flagging native code, and keeping online play fair

The game cannot make mods correct, but it can make their failures safe and visible. Recording the mods in each save also helps when diagnosing problems later.

cards.q: What decides which mod wins when two change the same entry?
cards.a:
The load order: later mods win

The base game is first; each mod in the list overrides what came before.

cards.q: Why are data and script mods safer than plugin DLLs?
cards.a:
They can only do what the game exposes

Many games limit mods to data and scripts for this reason.

cards.q: What does a mod's manifest typically contain?
cards.a:
Name, version, author, and requirements

The game uses it to list, order and check mods.

cards.q: What is a virtual file system for mods?
cards.a:
A layer that looks in enabled mods' folders before the base game

The game asks for `monsters.ini` and gets the highest-priority mod's copy, or the base game's if no mod has one.

cards.q: How does merging data from several mods work?
cards.a:
Apply each mod's keys over the base entries, in load order

Two mods changing different keys of the same file then both take effect.

cards.q: What should happen when a mod's script has an error?
cards.a:
Report it with the mod's name, disable that mod, and carry on

Naming the mod tells the player what to remove or update.

cards.q: In which order does the layered file system search?
cards.a:
Last mod first, down to the base game

The topmost layer that has the file wins.

cards.q: Two mods change different keys of `monsters.ini`. With merging, what happens?
cards.a:
Both changes apply

Merging overwrites only the keys each mod contains.

cards.q: Why reject `..` in file names requested by mods?
cards.a:
It could reach files outside the allowed folders

Mods must stay within their own layer.

cards.q: What are the host API and the plugin API?
cards.a:
What the game offers plugins, and what each plugin offers the game

Two tables, two directions: the game calls into plugins, and plugins call back into the game. The plugin API lets the game initialise, update and shut each plugin down.

cards.q: What may cross the plugin boundary?
cards.a:
Numbers, plain structs, C strings, function pointers and handles

Standard library types can differ in layout and heap between builds, so only simple C types are safe.

cards.q: How should errors cross the boundary?
cards.a:
As return codes; exceptions never cross

An exception thrown through a C interface into code built differently is undefined behaviour.

cards.q: Why is the plugin interface written in C rather than C++ classes?
cards.a:
Only plain C types are compatible across builds

Lesson 4.05's rules for DLL boundaries.

cards.q: Why does every API table start with a size and version?
cards.a:
So each side knows which functions the other has

Lesson 12.06's versioning, applied to function tables.

cards.q: What is the `void* user` parameter in the event callback for?
cards.a:
The plugin's own state, handed back to it

C function pointers carry no data; this pointer does.

cards.q: What are the steps of loading a plugin?
cards.a:
Load by full path, find and call its entry point, validate, then `init`

Every step can fail, and each failure must leave the game running without that plugin.

cards.q: In what order are plugins initialised and shut down?
cards.a:
By dependencies, and shut down in reverse

A plugin's dependencies are ready before it starts and still there while it shuts down.

cards.q: How does hot reloading work?
cards.a:
Load a copy of the new build, unload the old one cleanly, init the new

Loading a copy keeps the original file free for the compiler to overwrite next time. Remove the old plugin's callbacks before unloading it.

cards.q: What does a topological sort of mods produce?
cards.a:
An order with each mod after its requirements

A cycle in the requirements makes such an order impossible.

cards.q: Why copy a plugin DLL before loading it for hot reloading?
cards.a:
A loaded DLL's file is locked against writes

Loading the copy leaves the original free for the compiler.

cards.q: Why must a plugin's callbacks be removed before `FreeLibrary`?
cards.a:
Calling them later would jump into unloaded code

A dangling function pointer is as dangerous as a dangling data pointer.

cards.q: Name three designed-in instrumentation patterns.
cards.a:
Scoped timers, an event bus, and replaceable functions

These are observation points the program offers on purpose, so tools and plugins need no tricks.
cards.lessonTitle: Instrumenting Functions in Your Own Program

cards.q: How should a handler that unsubscribes itself during dispatch be handled?
cards.a:
It is marked as removed and actually removed after the dispatch loop finishes

Changing a list while iterating it can skip handlers or read freed memory.
cards.lessonTitle: Instrumenting Functions in Your Own Program

cards.q: When is compiler-inserted entry and exit instrumentation appropriate?
cards.a:
In special tracing builds of your own program

`/Gh` and `/GH` call a hook on every function entry and exit, which is far too slow for normal builds.
cards.lessonTitle: Instrumenting Functions in Your Own Program

cards.q: What problem does an event bus solve?
cards.a:
The sender need not know who reacts

Publishers and subscribers are decoupled.
cards.lessonTitle: Instrumenting Functions in Your Own Program

cards.q: Why must subscribing return something that can unsubscribe?
cards.a:
Handlers that go away must be removed

Lesson 13.04's unloading depends on it.
cards.lessonTitle: Instrumenting Functions in Your Own Program

cards.q: What do MSVC's `/Gh` and `/GH` options do?
cards.a:
Call hooks on every function entry and exit

You supply those functions, for example to trace calls.
cards.lessonTitle: Instrumenting Functions in Your Own Program

cards.q: What does the tweakable registry store for each entry?
cards.a:
Name, variable pointer, type, limits and description

With the pointer and type, the menu can show and change the real variable directly.
cards.lessonTitle: A Debug Menu Inside the Game

cards.q: Why must setting a tweakable from text clamp the value?
cards.a:
So typed or loaded values cannot go outside the range the game is designed for

A gravity of -9000 typed by mistake should not break the game.
cards.lessonTitle: A Debug Menu Inside the Game

cards.q: How do plugins add to the debug menu?
cards.a:
By registering a named section with a draw callback

Removing the section on unload prevents the menu calling into an unloaded DLL.
cards.lessonTitle: A Debug Menu Inside the Game

cards.q: What does registering a tweakable give you?
cards.a:
One table that the menu and console are built from

Register once, use everywhere.
cards.lessonTitle: A Debug Menu Inside the Game

cards.q: What does "immediate mode" mean for Dear ImGui?
cards.a:
The interface is described again every frame

No separate widget objects to keep in sync with the data.
cards.lessonTitle: A Debug Menu Inside the Game

cards.q: Why check `WantCaptureMouse` before handling game input?
cards.a:
So menu clicks do not also act in the game

The menu and the game must not both react to the same input.
cards.lessonTitle: A Debug Menu Inside the Game

cards.q: How is each kind of mod failure contained?
cards.a:
Each layer catches its own failures and disables that mod

Each layer stops the failure where it happens, so one broken mod does not take the others down. Bad data entries are skipped, script errors disable the mod's scripts, and plugin exceptions are caught at the boundary.
cards.lessonTitle: Architecture: Keeping Mods Modular and Stable

cards.q: What are the options for native plugins that might corrupt memory?
cards.a:
Diagnose well, prefer data and scripts, or use a separate process

A plugin in the same process can write anywhere, so it cannot be fully contained there.
cards.lessonTitle: Architecture: Keeping Mods Modular and Stable

cards.q: What should a log contain to make mod problems diagnosable?
cards.a:
The game version, the mod list, and the mod in each error

With that, a player's log alone usually shows which mod is at fault.
cards.lessonTitle: Architecture: Keeping Mods Modular and Stable

cards.q: A plugin's `update` throws a C++ exception every frame. What should the game do?
cards.a:
Catch it at the boundary, and disable the plugin

Failures stay local, and are reported.
cards.lessonTitle: Architecture: Keeping Mods Modular and Stable

cards.q: Why can a native plugin's memory corruption not be fully contained inside the game process?
cards.a:
It shares the game's memory, so it can damage anything

Isolation from memory corruption needs a separate process.
cards.lessonTitle: Architecture: Keeping Mods Modular and Stable

cards.q: What is safe mode for?
cards.a:
Starting with every mod disabled

Then bisect the mod list to find the culprit.
cards.lessonTitle: Architecture: Keeping Mods Modular and Stable

cards.q: What do official modding tools usually provide?
cards.a:
Mod kits, documented formats and an SDK

Official support defines what modders may change and how.
cards.lessonTitle: Working with a Game's Official Modding Tools

cards.q: What makes a mod survive game updates?
cards.a:
Documented interfaces, entry-level changes and namespaced ids

Replacing whole files throws away every change the update made to them.
cards.lessonTitle: Working with a Game's Official Modding Tools

cards.q: Which licences matter when releasing a mod?
cards.a:
The game's mod licence, and those of all content used

Your mod's licence only covers your own work; everything you use from others has its own terms.
cards.lessonTitle: Working with a Game's Official Modding Tools

cards.q: What is usually the first step with an unfamiliar mod kit?
cards.a:
Read the official documentation and start from an example mod

Mod kits encode how the developers intend mods to work.
cards.lessonTitle: Working with a Game's Official Modding Tools

cards.q: Why namespace the ids your mod adds?
cards.a:
So they cannot collide with the game's ids or other mods' ids

Two mods adding a `lantern` item would otherwise conflict.
cards.lessonTitle: Working with a Game's Official Modding Tools

cards.q: What do mod licences commonly allow and forbid?
cards.a:
Free sharing yes; selling or game assets no

Always read the specific game's terms.
cards.lessonTitle: Working with a Game's Official Modding Tools

cards.q: What state does an immediate-mode library keep between frames?
cards.a:
Small amounts keyed by widget id: which widget is active, plus things like window positions and scroll offsets

The widgets themselves are described again every frame; only small bits of interaction state persist.

cards.q: What are the hot and active widgets?
cards.a:
Hot is under the mouse; active is the one the button went down on

A button reports a click when the mouse is released while it is both hot and active.

cards.q: Why does immediate mode suit game tools?
cards.a:
Games redraw from data every frame anyway, so no syncing is needed

Retained-mode interfaces need code to keep widget objects in step with the data; immediate mode just reads the data.

cards.q: What is the main difference between immediate and retained mode?
cards.a:
Immediate re-describes the interface each frame; retained keeps widgets

No widget objects means nothing to keep in sync. Retained-mode widget objects must be kept in step with the data.

cards.q: When does an immediate-mode button report a click?
cards.a:
When the mouse is released over it after being pressed on it

Press and release on the same widget.

cards.q: Two "Delete" buttons in one window both react when either is clicked. Why?
cards.a:
They have the same label, so the same id

Use `Delete##1`, or `PushID` per row.

cards.q: Why does ImGui need separate platform and renderer back ends?
cards.a:
The core knows no platform or graphics API; back ends supply both

The same core works with SDL or Win32 for input and DirectX, OpenGL or Vulkan for drawing.

cards.q: How does ImGui fit into a game frame?
cards.a:
After the game draws, ImGui is described and drawn on top

Drawing the interface last puts it on top of the game.

cards.q: What should a game check before handling input when ImGui is active?
cards.a:
`io.WantCaptureMouse` and `io.WantCaptureKeyboard`

Clicking a slider should not also fire the player's weapon.

cards.q: What do ImGui's back ends do?
cards.a:
Connect the core to input, windows and a graphics API

The core only produces draw lists.

cards.q: What are the four steps of every ImGui frame?
cards.a:
New frame, describe the interface, render, draw the lists

Describe happens between `NewFrame` and `Render`.

cards.q: Where is the best reference for how to use a particular widget?
cards.a:
The demo window and `imgui_demo.cpp`

Every widget is shown there with the code that draws it.

cards.q: How does ImGui lay widgets out by default, and how do you change it?
cards.a:
One per line, top to bottom; `SameLine` keeps the next on the same line

Most layout is just the order of calls plus a few `SameLine`s.

cards.q: When should side effects of a widget be applied?
cards.a:
On the frame its function returns true

Applying effects every frame would, for example, re-send a command to the game sixty times a second.

cards.q: What do `BeginDisabled` and `EndDisabled` do?
cards.a:
Grey out and block the widgets between them

The widgets are still drawn, so the layout does not jump when the condition changes.

cards.q: What does a slider's return value mean?
cards.a:
The value was changed by the user this frame

Use it to apply side effects only when needed.

cards.q: How do you put a button to the right of a text label?
cards.a:
Call `SameLine()` between them

Widgets go top to bottom unless told otherwise.

cards.q: What does `"##floor"` do as a label?
cards.a:
Shows no text, with the id "floor"

Text after `##` is part of the id only.

cards.q: What do you need to do when the user clicks a sortable column header?
cards.a:
When the sort specs are dirty, sort your data and clear the flag

ImGui only records what the user asked for; your code owns and sorts the data.

cards.q: Why use a list clipper?
cards.a:
So only visible rows are described each frame

Describing ten thousand rows every frame is wasted work when only thirty are on screen.

cards.q: What is ImPlot for?
cards.a:
Full charts with series, axes and zooming

ImGui's own `PlotLines` is enough for a sparkline; ImPlot is for real charts.

cards.q: Who sorts a sortable ImGui table's data?
cards.a:
Your code, when ImGui reports the sort order changed

ImGui only tracks which column and direction the user chose.

cards.q: What does `ImGuiListClipper` do?
cards.a:
Tells you which rows are visible

Cost then depends on what is on screen.

cards.q: How does a tree node know whether to draw its children?
cards.a:
`TreeNodeEx` returns true when the node is open

Then draw the children and call `TreePop`.

cards.q: Where should a tool keep its layout and settings files?
cards.a:
In the user's settings folder, such as Local AppData

The current directory changes with how the tool is started, and the installation folder is often not writable.

cards.q: How should a settings loader treat missing, unknown and invalid keys?
cards.a:
Defaults for missing or invalid keys; keep unknown ones

A settings file from an older or newer version should still mostly work. Log each invalid value that was replaced.

cards.q: How do you make sure a restored window is visible?
cards.a:
Check it against the monitors' work areas and move it on if needed

A window saved on a monitor that is no longer connected would otherwise open where nobody can see it.

cards.q: What does ImGui save automatically?
cards.a:
Window positions, sizes and docking

Everything else is up to your code.

cards.q: What does the title `"Monsters (12)###monsters"` achieve?
cards.a:
It shows a count but keeps the id "monsters"

Text before `###` is shown; the id comes from after it.

cards.q: A saved window position is on a monitor that is no longer connected. What should the tool do?
cards.a:
Move it onto a monitor that exists

Otherwise the window opens where the user cannot see it.

cards.q: What does ImGui docking add to a tool?
cards.a:
Users can rearrange and tab panels, saved with the layout

Each user can arrange the panels the way they work, and it is restored next time.

cards.q: Why should views only draw and forward actions?
cards.a:
So all logic is in the model, where it can be tested

Logic inside drawing code can only be tested by clicking through the interface.

cards.q: What should a tool's status bar show?
cards.a:
The connection, the versions, and the last error

When something looks wrong, the status bar is the first place to see why.

cards.q: What are the three layers of the inspector?
cards.a:
A platform layer, a pure model, and views

Separating them keeps the logic testable and the views simple.

cards.q: How does the inspector change things in the game?
cards.a:
Through commands on the game's pipe

The game stays in charge of its own state.

cards.q: What does fuzzy matching in a command palette do?
cards.a:
Finds names containing the typed letters in order

`gt3` finds "Goto floor 3".

cards.q: What runs in kernel mode on Windows?
cards.a:
ntoskrnl, the HAL, device and file-system drivers, and win32k

Services and system DLLs run in user mode; ntdll only contains the stubs that make system calls.

cards.q: How does kernel address space differ from user address space?
cards.a:
The user half is per process; the kernel half is shared by all

One kernel serves every process, so its half of the address space is the same wherever you look. Only kernel-mode code can touch the kernel half.

cards.q: Name three ways kernel-mode mistakes are worse than user-mode ones.
cards.a:
Crashes stop the whole machine, leaks last until reboot, and bad pointers can silently corrupt any part of the system

A user-mode crash ends one process; a kernel-mode crash ends everything.

cards.q: What enforces the separation between user mode and kernel mode?
cards.a:
The processor itself, by faulting privileged use

Hardware privilege levels are the foundation.

cards.q: Why is the kernel half of the address space the same in every process?
cards.a:
One kernel serves the whole system, mapped alike

Supervisor-only pages keep user code out.

cards.q: Why does an unhandled fault in a driver stop the whole machine?
cards.a:
Nothing in the kernel is walled off from it

Continuing could corrupt data, so Windows bug-checks.

cards.q: What layers does a call to `CreateFileW` pass through?
cards.a:
kernelbase, ntdll's stub, `syscall`, the kernel, then the I/O manager

Only kernel code can reach drivers and hardware; the `syscall` instruction is the crossing. Inside the kernel the system service dispatcher calls the kernel's `NtCreateFile`, which reaches the drivers through the I/O manager.

cards.q: What are the three rules for handling user-mode data in the kernel?
cards.a:
Probe the range, capture the data once, and use exception handlers

Capturing once stops another user thread changing the data between the check and the use.

cards.q: What is an NTSTATUS?
cards.a:
A 32-bit status code, negative for errors

Win32 functions translate NTSTATUS values into the error codes `GetLastError` reports.

cards.q: What does a function in ntdll like `NtCreateFile` do?
cards.a:
Loads the call number and runs `syscall`

It is a tiny stub; the work happens in the kernel.

cards.q: Why must the kernel copy user data before checking and using it?
cards.a:
Another thread could change it between check and use

This is the time-of-check to time-of-use problem.

cards.q: What does probing a user buffer check?
cards.a:
That the whole range lies in user address space

Otherwise a caller could make the kernel touch kernel memory for it.

cards.q: What does an object header contain?
cards.a:
Its type, counts, security descriptor and name

The object is deleted when both counts reach zero.
cards.lessonTitle: Kernel Objects and the Object Manager

cards.q: How does the kernel use a handle passed in a system call?
cards.a:
Looks it up in the caller's table, checks access, holds a reference

The extra reference keeps the object alive even if another thread closes the handle mid-call.
cards.lessonTitle: Kernel Objects and the Object Manager

cards.q: How does a user-mode program open a device created by a driver?
cards.a:
It opens the driver's symbolic link, `\.\LinkName`, with `CreateFileW`

After that, the program talks to the driver with `ReadFile`, `WriteFile` and `DeviceIoControl` on the handle.
cards.lessonTitle: Kernel Objects and the Object Manager

cards.q: When is a kernel object deleted?
cards.a:
When its handle and reference counts reach zero

Kernel code's own references keep it alive too.
cards.lessonTitle: Kernel Objects and the Object Manager

cards.q: What does a handle table entry store?
cards.a:
The object pointer and the granted rights

Rights are checked once, at open time.
cards.lessonTitle: Kernel Objects and the Object Manager

cards.q: What does `\??\C:` refer to?
cards.a:
A symbolic link to a volume device

The object manager follows the link to the device.
cards.lessonTitle: Kernel Objects and the Object Manager

cards.q: Why does Windows have both paged and non-paged pool?
cards.a:
Code that cannot fault needs RAM-resident memory, which is scarce

Code running at DISPATCH_LEVEL or above cannot handle a page fault, so its data must always be in RAM.

cards.q: What happens to leaked pool memory?
cards.a:
It stays allocated until the machine reboots; pool tags help find which driver leaked it

The kernel has no per-process cleanup for pool, so the four-character tag is the main clue to the culprit.

cards.q: What are the steps for a driver to use a user buffer safely through an MDL?
cards.a:
Allocate an MDL, probe and lock the pages, map them, then unlock

Locking keeps the pages in RAM, and the system-space mapping stays valid whatever process is current.

cards.q: What is the difference between paged and non-paged pool?
cards.a:
Paged can go to disk; non-paged stays in RAM

High-IRQL code must only touch non-paged memory.

cards.q: What is a pool tag for?
cards.a:
Showing which driver owns each block

Tools like PoolMon show usage per tag.

cards.q: Why does a driver use an MDL rather than a user virtual address?
cards.a:
Its locked pages work from any process context

The user address only means something in the original process.

cards.q: What three things can a driver do with an IRP?
cards.a:
Complete it, pass it down to the next driver in the stack, or mark it pending and complete it later

Ignoring an IRP leaves the caller waiting forever; every IRP must eventually be completed.
cards.lessonTitle: The I/O Manager and the Driver Model

cards.q: What is the difference between a driver object and a device object?
cards.a:
The driver object holds the dispatch routines; IRPs go to device objects

One driver can manage many devices, each with its own device object.
cards.lessonTitle: The I/O Manager and the Driver Model

cards.q: Name the kinds of drivers in a device stack.
cards.a:
Bus drivers, function drivers and filter drivers

An IRP travels down the stack, and each driver can handle it or pass it on.
cards.lessonTitle: The I/O Manager and the Driver Model

cards.q: What is an IRP?
cards.a:
A structure describing one I/O request

Major function, parameters, buffers and status.
cards.lessonTitle: The I/O Manager and the Driver Model

cards.q: A filter driver receives an IRP it does not need to change. What does it do?
cards.a:
Passes it down with `IoCallDriver`

Filters add behaviour only where they need to.
cards.lessonTitle: The I/O Manager and the Driver Model

cards.q: Why is KMDF recommended over writing WDM drivers directly?
cards.a:
It gets the standard driver logic right for you

UMDF is the user-mode framework.
cards.lessonTitle: The I/O Manager and the Driver Model

cards.q: What two things are forbidden at DISPATCH_LEVEL and above?
cards.a:
Waiting, and touching paged memory or calling pageable code

The scheduler and the page-fault handler cannot run there, so a wait or page fault cannot be serviced.

cards.q: How is work split between an ISR, a DPC and a work item?
cards.a:
ISR does the minimum, the DPC the main work, a work item what must wait

Each step down lowers the IRQL, allowing more but giving up urgency. The ISR runs at device IRQL, the DPC at DISPATCH_LEVEL, and the work item at PASSIVE_LEVEL.

cards.q: What is the difference between a spin lock and a mutex?
cards.a:
A spin lock busy-waits at DISPATCH_LEVEL; a mutex sleeps

Sleeping is impossible at DISPATCH_LEVEL, which is why code there must spin instead. Spin locks are only for very short work but can be used with DPCs and ISRs; a mutex only works at low IRQL.

cards.q: At which IRQL do normal threads, including `DriverEntry`, run?
cards.a:
PASSIVE_LEVEL

Everything that may wait and use paged memory runs at PASSIVE_LEVEL.

cards.q: Why can code at DISPATCH_LEVEL not wait on an event?
cards.a:
The scheduler cannot switch it out to let it wait

Waiting there would hang that processor.

cards.q: What does acquiring a spin lock do to the IRQL?
cards.a:
Raises it to DISPATCH_LEVEL

So all DISPATCH_LEVEL rules apply while holding it.

cards.q: What is a DPC for?
cards.a:
An interrupt's follow-up work, so the ISR is short

Work that must wait goes further down, to a work item at PASSIVE_LEVEL.

cards.q: What does `KeBugCheckEx` do?
cards.a:
Stops every processor, writes a dump, and restarts

Continuing after a kernel fault could corrupt data, so Windows stops everything instead.
cards.lessonTitle: Why Kernel Bugs Take the Whole Machine Down

cards.q: Which WinDbg command is the first step with a kernel dump?
cards.a:
`!analyze -v`, after fixing the symbol path

It reports the bug check, its parameters, the faulting module and the stack. A dump cannot continue running.
cards.lessonTitle: Why Kernel Bugs Take the Whole Machine Down

cards.q: Why leave Driver Verifier on throughout driver development?
cards.a:
It makes rare driver bugs fail at once, with the rule named

A bug found the moment it happens, with the rule named, is far cheaper than one found months later.
cards.lessonTitle: Why Kernel Bugs Take the Whole Machine Down

cards.q: Why does Windows stop the whole machine on a kernel-mode fault?
cards.a:
The damage could be anywhere, so going on risks data

Stopping with a dump is the safe choice.
cards.lessonTitle: Why Kernel Bugs Take the Whole Machine Down

cards.q: What usually causes bug check `0xD1`?
cards.a:
Touching paged memory at DISPATCH_LEVEL

Parameter 4 is the faulting address in the driver.
cards.lessonTitle: Why Kernel Bugs Take the Whole Machine Down

cards.q: What does Driver Verifier do?
cards.a:
Makes rare driver bugs fail clearly

It turns occasional crashes into reproducible ones.
cards.lessonTitle: Why Kernel Bugs Take the Whole Machine Down

cards.q: What does the lab VM need before chapter 16?
cards.a:
Test signing, kernel debugging, dumps, and a clean snapshot

The clean snapshot is what lets you undo any mistake in seconds.

cards.q: How does WinDbg on the host debug the guest's kernel?
cards.a:
Through a network kernel-debugging connection set up with `kdnet` in the guest, using the port and key it prints

When you break in, the whole guest stops, which is only possible because the debugger is outside it.

cards.q: What is the rule about where development drivers are loaded?
cards.a:
Only ever in the lab VM, never on your everyday machine

A driver bug can crash or corrupt the whole system it runs on.

cards.q: Why develop drivers in a virtual machine?
cards.a:
Crashes stay in the VM, and snapshots undo them

And it keeps test signing off your everyday system.

cards.q: What does `bcdedit /set testsigning on` do?
cards.a:
Lets test-signed drivers load

Lab VM only.

cards.q: What happens to the guest when you break into it with the kernel debugger?
cards.a:
The whole guest freezes until you continue

So nothing changes while you inspect it.

cards.q: What does the WDK add to Visual Studio?
cards.a:
Kernel headers and libraries, driver templates and driver tools

Visual Studio, the SDK and the WDK must be versions that match, so they work together.

cards.q: Name three ways building kernel code differs from user code.
cards.a:
No C runtime or standard library, no exceptions, and a tiny stack

That is why a driver cannot call `printf` or use `std::vector`. Drivers can be written in C++ and are built optimised. Every function also has IRQL rules about where it may be called.

cards.q: What files does a driver build produce?
cards.a:
The `.sys` file, its `.pdb`, and a test certificate

The `.pdb` is what lets the kernel debugger show your driver's source and names.

cards.q: Where are the Visual Studio, SDK and WDK installed?
cards.a:
On the host; the VM only runs the driver

Build on the host, test in the VM.

cards.q: Why can a driver not call `printf` or use `std::vector`?
cards.a:
The C and C++ libraries are not in the kernel

`KdPrint` and the pool allocation functions take their place.

cards.q: Roughly how big is a kernel thread's stack on x64?
cards.a:
12 KB to 24 KB

So large locals and deep recursion are out.

cards.q: What are the two functions every unloadable driver needs?
cards.a:
`DriverEntry` and an unload routine

Without an unload routine the driver can be loaded but never unloaded until reboot.

cards.q: How is a software-only driver loaded for testing?
cards.a:
With `sc create ... type= kernel` and `sc start`, in the VM

Loading happens only in the lab VM, where a crash costs nothing but a snapshot restore.

cards.q: How do you break into a driver as soon as it loads?
cards.a:
Set `bu Driver!DriverEntry` before starting it

`bu` is resolved when the module loads; `bp` needs the module to be loaded already.

cards.q: When is `DriverEntry` called, and at which IRQL?
cards.a:
Once, when the driver is loaded, at PASSIVE_LEVEL

It is the driver's equivalent of `main`.

cards.q: What happens if `DriverEntry` returns a failure status?
cards.a:
It is unloaded without its unload routine

Lesson 16.03 handles partial set-up.

cards.q: Where does `KdPrint` output go?
cards.a:
To an attached kernel debugger

It compiles away in Release builds.

cards.q: Why must a driver's unload routine leave nothing behind?
cards.a:
Its code is unmapped, so leftovers would later reach freed code

A forgotten timer firing later jumps into unmapped code, which is a bug check.

cards.q: How should `DriverEntry` handle a failure partway through?
cards.a:
Undo, in reverse order, exactly the steps that succeeded, then return the failure status

The unload routine is not called when `DriverEntry` fails, so it must clean up itself.

cards.q: Why can `sc stop` fail while a program has the device open?
cards.a:
A driver with open device handles is not unloaded

Close the client program's handle first, then stop the driver.

cards.q: What happens to a timer the driver forgot to cancel when it unloads?
cards.a:
It fires into unloaded code: a bug check

Bug check `0xCE` is exactly this.

cards.q: In which order does unload release resources?
cards.a:
The reverse of creation

Later resources may depend on earlier ones.

cards.q: `DriverEntry` created a device, then failed to create the link. What must it do?
cards.a:
Delete the device and return the failure status

The unload routine is not called when `DriverEntry` fails.

cards.q: What do `IoCreateDevice` and `IoCreateSymbolicLink` each create?
cards.a:
A device object, and a name user mode can open

User mode cannot open names in `\Device` directly, which is why the link is needed.

cards.q: Why handle `IRP_MJ_CREATE` and `IRP_MJ_CLOSE`?
cards.a:
Opening and closing send them; unhandled, they fail

The handlers can be tiny, just completing the request successfully.

cards.q: How do you restrict who may open a device?
cards.a:
Use `IoCreateDeviceSecure` with an SDDL string

A secret name is not security: anyone can list the object namespace. Each IOCTL should also require specific access rights.

cards.q: How does a user-mode program open the device `\Device\XenonEcho`?
cards.a:
As `\.\XenonEcho`, through its link

The link gives the device a name in the DOS device directory.

cards.q: What is the device extension?
cards.a:
Per-device state memory

Its size is passed to `IoCreateDevice`.

cards.q: What must a dispatch routine always do with an IRP it handles itself?
cards.a:
Complete it exactly once

Lesson 15.05's rules.

cards.q: Which ranges should your own device types and function numbers use?
cards.a:
Device types `0x8000` and above; function numbers `0x800` and above

The lower ranges are reserved for Microsoft.

cards.q: What does the dispatch routine do with an unknown control code?
cards.a:
Completes it with `STATUS_INVALID_DEVICE_REQUEST`

Every IRP must be completed; an unknown request gets a clear error.

cards.q: Why should the IOCTL definitions live in a shared header?
cards.a:
So the driver and its user-mode client use exactly the same codes and structures

Two hand-copied definitions drift apart and produce baffling mismatches.

cards.q: What four fields make up an IOCTL code?
cards.a:
Device type, required access, function number and buffering method

Packed by the `CTL_CODE` macro into 32 bits.

cards.q: Who enforces an IOCTL's access bits?
cards.a:
The I/O manager, before the driver sees it

A handle without the required access cannot send the code.

cards.q: What does `IoStatus.Information` hold when completing a buffered IOCTL?
cards.a:
The output byte count to copy back

It must never exceed the output buffer's length.

cards.q: How does a client open a driver's device?
cards.a:
`CreateFileW` on the link's name, `\.\Name`

In C++ source the backslashes are doubled: `L"\\\\.\\XenonEcho"`.

cards.q: What arguments does `DeviceIoControl` take?
cards.a:
A handle, a code, input and output buffers and sizes, and more

The bytes-returned value comes from the `Information` field the driver set when completing the request. The rest is a place for the bytes returned and an optional OVERLAPPED structure.

cards.q: Why treat the client–driver protocol like a plugin API?
cards.a:
Both are built separately and need a shared, versioned contract

The same lessons as chapter 13 apply: an interface between separately built pieces needs a contract.

cards.q: The client's `CreateFileW(L"\\\\.\\XenonEcho", ...)` fails with error 2. What is the likely cause?
cards.a:
The driver is not loaded, so no link exists

Error 5 would suggest access denied.

cards.q: How does a driver's NTSTATUS reach the client?
cards.a:
`DeviceIoControl` fails; `GetLastError` maps it

For example `STATUS_BUFFER_TOO_SMALL` becomes `ERROR_INSUFFICIENT_BUFFER`.

cards.q: What does the `returned` argument of `DeviceIoControl` receive?
cards.a:
The Information byte count the driver set

Size results by it, and check it.

cards.q: What are the three buffering methods, and which is safest?
cards.a:
Buffered, direct and neither; buffered is safest

With buffered I/O the driver never touches user memory directly; with neither, it must probe and capture everything itself. Buffered uses a system buffer, direct uses MDLs of locked pages, and neither passes raw user pointers.

cards.q: What are the main rules for handling a request?
cards.a:
Check lengths, distrust fields, report exact sizes, leak nothing

Each rule closes a way for a hostile caller to read or corrupt kernel memory. Also handle every failure and synchronise shared state.

cards.q: Why are vulnerable drivers such a concern?
cards.a:
A validation bug can hand a caller the kernel

Attackers even load old, signed but vulnerable drivers on purpose to get into the kernel.

cards.q: With `METHOD_BUFFERED`, what does the driver work with?
cards.a:
A system buffer the I/O manager copies

The driver never touches user memory directly.

cards.q: Why must `Information` never exceed the bytes actually written?
cards.a:
Extra bytes copied back leak kernel memory

An information leak can reveal kernel addresses and data.

cards.q: A request contains a count of items. How should the driver treat it?
cards.a:
As hostile: check it and its arithmetic first

Fields inside requests are as hostile as the lengths.

cards.q: How do you see a driver's dispatch table in WinDbg?
cards.a:
`!drvobj <name> 7`

It lists the driver's device objects and the routine for each IRP major function.

cards.q: Where is the IRP when a dispatch routine starts, and how do you look at it?
cards.a:
In `rdx`; look with `!irp @rdx`

A dispatch routine's arguments are the device object (`rcx`) and the IRP (`rdx`).

cards.q: What does a bug check's stack show for a request from user mode?
cards.a:
The path from the client, through the kernel, to the driver

Frames such as `nt!NtDeviceIoControlFile` mark where the request entered the kernel.

cards.q: Why use `bu` rather than `bp` for `DriverEntry`?
cards.a:
It resolves when the driver loads

Unresolved breakpoints wait for the module.

cards.q: What does `!drvobj XenonEcho 7` show?
cards.a:
Its devices and dispatch routines

A quick check that DriverEntry set things up correctly.

cards.q: In the bug check stack, what does `nt!NtDeviceIoControlFile` represent?
cards.a:
The kernel side of the system call

Lesson 15.02's path, seen in a real stack.

cards.q: Why does 64-bit Windows require signed drivers?
cards.a:
Drivers control everything, so they must be accountable

A signature also proves the file has not been changed since it was signed.

cards.q: How is a driver test-signed in Visual Studio?
cards.a:
Set Sign Mode to Test Sign; the build signs it

Test signatures are only accepted when the machine has test signing turned on. The test machine must also be running in test mode.

cards.q: Why must test mode never be used on an everyday computer?
cards.a:
It lets anyone's test-signed drivers load

Anyone can make a test certificate, so test mode trusts anyone.

cards.q: What does driver signature enforcement do?
cards.a:
Loads only validly signed drivers

Without it, any program could load code into the kernel.

cards.q: What does test mode (`bcdedit /set testsigning on`) allow?
cards.a:
Loading drivers signed with test certificates, for development

Only ever in a lab machine.

cards.q: What does a valid signature prove?
cards.a:
Who published it, and that it is unchanged

Signed drivers can still be vulnerable.

cards.q: What does the XenonEcho driver do on load, and undo on unload?
cards.a:
Creates its device and link; unload deletes them in reverse

Unload undoes the steps in reverse order: link first, then device.
cards.lessonTitle: Project: An Echo Driver in a Virtual Machine

cards.q: Which rules from lesson 16.07 does the echo handler apply?
cards.a:
Length checks, exact byte counts, zeroed output and atomic statistics

Even buffered I/O needs length checks, and zeroing prevents leaking uninitialised kernel memory.
cards.lessonTitle: Project: An Echo Driver in a Virtual Machine

cards.q: What does a complete test of a driver include besides correct requests?
cards.a:
Hostile inputs, concurrency, fuzzing, all under Verifier

Correct requests only prove the easy path works; drivers fail on the hostile ones.
cards.lessonTitle: Project: An Echo Driver in a Virtual Machine

cards.q: Why are the statistics updated with interlocked operations?
cards.a:
Several processors may handle requests at once

Lesson 6.06's data races, in the kernel.
cards.lessonTitle: Project: An Echo Driver in a Virtual Machine

cards.q: What does the driver do with an undefined control code?
cards.a:
Fails it as invalid

Only defined codes are handled.
cards.lessonTitle: Project: An Echo Driver in a Virtual Machine

cards.q: What must be true after `sc stop` for the driver to have unloaded cleanly?
cards.a:
Nothing remains: no device, link, work or pool

Lesson 16.03's rule: leave nothing behind.
cards.lessonTitle: Project: An Echo Driver in a Virtual Machine

cards.q: What makes code easy to unit test?
cards.a:
Small functions that take clocks and data as parameters

A function that reads the system clock itself cannot be tested at a chosen time; one given a clock can. Platform calls are kept in a separate layer, so the logic runs without them.

cards.q: What kinds of cases should tests cover?
cards.a:
Normal cases, edges, bad input, regressions and round trips

Edges and invalid input are where low-level code most often breaks.

cards.q: Why run the test suite under AddressSanitizer?
cards.a:
So the tests also catch overruns and use-after-free

A test can pass while silently overrunning a buffer; ASan turns that into a clear failure.

cards.q: Why pass a clock into a cooldown timer instead of reading the system time inside it?
cards.a:
So a test can control time exactly

A fake clock makes timing logic testable.

cards.q: What is a regression test?
cards.a:
A test that keeps a fixed bug from returning

Every fixed bug deserves one.

cards.q: Which code benefits most from tests with truncated and nonsense inputs?
cards.a:
Parsers of untrusted data, such as saves

Then fuzz them too.

cards.q: Which sanitizers can you use with Visual Studio on Windows?
cards.a:
ASan with MSVC or clang-cl, and UBSan with clang-cl

MSVC itself supports ASan; clang-cl adds UBSan. ThreadSanitizer and MemorySanitizer need Linux builds.

cards.q: What does `/analyze` add beyond compiler warnings?
cards.a:
Path-sensitive checks for nulls, overruns and leaks, using SAL

It reasons about the paths through a function without running it, which plain warnings do not.

cards.q: How should a genuine false alarm be suppressed?
cards.a:
Narrowly, on the one line, with a comment why it is safe

A project-wide switch hides the real bugs the warning would find elsewhere.

cards.q: What is the main difference between a sanitizer and static analysis?
cards.a:
Sanitizers check running code; static analysis reads the source

They complement each other.

cards.q: Which tool catches signed integer overflow as it happens?
cards.a:
UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer

ASan is about memory accesses.

cards.q: What does a SAL annotation like `_Out_writes_z_(destSize)` give the analyzer?
cards.a:
The size of the buffer it writes

The Windows headers use these throughout.

cards.q: What makes a good fuzz target?
cards.a:
It feeds the bytes to one parser, fast, deterministic, side-effect free

Randomness or side effects make crashes impossible to reproduce from the saved input. It should also check invariants, not only wait for crashes.

cards.q: How do you run libFuzzer with MSVC?
cards.a:
Build with `/fsanitize=fuzzer,address`, run it on a corpus folder

libFuzzer supplies `main` itself and calls your `LLVMFuzzerTestOneInput` with each input.

cards.q: What should happen to every input a fuzzer finds?
cards.a:
Minimise it, fix the bug, and keep it as a regression test

The regression test makes sure the same bug cannot quietly come back.

cards.q: What makes a coverage-guided fuzzer better than random inputs?
cards.a:
It keeps and mutates inputs that reach new code

New coverage guides the search.

cards.q: Why run a fuzz target with AddressSanitizer?
cards.a:
So silent memory errors are caught at once

Silent overruns become clear failures.

cards.q: What does minimising a crashing input achieve?
cards.a:
The smallest input that still fails

Then add it as a regression test.

cards.q: What is a trust boundary?
cards.a:
Where data you do not control enters, and must be validated

Files, mods, network messages and other processes all cross trust boundaries.
cards.lessonTitle: Secure Coding: Buffers, Integers and Trust

cards.q: Name five classic bug classes.
cards.a:
Overruns, integer overflow, use after free, uninitialised reads, path traversal

Each of these has caused real security vulnerabilities in games and drivers. Format strings, time-of-check to time-of-use, and injection are classic too.
cards.lessonTitle: Secure Coding: Buffers, Integers and Trust

cards.q: What does "defence in depth" mean here?
cards.a:
Several layers, so a bug past one is stopped by another

No single layer is perfect, so several independent layers are used together. The layers are correct code, testing and analysis tools, platform mitigations and least privilege.
cards.lessonTitle: Secure Coding: Buffers, Integers and Trust

cards.q: Where should untrusted input be validated?
cards.a:
At the boundary where it enters

Then the inside of the program can rely on it.
cards.lessonTitle: Secure Coding: Buffers, Integers and Trust

cards.q: A mod asks the game to load `..\..\saves\other.sav`. What bug class is this?
cards.a:
Path traversal

Reject parent-directory components and check the resolved path stays inside the mod's folder.
cards.lessonTitle: Secure Coding: Buffers, Integers and Trust

cards.q: Why use `std::span` for buffer parameters?
cards.a:
It keeps the pointer and length together

Lost lengths are the root of many overruns.
cards.lessonTitle: Secure Coding: Buffers, Integers and Trust

cards.q: What are the four questions of threat modelling?
cards.a:
What are we building, what can go wrong, what are we going to do about it, and did we do a good job

They work for any system, from a save file to an online game.

cards.q: What does STRIDE stand for?
cards.a:
Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information disclosure, Denial of service and Elevation of privilege

Each letter is a kind of threat against one security property, such as tampering against integrity.

cards.q: What are the possible responses to a threat?
cards.a:
Mitigate it, design it out, or accept it, and record why

Players editing their own single-player saves only affect themselves, which is why accepting that threat is reasonable. Accepting fits when the risk is low or falls only on the person causing it.

cards.q: What does the T in STRIDE stand for, and which property does it violate?
cards.a:
Tampering, which violates integrity

Changing data or code without permission.

cards.q: Why is "accept" a valid response for players editing their own single-player saves?
cards.a:
The impact falls only on the person making the change

Effort goes to threats that harm others.

cards.q: Where do trust boundaries appear on a data-flow diagram?
cards.a:
Wherever data crosses between trust levels

Those are where validation is needed.

cards.q: What is the most important rule of game security?
cards.a:
Never trust the client; decide on the server

Encryption and obfuscation only slow tampering down; server authority makes it irrelevant for what matters. Anything on the player's machine can be changed, so decisions that affect others must be made or checked on the server.
cards.lessonTitle: Software Integrity, Anti-Tamper and Fair Play

cards.q: How do you verify the integrity of your own shipped files and updates?
cards.a:
Hash manifests, Authenticode signing, and signed updates

Signing proves who made a file and that it has not changed since. Also load DLLs only by full path from your own folder.
cards.lessonTitle: Software Integrity, Anti-Tamper and Fair Play

cards.q: What are the costs of kernel-mode anti-cheat?
cards.a:
Players must trust it fully, and its bugs can crash the system

It sits at the highest privilege level, with all the risks of any kernel driver. It also handles personal data, with the privacy obligations that brings.
cards.lessonTitle: Software Integrity, Anti-Tamper and Fair Play

cards.q: Why can client-side protection never fully stop tampering?
cards.a:
It runs on the player's own machine, which they control completely

Protection there can only raise the cost.
cards.lessonTitle: Software Integrity, Anti-Tamper and Fair Play

cards.q: In an authoritative-server design, what do clients send?
cards.a:
Their inputs, which the server validates and simulates to decide the results

The server owns the game state.
cards.lessonTitle: Software Integrity, Anti-Tamper and Fair Play

cards.q: What does code signing an update prove?
cards.a:
Who published it, and that it is unchanged

The updater checks the signature before installing.
cards.lessonTitle: Software Integrity, Anti-Tamper and Fair Play

cards.q: What is the measurement loop?
cards.a:
Measure, change one thing, measure again, keep it only if better

Changing one thing at a time is the only way to know which change helped.

cards.q: How does a sampling profiler work?
cards.a:
It records what code is running, many times a second

Instrumenting every function is a different technique and slows the program much more.

cards.q: What are the usual real causes of slow C++ code?
cards.a:
Cache misses, hot-loop allocations and poor algorithms

`const`, references and comments cost nothing at run time. Repeated work, blocking waits, and measuring a Debug build are other usual culprits.

cards.q: What is the frame budget at 60 frames per second?
cards.a:
About 16.7 milliseconds

1000 ms divided by 60.

cards.q: Why report the median and p95 rather than only the mean?
cards.a:
A few slow runs skew the mean

Distributions, not single numbers.

cards.q: Why store a benchmark's result in a `volatile` variable?
cards.a:
So the optimiser cannot remove the work

Unused results invite dead-code elimination.

cards.q: What does each part of a semantic version mean?
cards.a:
MAJOR: incompatible; MINOR: new features; PATCH: fixes

A change that breaks old saves is incompatible, so it needs a new MAJOR version.
cards.lessonTitle: Shipping and Maintaining What You Build

cards.q: What makes a Release build reproducible?
cards.a:
One documented command, pinned dependencies, and CI builds

Anyone, on any machine, can then make the same build from the same source.
cards.lessonTitle: Shipping and Maintaining What You Build

cards.q: What is needed to debug a crash reported by a user?
cards.a:
A minidump from the user's machine and the exact PDB files from the build they were running

Without the matching PDBs, the dump's call stack is just raw addresses.
cards.lessonTitle: Shipping and Maintaining What You Build

cards.q: A change makes old save files fail to load. Which part of the version increases?
cards.a:
MAJOR

It breaks compatibility.
cards.lessonTitle: Shipping and Maintaining What You Build

cards.q: Why keep the PDB files of every release?
cards.a:
Only they can read that build's dumps

Without them a dump is just addresses.
cards.lessonTitle: Shipping and Maintaining What You Build

cards.q: Where should a game store its saves?
cards.a:
In the user's folders, such as Saved Games or AppData

Per-user, writable, and untouched by updates.
cards.lessonTitle: Shipping and Maintaining What You Build

cards.q: What are the inspector's scope rules?
cards.a:
Only processes from your build folder, read-only, minimum rights

Keeping the tool to your own builds and read-only access keeps it safe and within the course's ground rules. It also uses documented APIs only and never needs administrator rights.
cards.lessonTitle: Capstone: A Memory Inspector with a Full Interface

cards.q: How is the inspector structured so it can be tested?
cards.a:
Tested pure logic, one Windows access layer, and drawing-only panels

Pure logic can be tested without any process to read, which is why it is kept away from Windows calls.
cards.lessonTitle: Capstone: A Memory Inspector with a Full Interface

cards.q: How should the hex view handle a page that cannot be read?
cards.a:
Show `??` for those bytes and keep working

Zeros would look like real data; `ReadProcessMemory` may fail or read only part of a range, so the view must cope.
cards.lessonTitle: Capstone: A Memory Inspector with a Full Interface

cards.q: Why is the process scope check done on the full executable path after normalising it?
cards.a:
So `..`, case or short names cannot evade it

The same lessons as safe path joining.
cards.lessonTitle: Capstone: A Memory Inspector with a Full Interface

cards.q: Why read only the visible rows of the hex view?
cards.a:
Reading large ranges every frame is slow

Read what you show.
cards.lessonTitle: Capstone: A Memory Inspector with a Full Interface

cards.q: Which access rights does the inspector need?
cards.a:
`PROCESS_QUERY_INFORMATION` and `PROCESS_VM_READ`

The least rights for a read-only tool.
cards.lessonTitle: Capstone: A Memory Inspector with a Full Interface

cards.q: What does each mod's manifest contain?
cards.a:
Its id, version, target API, requirements and content paths

Absolute paths would break on every other machine; the manifest lists paths relative to the mod.
cards.lessonTitle: Capstone: A Moddable Game with a Plugin System

cards.q: How is the load order computed?
cards.a:
A topological sort of `requires` and `after`, ties alphabetical

Alphabetical tie-breaking makes the order the same every time for the same set of mods. Any cycle is reported and the mods in it are disabled.
cards.lessonTitle: Capstone: A Moddable Game with a Plugin System

cards.q: How does the game protect itself from native plugins?
cards.a:
Version checks, full-path loading, and catching failures

None of this makes a native plugin safe, which is why players are warned, but it contains ordinary failures. It also keeps the API in plain C, disables failing plugins, and warns that plugins run with the game's rights.
cards.lessonTitle: Capstone: A Moddable Game with a Plugin System

cards.q: Why is alphabetical order used to break ties in the load order?
cards.a:
So the order is the same every time

The same mods must load the same way everywhere.
cards.lessonTitle: Capstone: A Moddable Game with a Plugin System

cards.q: Why does each API table start with its `size`?
cards.a:
So each side can tell which fields exist

A common pattern for versioned C interfaces.
cards.lessonTitle: Capstone: A Moddable Game with a Plugin System

cards.q: A plugin throws an exception during initialisation. What should the game do?
cards.a:
Catch it, disable that plugin, and carry on

Mods must not be able to break the game.
cards.lessonTitle: Capstone: A Moddable Game with a Plugin System

cards.q: What does the XenonLog driver do, and what does it never do?
cards.a:
Keeps a bounded log via validated IOCTLs; never touches other processes

The project is deliberately limited to its own buffer, which is what makes it a safe learning driver. It also never registers callbacks on other processes, hides anything, or runs outside the lab VM.
cards.lessonTitle: Capstone: A Driver and Client Pair in a Virtual Machine

cards.q: Name four engineering requirements for the driver.
cards.a:
Validate lengths, set exact byte counts, lock correctly, free in unload

Restricting device access and passing warnings and Code Analysis are also required.
cards.lessonTitle: Capstone: A Driver and Client Pair in a Virtual Machine

cards.q: How is the driver verified?
cards.a:
Unit tests, Driver Verifier, kernel debugging, fuzzing and reload cycles

Repeated load and unload cycles catch anything the unload routine forgot to release.
cards.lessonTitle: Capstone: A Driver and Client Pair in a Virtual Machine

cards.q: Why does every XenonLog request start with a version and a size?
cards.a:
So mismatched requests are rejected first

Check the header first.
cards.lessonTitle: Capstone: A Driver and Client Pair in a Virtual Machine

cards.q: What happens when the ring buffer is full and a new message arrives?
cards.a:
The oldest message is dropped and the dropped count increases

Bounded memory, visible behaviour.
cards.lessonTitle: Capstone: A Driver and Client Pair in a Virtual Machine

cards.q: Where must all XenonLog testing happen?
cards.a:
In the lab virtual machine with test signing and a snapshot

The rules from chapters 15 and 16 do not change.
cards.lessonTitle: Capstone: A Driver and Client Pair in a Virtual Machine

cards.q: Which targets are suitable for this capstone?
cards.a:
Permitted, checkable programs, such as open source you build

Not commercial software that forbids it, protected or online games, or anything analysed to defeat a protection. Practice programs published for analysis, a classmate's program, and your own old programs also qualify.
cards.lessonTitle: Capstone: Analysing and Documenting a Program You Did Not Write

cards.q: What are the six steps of the method?
cards.a:
Triage, observe, find code via strings, understand, confirm, document

Confirming dynamically is what turns a reading of the code into a verified claim.
cards.lessonTitle: Capstone: Analysing and Documenting a Program You Did Not Write

cards.q: What makes the report trustworthy?
cards.a:
Recorded permission, a method, verified claims and confidence levels

Saying how confident you are, and why, is more useful to a reader than hiding the uncertain parts.
cards.lessonTitle: Capstone: Analysing and Documenting a Program You Did Not Write

cards.q: Why is an open-source program built yourself a good target?
cards.a:
It is permitted, and the source checks you

An answer key, with permission.
cards.lessonTitle: Capstone: Analysing and Documenting a Program You Did Not Write

cards.q: What is the best starting point for finding a program's interesting code?
cards.a:
Strings and imports, then their xrefs

Work from what you can observe.
cards.lessonTitle: Capstone: Analysing and Documenting a Program You Did Not Write

cards.q: Why does the function map have a confidence column?
cards.a:
To show which claims were confirmed

Honest uncertainty makes a report trustworthy.
cards.lessonTitle: Capstone: Analysing and Documenting a Program You Did Not Write
